"Loath" is an adjective meaning reluctant, and it is followed by "to" plus a verb, which is the pattern the sentence uses. The reluctance is given a cause and an end point: suspicion of a strange crop, lifted by visible example from people of standing. It is worth keeping the adjective apart from the verb "loathe", which means to detest.

Unwillingness that persists until reassurance arrives is what the adjective names, so this line holds.

**E) Adoption became "widespread" only after two generations had watched their neighbours survive a bad grain year on potatoes.**

"Widespread" is a claim about extent, and the sentence carefully dates the point at which extent was reached. Two generations of observed evidence is the mechanism by which a local practice becomes a general one, so the timing clause supports rather than undercuts the word. Nothing here suggests the crop was universal, only that it spread broadly.

Broad uptake arriving late but genuinely arriving is what the adjective claims, so the sentence works.
tasks.solution_overview: This set rewards attention to degree and to grammar: mitigate lessens rather than ends, loath takes "to" and describes reluctance, and adverse sits in front of the conditions it describes. For diligently and widespread, ask whether the sentence shows sustained care and genuine extent instead of merely asserting them. When every clause supplies supporting evidence rather than a contradiction, the word usually belongs.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five sentences about the factories that make advanced chips. Decide whether each quoted word is used in a defensible way.
statements: A supply forecast is "credible" when it matches the capacity actually installed in the plants it describes.
The legacy production line proved "lucrative", running at a loss in every quarter since it opened.
Export rules that name a precise transistor density are "ambiguous", since lawyers can read them in only one way.
Extreme precision is "intrinsic" to advanced lithography, where a few nanometres of drift ruins an entire wafer.
The manufacturer's "elaborate" explanation of the shortage was a two-word statement issued shortly after midnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A supply forecast is "credible" when it matches the capacity actually installed in the plants it describes.**

"Credible" means worth believing, and the sentence gives the ground on which belief rests: agreement with physical capacity that already exists. Forecasts lose credibility when they assume output no factory can produce, so the test named here is the right one. The word is about acceptance by informed readers, not about the forecast turning out correct.

Believability anchored to verifiable capacity is exactly the sense required, so the usage is right.

**B) The legacy production line proved "lucrative", running at a loss in every quarter since it opened.**

"Lucrative" means it makes money, and a good deal of it. A line that has lost money in every quarter of its life is the clearest possible counterexample, however strategically useful it may be to keep it open. Strategic and profitable are different claims, and only the second is what this adjective asserts.

Unbroken quarterly losses rule the word out, so the description fails on its own figures.

**C) Export rules that name a precise transistor density are "ambiguous", since lawyers can read them in only one way.**

"Ambiguous" means capable of more than one interpretation, which is why vague thresholds cause disputes. A numeric density is the standard cure for ambiguity, and the sentence admits as much by conceding that only one reading is available. The "since" clause is therefore arguing against the adjective it was meant to justify.

A single available reading is the definition of unambiguous, so the sentence contradicts itself.

**D) Extreme precision is "intrinsic" to advanced lithography, where a few nanometres of drift ruins an entire wafer.**

"Intrinsic" marks a property as belonging to the nature of the process rather than being imposed by choice. Because tolerances of a few nanometres decide whether the wafer works at all, precision is not an optional standard here but a condition of the process existing. The relative clause supplies that proof directly.

A requirement without which the activity cannot happen is intrinsic in the strict sense, so the word fits.

**E) The manufacturer's "elaborate" explanation of the shortage was a two-word statement issued shortly after midnight.**

"Elaborate" implies detail carefully worked out and set out at length. Two words issued in the middle of the night is minimal disclosure, and the timing detail underlines that the company wanted the matter closed rather than explained. Terse or evasive would describe what actually appeared.

A two-word release cannot carry an elaborate explanation, so the adjective is the wrong one for this statement.
tasks.solution_overview: Look for the clause beginning with "since", "where" or "running", because in each line that clause is the evidence the adjective must survive. Credible and intrinsic are supported when the sentence names a verifiable anchor or an unavoidable condition, while lucrative and elaborate are claims about quantity that a single figure can destroy. Ambiguous is the sharpest test of all, since a sentence admitting only one reading has already answered it.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five sentences about fieldwork on a fast-retreating glacier. Decide whether the quoted word describes what the sentence reports.
statements: Drilling through half a kilometre of ice became "feasible" once hot-water systems light enough to fly in were developed.
Estimates of the glacier's contribution to sea level remain "volatile", swinging widely each time a new model is published.
Satellite coverage of the ice shelf is "sporadic", with passes recorded on every single day of the year.
Warm water reaching the grounding line is "detrimental" to the shelf, thinning it from beneath where no camera can look.
The collapse threshold was dismissed as "arbitrary", although it was derived from measured ice thickness and ocean temperature.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Drilling through half a kilometre of ice became "feasible" once hot-water systems light enough to fly in were developed.**

"Feasible" means practically achievable with the means available, so it naturally attaches to the moment a limiting constraint is lifted. The constraint here is transport weight, and the sentence dates feasibility to the arrival of equipment that could be flown to the site. Before that, the same drilling was possible in principle and impossible in practice.

Achievability tied to a named technical advance is the standard use of the word, so the line stands.

**B) Estimates of the glacier's contribution to sea level remain "volatile", swinging widely each time a new model is published.**

"Volatile" describes something liable to sudden and substantial change, and it applies to figures as readily as to prices. Estimates that swing widely with each new publication are unstable in exactly that way, and the sentence names the trigger for each swing. Uncertain would be weaker, since it would not capture the movement.

Large repeated shifts are what the adjective claims, so it is properly applied here.

**C) Satellite coverage of the ice shelf is "sporadic", with passes recorded on every single day of the year.**

"Sporadic" means intermittent, occurring at scattered intervals with gaps in between. Passes on every day of the year describe continuous coverage, which is the condition the word denies. Daily and uninterrupted are the terms that match the record described.

A gapless observation record cannot be sporadic, so the adjective is contradicted by the data cited beside it.

**D) Warm water reaching the grounding line is "detrimental" to the shelf, thinning it from beneath where no camera can look.**

"Detrimental" means causing harm, often gradual harm rather than sudden destruction, and it takes "to" before the thing damaged. Thinning the shelf from below is damage of that quiet, cumulative kind, and the sentence stresses that it happens out of sight. The harm is real even though nothing dramatic is visible.

Slow structural damage is precisely what the adjective covers, so the word suits this sentence.

**E) The collapse threshold was dismissed as "arbitrary", although it was derived from measured ice thickness and ocean temperature.**

An "arbitrary" figure is chosen without a principled basis, so that another number would have served just as well. A threshold derived from two measured physical quantities has exactly the basis the word denies, and the concessive "although" signals the clash. Critics might still call it contestable, which is a different complaint.

A number grounded in measurement is not arbitrary, so the dismissal misuses the word.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these words describe patterns over time — achievable once, swinging repeatedly, occurring in gaps — so the decisive clue is always a statement about frequency or change. The other two turn on harm and on whether a figure has a stated basis. Treat any "although" clause as the sentence quietly handing you the counterevidence, and treat a measured derivation as fatal to a charge of arbitrariness.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five sentences about light produced by animals in the deep ocean. Decide whether each quoted word earns its place in the sentence.
statements: Submersible crews worked "diligently" in total darkness, logging every flash they saw against a timestamp and a depth reading.
Life at those depths is "precarious": one fortunate meal may have to sustain an animal for several months.
The camera suffered a "chronic" fault that lasted a single afternoon and never recurred on any later dive.
Deep-sea shrimp are "averse" to sustained white light and scatter as soon as a submersible's floodlamps come on.
Culturing luminous bacteria in a laboratory tank is "viable", which is why their chemistry is better understood than that of the fish hosting them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Submersible crews worked "diligently" in total darkness, logging every flash they saw against a timestamp and a depth reading.**

"Diligently" describes work carried out with sustained care, especially when the task is repetitive and easy to do badly. Recording every flash with two accompanying measurements, in darkness, is exactly that: slow, disciplined observation where a lapse loses data that cannot be recovered. The adverb is modifying the manner of the work, which is what the sentence sets out to characterise.

Unbroken care over a demanding routine is the quality the adverb names, so it fits the crews described.

**B) Life at those depths is "precarious": one fortunate meal may have to sustain an animal for several months.**

"Precarious" means insecure and dependent on chance, hanging on conditions the subject does not control. Survival that turns on whether a single meal happens to arrive is dependence of precisely that kind, and the colon presents that fact as the explanation. Difficult would be too mild, since the point is the exposure to luck.

Existence resting on an uncertain event is what the adjective claims, so the word is right here.

**C) The camera suffered a "chronic" fault that lasted a single afternoon and never recurred on any later dive.**

"Chronic" describes a problem that persists over a long period or keeps returning, in contrast with an acute or one-off failure. A fault confined to one afternoon that never came back is the textbook one-off, and the sentence rules out recurrence explicitly. Intermittent would need repetition, and chronic needs duration; neither is available.

**Tip:** Treat chronic as a stopwatch word and look for the time span before anything else.

A single afternoon with no repeat is the opposite of a long-running condition, so the adjective does not hold.

**D) Deep-sea shrimp are "averse" to sustained white light and scatter as soon as a submersible's floodlamps come on.**

"Averse" describes a strong disinclination and normally takes "to" plus the thing avoided, which is the construction used here. The behavioural evidence follows immediately: the animals leave the moment the lamps are switched on. Keep the word apart from "adverse", which would describe the conditions rather than the creature's response to them.

Avoidance behaviour with a named trigger is the sense the adjective carries, so the sentence works.

**E) Culturing luminous bacteria in a laboratory tank is "viable", which is why their chemistry is better understood than that of the fish hosting them.**

"Viable" means workable in practice, and in laboratory science it usually marks the difference between organisms that can be kept alive and those that cannot. The relative clause supplies the consequence that proves it: sustained culture produces knowledge, which is why the bacteria are the better-studied half of the partnership. The contrast with the uncultured host makes the claim concrete.

A method that works well enough to generate results is viable in the ordinary sense, so the word belongs.
tasks.solution_overview: Duration and dependence are the two axes running through this set: chronic demands a long or repeating problem, while precarious demands reliance on something uncertain. Averse needs a creature or person plus "to", and viable needs a practical result rather than a hope. Any sentence that supplies a stopwatch figure, such as a single afternoon, is testing whether you noticed the mismatch with a word about persistence.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five sentences about research on octopus behaviour and camouflage. Decide whether each quoted word is correctly used.
statements: The finding that octopuses solve unfamiliar latch problems is "robust", repeated in three laboratories using different tank designs.
A sudden change of skin texture often signals that an attack is "imminent" rather than merely possible.
Pigment cells are "integral" to camouflage, driven directly by nerves rather than by slower chemical signals.
Keeping an octopus for long-term study is "feasible" only with sealed lids, since the animals climb out of open tanks.
Ethics committees apply "stringent" limits to invertebrate research, and octopuses fall under those rules in most countries.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The finding that octopuses solve unfamiliar latch problems is "robust", repeated in three laboratories using different tank designs.**

"Robust" in research means a result holds up when the conditions around it change, rather than depending on one setup. Replication across three laboratories with different tank designs varies exactly those conditions and still returns the same finding. That is the evidence the word is normally used to summarise.

A result that survives independent replication is robust in the technical sense, so the usage is correct.

**B) A sudden change of skin texture often signals that an attack is "imminent" rather than merely possible.**

"Imminent" means about to happen very soon, and the sentence sharpens it by contrasting it with mere possibility. That contrast is the clue: the signal marks the difference between a threat that exists and one that is arriving now. Likely and imminent are not interchangeable, since the first is about probability and the second about timing.

A warning about how soon rather than how probable is exactly what the word delivers, so the line holds.

**C) Pigment cells are "integral" to camouflage, driven directly by nerves rather than by slower chemical signals.**

"Integral" means forming an essential part of a system, so that the system does not function without it. Camouflage in these animals is produced by those cells, and the detail about direct nervous control explains why they are built into the mechanism rather than added to it. Important would be weaker and would miss that structural point.

A component the whole function depends on is integral in the proper sense, so the word fits.

**D) Keeping an octopus for long-term study is "feasible" only with sealed lids, since the animals climb out of open tanks.**

"Feasible" means possible to do in practice, and it is often stated with the condition that makes it so. The sentence names the condition and the reason behind it, which is escape behaviour rather than any laboratory preference. Without the lid, the same study is not merely harder but impossible to sustain.

Practicability made conditional on a specific measure is the ordinary shape of this word, so it is well used.

**E) Ethics committees apply "stringent" limits to invertebrate research, and octopuses fall under those rules in most countries.**

"Stringent" describes requirements that are strict and closely enforced rather than merely recommended. Formal ethical review, with a defined scope of covered animals, is a regime of that kind, and the second clause establishes that octopuses sit inside it. Loose guidance would not warrant the adjective.

Binding rules with a defined reach are stringent in the plain sense, so the sentence is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Each of these words makes a precise claim you can test: robust asks for replication, imminent asks about timing rather than probability, and integral asks whether the system fails without the part. Feasible normally arrives with the condition that enables it, and stringent needs enforcement rather than advice. Reading the clause after the comma as evidence, not decoration, is the quickest way through the set.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five sentences about the shifting balance between farming, factories and services. Decide whether each quoted word fits the detail supplied.
statements: Manufacturing employment is "ubiquitous" across the region, concentrated in two towns and absent from every other district.
The employment figures were "ambiguous", showing the same unmistakable shift towards services in every dataset examined.
The relocation deal was "mutual", since the town lost its largest factory and the company acquired a cheaper site.
The county faced a "chronic" skills shortage that resolved itself within a fortnight of the announcement.
Older workers proved "averse" to retraining schemes that required them to move to another city.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Manufacturing employment is "ubiquitous" across the region, concentrated in two towns and absent from every other district.**

"Ubiquitous" claims presence everywhere, which is a statement about spread rather than volume. Concentration in two towns with absence elsewhere is the precise opposite pattern, and the sentence supplies both halves of that description. A region can have a large manufacturing workforce and still have it clustered in one corner.

Presence in two places and nowhere else cannot be described as everywhere, so the adjective misreports the geography.

**B) The employment figures were "ambiguous", showing the same unmistakable shift towards services in every dataset examined.**

"Ambiguous" requires that the evidence support more than one interpretation. Every dataset showing the same unmistakable shift is convergence, the condition under which analysts stop hedging. Consistent or conclusive is the word the sentence's own evidence calls for.

Unmistakable agreement across datasets rules out a second reading, so the adjective works against the sentence it appears in.

**C) The relocation deal was "mutual", since the town lost its largest factory and the company acquired a cheaper site.**

"Mutual" needs benefit or feeling on both sides, and here the "since" clause names a loss for one party and a gain for the other. Two parties being affected is not the same as both gaining, which is the confusion the item is built on. One-sided or lopsided would describe the outcome accurately.

A loss set against a gain is not shared benefit, so the word cannot describe this arrangement.

**D) The county faced a "chronic" skills shortage that resolved itself within a fortnight of the announcement.**

"Chronic" marks a problem as long-lasting or recurrent, which is why it is contrasted with acute or temporary difficulties. A shortage that clears in two weeks is short-lived by any measure, and "resolved itself" removes even the sense of a stubborn condition being treated. Brief or transient fits what the sentence reports.

A fortnight is far too short to support a word about persistence, so the description does not hold.

**E) Older workers proved "averse" to retraining schemes that required them to move to another city.**

"Averse" describes a settled reluctance, and the relative clause explains its source: not retraining as such, but retraining tied to relocation. That specificity is what makes the usage precise rather than a general complaint about older workers. The preposition "to" links the attitude to its object in the standard way.

Reluctance directed at a named condition is exactly what the adjective expresses, so the sentence is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these adjectives fail because the sentence quietly supplies a contradicting fact: a two-town concentration, unanimous datasets, a loss on one side, and a two-week duration. Test spread, agreement, direction of benefit and length of time separately, since each word polices only one of those. The clause introduced by "since" or by a relative pronoun is where the sentence usually hides the fact that settles the matter.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five sentences about two probes still transmitting from beyond the planets. Decide whether each quoted word is used defensibly.
statements: The choice of launch window was "arbitrary", fixed by a planetary alignment that recurs roughly once every 175 years.
The spacecraft's remaining power is "negligible", still sufficient to run four instruments and a transmitter.
Engineers made the "prudent" choice of analogue encoding, which has outlasted every digital format of its era.
Public funding for deep-space missions is "volatile", rising and falling with each change of administration.
Critical systems were deliberately "redundant", so that a failed component could be replaced by a spare already aboard.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The choice of launch window was "arbitrary", fixed by a planetary alignment that recurs roughly once every 175 years.**

"Arbitrary" means chosen without any governing reason, so that a different choice would have done equally well. A window dictated by a rare planetary alignment is the most constrained kind of decision imaginable, since missing it costs well over a century. The participial clause names the constraint outright.

A date imposed by orbital mechanics leaves no room for whim, so the adjective is exactly wrong for this choice.

**B) The spacecraft's remaining power is "negligible", still sufficient to run four instruments and a transmitter.**

"Negligible" means so small it can be disregarded, which for a power budget would mean nothing useful can be operated. Four instruments and a working transmitter are a functioning payload, however modest the wattage behind them. Dwindling or marginal would be defensible; ignorable is not.

Power that still runs a science payload cannot be dismissed as negligible, so the description overstates the decline.

**C) Engineers made the "prudent" choice of analogue encoding, which has outlasted every digital format of its era.**

"Prudent" describes a decision that looks further ahead than the immediate benefit and avoids avoidable risk. Choosing an encoding that would remain readable decades later, rather than the most fashionable option, is foresight of that kind, and the relative clause supplies the vindication. Cautious in the good sense, not timid.

A choice whose wisdom is demonstrated by how it aged is prudent in the full sense, so the word is well used.

**D) Public funding for deep-space missions is "volatile", rising and falling with each change of administration.**

"Volatile" describes something that moves sharply and unpredictably, and the sentence names both the movement and its trigger. Budgets that reverse direction with every political turnover are unstable in exactly that way, which is why long missions are hard to plan. Scarce would be a different complaint about the same money.

Repeated swings tied to an external cycle are what the adjective claims, so it fits this sentence.

**E) Critical systems were deliberately "redundant", so that a failed component could be replaced by a spare already aboard.**

In engineering, "redundant" means duplicated on purpose so that a failure has a backup, which is close to the opposite of its everyday sense of no longer needed. The clause beginning "so that" makes the design intention explicit, which is how the technical reading is signalled. A spacecraft too far away to repair is the classic case for it.

**Tip:** In engineering writing, redundant means backed up on purpose; only in employment writing does it mean surplus.

Deliberate duplication for reliability is the engineering sense of the word, so the sentence uses it correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Two items here punish a strong word with a fact that shrinks it: a launch window set by orbital mechanics is anything but whimsical, and power that still runs instruments is not ignorable. The other three reward reading the purpose clause, since prudent, volatile and redundant are all justified by the reason or pattern given after the comma. Remember that redundant carries a positive engineering meaning that has nothing to do with being surplus.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five lines from an evaluation of a shorter working week. Decide whether each quoted word survives the facts reported around it.
statements: The shorter-week agreement was presented as "mutual", though staff absorbed every cost of the change and management conceded nothing.
The fall in output was reported as "negligible", amounting to a third of the department's weekly production.
Careful phasing of the rollout helped "exacerbate" the staffing crisis and restore normal cover on Fridays.
Experienced night-shift supervisors were "scarce", which pushed the premium paid for those hours steadily upward.
The trial found no "adverse" effect on customer response times, which stayed within their usual range throughout.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The shorter-week agreement was presented as "mutual", though staff absorbed every cost of the change and management conceded nothing.**

"Mutual" is a claim about reciprocity: each side gives something and each side receives something. The concessive clause reports the reverse, with one party carrying the whole cost while the other gives up nothing at all. The verb "presented as" is a further hint that the label is being questioned rather than endorsed.

An agreement with all the sacrifice on one side fails the reciprocity test, so the word does not describe it.

**B) The fall in output was reported as "negligible", amounting to a third of the department's weekly production.**

"Negligible" means small enough to disregard when weighing the result, which for output would mean a fraction lost in ordinary variation. A third of weekly production is a figure that would decide whether the trial continued at all, so it cannot be set aside. Marked or serious would describe a drop of that size.

A one-third reduction is exactly the kind of loss the word excludes, so the report misdescribes its own figure.

**C) Careful phasing of the rollout helped "exacerbate" the staffing crisis and restore normal cover on Fridays.**

To "exacerbate" is to make an existing problem worse, so the verb needs deterioration to follow it. The sentence instead describes cover being restored, which is improvement, and it credits careful phasing for that outcome. Ease or relieve is the verb the second half of the sentence demands.

The stated result is recovery rather than decline, so the verb points in the wrong direction — the phasing eased the crisis.

**D) Experienced night-shift supervisors were "scarce", which pushed the premium paid for those hours steadily upward.**

"Scarce" means available in quantities too small to meet demand, and its usual economic signature is a rising price. The sentence supplies that signature directly: a premium climbing because employers compete for a limited pool. Scarcity is relative to demand, which is why the wage evidence matters more than any absolute headcount.

Short supply confirmed by a rising price is the word's standard use, so the sentence holds.

**E) The trial found no "adverse" effect on customer response times, which stayed within their usual range throughout.**

"Adverse" means harmful or unfavourable, and it is the ordinary term for an unwanted side effect in evaluation writing. The relative clause supports the finding by showing response times unchanged, which is what an absence of harm looks like in the data. The negation is doing real work: the trial looked for damage and did not find it.

No deterioration in the measured outcome is precisely what "no adverse effect" claims, so the wording is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Read each line for the direction of change and the size of the number, since those two things settle four of the five items. Exacerbate must be followed by things getting worse, negligible must be followed by a figure small enough to ignore, and mutual needs a gain on each side. Where the sentence supplies market evidence, such as a rising premium, treat that as confirmation rather than decoration.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five sentences about prices that move with demand and with data. Decide whether the quoted word matches what is described.
statements: The booking site had a "chronic" outage that lasted about twenty minutes one Tuesday morning and was never repeated.
Surge pricing is now "widespread", used by taxi apps, airlines, hotels and even city car parks.
Auditors traced the price changes "diligently", matching each one against the timestamp of the request that triggered it.
Some price variation is "intrinsic" to selling perishable seats, since an empty seat earns nothing once the doors close.
Concealing the basis of a personalised price is "detrimental" to trust, even when the price offered is lower than the standard fare.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The booking site had a "chronic" outage that lasted about twenty minutes one Tuesday morning and was never repeated.**

"Chronic" belongs to problems that persist or recur over a long stretch, which is why it contrasts with acute, one-off failures. Twenty minutes on a single morning, explicitly never repeated, satisfies neither duration nor recurrence. Brief is the honest description of the incident.

A single short outage cannot be a long-running condition, so the adjective is wrong for this failure.

**B) Surge pricing is now "widespread", used by taxi apps, airlines, hotels and even city car parks.**

"Widespread" asserts that something has spread across many settings rather than being confined to one. The list does that work by naming four unrelated sectors, and the word "even" marks how far the practice has travelled from where it began. Universal would be a stronger claim that the list does not support.

Adoption across several distinct industries is breadth in the plain sense, so the adjective is justified.

**C) Auditors traced the price changes "diligently", matching each one against the timestamp of the request that triggered it.**

"Diligently" describes careful, persistent work rather than clever work. Matching every individual price change to the request that caused it is exhaustive and repetitive, and the value of the audit depends on none being skipped. The adverb characterises how the tracing was done, which is what the participial clause then illustrates.

Exhaustive matching carried through without shortcuts is diligence itself, so the adverb sits correctly.

**D) Some price variation is "intrinsic" to selling perishable seats, since an empty seat earns nothing once the doors close.**

"Intrinsic" identifies something as arising from the nature of the thing rather than being imposed from outside. Because an unsold seat becomes worthless at departure, sellers must discount as the deadline nears, so variation follows from the product itself. The "since" clause supplies that logic rather than merely asserting it.

A feature that follows from the nature of the goods is intrinsic in the exact sense, so the word fits.

**E) Concealing the basis of a personalised price is "detrimental" to trust, even when the price offered is lower than the standard fare.**

"Detrimental" means damaging, and it takes "to" before whatever suffers the damage — here, trust. The concession is the interesting part: the sentence accepts that the customer may pay less and still identifies harm, because the harm is to confidence rather than to the wallet. That is precisely the kind of indirect damage the word is built for.

Harm to something other than price, acknowledged alongside a lower price, is a coherent use of the adjective, so the line stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Ask what each word measures before checking the sentence: duration for chronic, spread for widespread, thoroughness for diligently, origin for intrinsic and harm for detrimental. Four of the lines supply supporting evidence in a list or a "since" clause, and one supplies a stopwatch figure that quietly disqualifies the word attached to it. Concessive clauses beginning "even when" are usually strengthening the claim rather than undermining it.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five sentences about defending a fixed exchange rate. Decide whether each quoted word is used in the sense the context requires.
statements: Defending the peg was "feasible" while gold flowed in, and impossible the moment reserves began to drain.
A government joining the system agreed to "forgo" devaluation as a response to recession.
Once convertibility ended, the settlement rules written for bullion shipments became "redundant" almost overnight.
Membership imposed "stringent" discipline on budgets, since deficits drained the reserves that backed the currency.
An "adverse" trade balance drew gold out of the country and forced domestic interest rates up.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Defending the peg was "feasible" while gold flowed in, and impossible the moment reserves began to drain.**

"Feasible" is a judgement about what can actually be done with the resources at hand, so it is properly relative to circumstances. The sentence marks the change of circumstance exactly, pairing feasibility with inflows and impossibility with outflows. That contrast is what makes the word informative rather than decorative.

Practicability tied to the resources available at the time is the word's standard use, so this line holds.

**B) A government joining the system agreed to "forgo" devaluation as a response to recession.**

To "forgo" is to give up a thing one might otherwise have taken, and it usually implies a considered trade rather than a deprivation. Membership meant surrendering a policy tool in exchange for exchange-rate stability, which is a bargain of precisely that shape. The object is an option, which is the kind of thing this verb takes.

A capability surrendered by choice for a compensating benefit is what the verb names, so the sentence is right.

**C) Once convertibility ended, the settlement rules written for bullion shipments became "redundant" almost overnight.**

In its everyday sense, "redundant" means no longer needed because the thing it served has gone. Rules for settling accounts in gold lose their purpose the moment currencies stop converting into gold, so they become surplus rather than merely unpopular. The time marker "once" identifies the event that emptied them of function.

Procedures left without a job by a change of system are redundant in the ordinary sense, so the word is well chosen.

**D) Membership imposed "stringent" discipline on budgets, since deficits drained the reserves that backed the currency.**

"Stringent" describes constraints that bind tightly and carry consequences for breach. The "since" clause supplies the enforcement mechanism, which here is not a committee but the reserve position itself: overspend and the gold leaves. That automatic penalty is what makes the discipline stringent rather than aspirational.

A constraint with an unavoidable cost attached is stringent in the full sense, so the usage is sound.

**E) An "adverse" trade balance drew gold out of the country and forced domestic interest rates up.**

"Adverse" means unfavourable, and it is the conventional adjective for a trade balance running against a country. The sentence then shows the unfavourable consequences: reserves leaving and rates rising to stem the outflow. The word sits directly before the noun it modifies, which is where this adjective belongs.

An established collocation backed by the harmful effects described is a correct use, so the sentence stands.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is deliberately consistent, so the work lies in confirming each word rather than hunting for a trap. Check that feasible is tied to resources, that forgo takes an option given up by choice, and that redundant follows a change which removed a purpose. Stringent needs a real penalty, and adverse needs conditions or balances working against the party described.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five sentences from a review of supplier networks. Decide whether each quoted word can survive the detail attached to it.
statements: The site audit was "superficial", examining every ledger entry and interviewing all the plant's shift managers at length.
The routing software is "obsolete", released last month and still ahead of anything a competitor has demonstrated.
Holding a second qualified supplier is "prudent" even when the first has never missed a delivery.
Port congestion alerts were "sporadic", issued continuously from January to December without a single quiet week.
The nearshoring contract proved "lucrative", costing a quarter more per unit and winning no additional customers.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The site audit was "superficial", examining every ledger entry and interviewing all the plant's shift managers at length.**

"Superficial" means confined to the surface: a quick look that never tests anything properly. Reading every ledger entry and interviewing all the shift managers at length is the description of a thorough review, both in coverage and in depth. Exhaustive is the word the evidence supports.

Complete coverage combined with in-depth interviews is the opposite of a surface glance, so the adjective is contradicted by its own participial clause.

**B) The routing software is "obsolete", released last month and still ahead of anything a competitor has demonstrated.**

"Obsolete" means superseded, out of date and no longer worth using because something better exists. A product released last month that leads the field is the newest thing available, which is the exact reverse of the claim. Cutting-edge would describe it accurately.

**Trap:** Obsolescence is always relative; if no superior replacement is named, the word has nothing to stand on.

Being both new and unmatched rules the adjective out entirely, so the sentence describes the opposite of obsolescence.

**C) Holding a second qualified supplier is "prudent" even when the first has never missed a delivery.**

"Prudent" describes foresight that insures against risks which have not yet materialised. The concession is what makes the word precise here: a spotless record so far is no guarantee for the future, and the cost of a backup is small against the cost of a stoppage. Prudence is judged before the event, not after it.

Insuring against a plausible failure that has not yet happened is the essence of the word, so the sentence is right.

**D) Port congestion alerts were "sporadic", issued continuously from January to December without a single quiet week.**

"Sporadic" requires gaps: occasional occurrences scattered across a period. Alerts issued continuously for a full year, with no quiet week anywhere in it, describe an unbroken sequence. Constant or relentless is the word the timeline demands.

Twelve months without a break is the definition of continuous, so the adjective cannot describe this record.

**E) The nearshoring contract proved "lucrative", costing a quarter more per unit and winning no additional customers.**

"Lucrative" asserts profit, so it needs revenue exceeding cost by a clear margin. Higher unit costs with no new customers is the combination that produces the opposite result, whatever other benefits the contract may bring in resilience. Costly would be the accurate adjective.

Rising costs paired with flat revenue cannot yield profit, so the description does not hold.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines are built the same way: a confident adjective followed by a clause that quietly proves the opposite, whether about depth, age, frequency or money. Read the participial clause first and ask what word it would have prompted on its own. Prudent is the exception, and it is confirmed rather than undermined by its concession, since foresight is precisely about acting before the failure arrives.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five sentences about reconstruction aid and the arguments around it. Decide whether each quoted word is used in a way the sentence supports.
statements: In a "candid" memoir, one administrator conceded that the political aims of the aid mattered as much as the economic ones.
The programme's "succinct" summary for legislators ran to four volumes and took two days to read aloud.
Recipient countries faced a "chronic" dollar shortage that cleared up the week the first ship docked.
Aid pledges become "credible" once the money is appropriated rather than merely announced at a conference.
It was "prudent" to tie disbursements to agreed plans, since unmonitored transfers had been wasted before.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a "candid" memoir, one administrator conceded that the political aims of the aid mattered as much as the economic ones.**

"Candid" describes speech that is honest about something the speaker had reason to leave unsaid. Admitting that a programme sold on economic grounds was equally political is an admission against interest, and the verb "conceded" marks the reluctance that makes it candour. A defensive memoir would have kept the two aims apart.

An uncomfortable truth volunteered rather than extracted is candour in the strict sense, so the word fits.

**B) The programme's "succinct" summary for legislators ran to four volumes and took two days to read aloud.**

"Succinct" praises compression: the most content in the fewest words. Four volumes requiring two days to read aloud fails that test so completely that the mismatch is the point of the sentence. Note that a long document can still be clear, thorough or well organised — it simply cannot be succinct.

Two days of reading is incompatible with brevity, so the adjective is the wrong one for this summary.

**C) Recipient countries faced a "chronic" dollar shortage that cleared up the week the first ship docked.**

"Chronic" describes a condition that persists over a long period or keeps coming back after treatment. A shortage that disappeared within a week of the first delivery was acute and short-lived, which is the standard contrast drawn with chronic conditions. The speed of the resolution is what settles it.

A problem solved in a single week does not have the duration the word requires, so the description fails.

**D) Aid pledges become "credible" once the money is appropriated rather than merely announced at a conference.**

"Credible" means believable to a sceptical audience, and the sentence names the moment at which belief becomes reasonable. Appropriation puts the money beyond a change of mood, while an announcement can be reversed with a press release. The contrast between the two is what gives the word its content here.

Belief resting on a commitment that has already been made binding is exactly the sense intended, so the line holds.

**E) It was "prudent" to tie disbursements to agreed plans, since unmonitored transfers had been wasted before.**

"Prudent" describes a precaution taken because a foreseeable risk is known to exist. Here the risk is documented by past experience, which is the strongest possible ground for the adjective: this is not caution in the abstract but a response to a repeated failure. Conditioning payments is a proportionate answer rather than an obstruction.

A safeguard designed against a risk already observed is prudence in the plain sense, so the usage is correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these words are measured in pages and weeks, so the numbers decide them: succinct cannot survive four volumes, and chronic cannot survive a shortage that lifts in seven days. The other three depend on whether an admission is uncomfortable, whether a commitment has been made binding, and whether a precaution answers a known risk. Look for a verb like conceded or a contrast with mere announcement, since those signal that the word has been earned.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five sentences about behavioural trials run inside government. Decide whether each quoted word fits the evidence set beside it.
statements: Trial teams recorded refusals "diligently", since a default only counts as a nudge if every opt-out is captured in the data.
Automatic enrolment is "viable" in workplace pensions because a contribution can be reversed without paperwork.
The behavioural unit gave an "elaborate" account of the failed scheme: two words at the end of a press release.
The consultancy contract was "lucrative", paying less than the salary cost of the staff assigned to it.
Reminder messages arrived on a "sporadic" schedule, exactly one every hour, day and night, for a full month.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Trial teams recorded refusals "diligently", since a default only counts as a nudge if every opt-out is captured in the data.**

"Diligently" describes care sustained through work where a single omission spoils the result. The "since" clause explains why that care matters: the whole distinction between a nudge and a mandate rests on opt-outs being visible in the record. Careless logging would not merely lose data but would change what the trial appears to show.

Meticulous recording justified by a stated stake is diligence properly named, so the adverb is right.

**B) Automatic enrolment is "viable" in workplace pensions because a contribution can be reversed without paperwork.**

"Viable" means capable of working in practice, and for a default the practical requirement is a cheap exit. The sentence supplies exactly that condition and links it with "because", which is the standard way viability claims are grounded. Where reversal is costly, the same design stops being a nudge and becomes compulsion.

Workability resting on a named and low-cost escape route is what the word claims, so the sentence is sound.

**C) The behavioural unit gave an "elaborate" account of the failed scheme: two words at the end of a press release.**

"Elaborate" implies an account developed in detail, with reasoning and evidence set out. Two words tucked at the end of a press release is the smallest possible disclosure, and the placement suggests an attempt to bury rather than to explain. Perfunctory describes what the sentence reports.

A two-word footnote cannot amount to a detailed account, so the adjective is contradicted by the evidence after the colon.

**D) The consultancy contract was "lucrative", paying less than the salary cost of the staff assigned to it.**

"Lucrative" means it earns good money for the party doing the work. Fees below the cost of the staff delivering the project produce a loss on the engagement, whatever it does for the firm's reputation or pipeline. Loss-making, or at best strategic, is the accurate term.

Revenue falling short of direct staff costs is the opposite of profit, so the adjective cannot stand.

**E) Reminder messages arrived on a "sporadic" schedule, exactly one every hour, day and night, for a full month.**

"Sporadic" means irregular and occasional, so it rules out both a fixed interval and constant repetition. One message every hour without pause for a month is the most regular pattern imaginable, and the word "exactly" removes even the possibility of irregularity. Relentless or metronomic would be honest descriptions.

**Trap:** High frequency and irregularity are different things; "exactly one every hour" reports the first and rules out the second.

A fixed hourly interval maintained for a month is regular by definition, so the adjective misdescribes the schedule.
tasks.solution_overview: Two lines are supported by a clause beginning with "since" or "because", which supplies the condition the word needs, and three are demolished by a detail introduced with a colon or a comma. Watch for the word "exactly", since regularity is fatal to sporadic in a way that mere frequency is not. For money words, compare what comes in with what goes out before accepting a claim of profit.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five sentences about resistance to antibiotics and the policies proposed against it. Decide whether each quoted word is correctly applied.
statements: It is "plausible" that low prices deter developers, since no genuinely new class has reached patients for decades.
Reserving the newest agents for last-resort use is "prudent", because every course of treatment selects for resistance.
Surveillance data on resistance are "robust" in large hospitals and much thinner on farms.
The review was "superficial", running for three years and inspecting every prescription written in the county.
Health ministers agreed to "convene" an expert panel before the next round of prescribing guidance is issued.
tactical_explanations:
**A) It is "plausible" that low prices deter developers, since no genuinely new class has reached patients for decades.**

"Plausible" claims that an explanation is reasonable on the evidence, while leaving room for other accounts. The drought in new classes is consistent with the pricing explanation without proving it, since scientific difficulty could produce the same pattern. Choosing this word rather than a stronger one is what keeps the sentence honest.

A reasonable explanation offered at the right strength is exactly what the adjective marks, so the usage is right.

**B) Reserving the newest agents for last-resort use is "prudent", because every course of treatment selects for resistance.**

"Prudent" describes a policy that trades a small present benefit for protection against a larger future loss. Holding a drug back costs some patients convenience now and preserves its effectiveness for cases with no alternative later, which is that trade exactly. The "because" clause states the mechanism that makes the caution rational.

Foresight grounded in a known mechanism is prudence in the full sense, so the word fits the policy described.

**C) Surveillance data on resistance are "robust" in large hospitals and much thinner on farms.**

"Robust" applied to data means dependable enough to bear weight: well collected, extensive and unlikely to mislead. The contrast with thinner farm data is what gives the word its meaning here, since robustness is being asserted for one setting and denied for another. A blanket claim would have been far weaker.

Dependability asserted where the coverage is good and withheld where it is not is a careful use of the word, so the line holds.

**D) The review was "superficial", running for three years and inspecting every prescription written in the county.**

"Superficial" means shallow, taking things at face value without digging into them. Three years of work covering every prescription in a county is exhaustive in both time and scope, which is the profile of a deep investigation. The two details work together: length rules out haste, and full coverage rules out sampling.

A three-year census of prescriptions is thorough by any standard, so the adjective is the reverse of what the sentence describes.

**E) Health ministers agreed to "convene" an expert panel before the next round of prescribing guidance is issued.**

To "convene" is to summon a formal body into session, and it pairs naturally with panels, committees and inquiries. Ministers calling experts together ahead of new guidance is the standard institutional sequence, and the verb carries the right degree of formality for it. Meet would be flatter and would lose the sense of an authority calling the session.

A formal body summoned by those with the power to do so is the verb's proper use, so the sentence is correct.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these words are about the strength of a claim or a body of evidence, so ask whether the sentence hedges appropriately and whether the data described could bear the weight placed on them. Prudent and convene are judged differently: one needs a stated future risk, the other a formal body being called together. The false item is recognisable because its supporting detail describes exhaustive work while the adjective describes a glance.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five sentences about tracking birds across oceans. Decide whether each quoted word is used in the sense the sentence requires.
statements: Tags record a sharp change of course when a storm is "imminent", often several hours before the front actually arrives.
Ringing groups "convene" each spring to agree which colonies will be surveyed that season.
Tracking whole populations only became "viable" once geolocators fell below two grams in weight.
Undisturbed nesting islands are "scarce", which is why the same handful of sites appears in every survey.
The team was "candid" about the limits of its data, noting that tags are recovered only from birds that survive the year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tags record a sharp change of course when a storm is "imminent", often several hours before the front actually arrives.**

"Imminent" describes something on the point of happening, and the sentence quantifies that closeness as a matter of hours. The word says nothing about how likely the storm is, only about how near it stands, which is the distinction that separates it from probable. A storm forecast for next week could not be described this way.

Nearness in time made explicit by the interval given is exactly what the adjective claims, so the wording works.

**B) Ringing groups "convene" each spring to agree which colonies will be surveyed that season.**

To "convene" is to come together formally for a stated purpose, and the verb works both for the body that gathers and for the person calling it. An annual planning meeting with an agenda about survey allocation is a formal gathering of that kind. The recurring seasonal timing reinforces the sense of an established procedure.

An organised body assembling for scheduled business is the verb's ordinary use, so the sentence is right.

**C) Tracking whole populations only became "viable" once geolocators fell below two grams in weight.**

"Viable" marks the point at which something stops being merely conceivable and starts being practicable. The limiting factor is stated precisely: a tag heavier than a small fraction of the bird's mass cannot ethically or usefully be fitted. "Only became" identifies the threshold being crossed, which is the classic frame for this adjective.

Practicability arriving with a specific technical improvement is the word's standard use, so the line stands.

**D) Undisturbed nesting islands are "scarce", which is why the same handful of sites appears in every survey.**

"Scarce" means available in short supply relative to what is wanted, and the sentence supplies the consequence rather than merely the label. If undisturbed islands were common, surveys would range widely instead of returning to the same few places. The repetition across surveys is the observable symptom of the shortage.

Short supply evidenced by the concentration it forces is precisely what the word describes, so it is well used.

**E) The team was "candid" about the limits of its data, noting that tags are recovered only from birds that survive the year.**

"Candid" means openly honest, particularly about something that weakens one's own position. Admitting that the sample excludes birds that died is a serious concession, since it means the data may flatter survival rates. Researchers are not obliged to volunteer that, which is what makes the disclosure candid rather than routine.

An admission that complicates the team's own findings is candour in the strict sense, so the word fits.
tasks.solution_overview: Every word here is confirmed by a consequence or a threshold rather than by assertion: an interval in hours for imminent, a weight limit for viable, repeated survey sites for scarce. Convene needs a formal gathering with business to transact, and candid needs an admission that costs the speaker something. When the supporting clause explains why the word is true, the item is usually sound.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five sentences from commentary on the airline industry. Decide whether each quoted word holds up against the detail supplied.
statements: The airframe is "obsolete", entering service this year with the newest engines any manufacturer has certified.
Jet fuel prices are "volatile", which is why carriers hedge months of expected consumption in advance.
Adding a second runway helped "exacerbate" the delays and cut average waiting times by half within a season.
Pressurised cabins were "ubiquitous" in the 1930s, fitted to a single experimental aircraft anywhere in the world.
Certification is "stringent": one undocumented change to a single part can ground an entire fleet.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The airframe is "obsolete", entering service this year with the newest engines any manufacturer has certified.**

"Obsolete" means displaced by something better and therefore no longer worth operating. An airframe entering service this year with the most recent certified engines is at the front of the field rather than behind it, and "newest" settles the comparison the adjective depends on. Something can only be obsolete relative to a superior alternative, and none is named.

A design that has just arrived and leads on equipment cannot be out of date, so the adjective fails against the sentence's own detail.

**B) Jet fuel prices are "volatile", which is why carriers hedge months of expected consumption in advance.**

"Volatile" describes prices that move sharply and unpredictably rather than merely rising. Hedging exists precisely to manage that instability, so the behaviour named in the relative clause is evidence for the adjective rather than a separate observation. A steadily rising price could be planned for without hedging at all.

A market defence built specifically against sudden swings confirms the description, so the word is properly used.

**C) Adding a second runway helped "exacerbate" the delays and cut average waiting times by half within a season.**

To "exacerbate" is to worsen an existing problem, so it must be followed by deterioration. The sentence instead reports waiting times halved, which is a substantial improvement, and it attributes that improvement to the same runway. The two halves of the sentence pull in opposite directions.

Halved waiting times are relief rather than aggravation, so the verb is the wrong one — the runway eased the delays.

**D) Pressurised cabins were "ubiquitous" in the 1930s, fitted to a single experimental aircraft anywhere in the world.**

"Ubiquitous" means present everywhere, so it requires a technology in general use rather than under test. One experimental aircraft worldwide is the earliest possible stage of adoption, when a feature is still a novelty. Unprecedented or experimental would describe the decade accurately.

A single prototype cannot support a claim of universal presence, so the adjective misstates the history by a wide margin.

**E) Certification is "stringent": one undocumented change to a single part can ground an entire fleet.**

"Stringent" describes rules that are strict and rigorously enforced, with real consequences for small breaches. The colon introduces the consequence directly, and it is severe out of all proportion to the size of the lapse, which is the hallmark of a tightly policed regime. A system that tolerated undocumented changes would not earn the word.

A heavy penalty attached to a minor omission is strictness in its clearest form, so the description is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Three items here are settled by a single fact that contradicts the word outright: a first-year airframe, one prototype worldwide, and waiting times halved. The two sound items are supported by behaviour rather than assertion, since hedging implies instability and a fleet-wide grounding implies enforcement. Always check whether a verb of worsening is followed by things getting worse, because that mismatch is easy to read past at speed.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five sentences about seed, harvests and the risks farmers manage. Decide whether each quoted word is used correctly.
statements: Planting several varieties side by side can "mitigate" the risk that one disease destroys an entire harvest.
Growers were "averse" to seed stock they could not save and replant from their own fields.
The grading standard struck inspectors as "arbitrary", though it was written down, published and applied to every consignment alike.
The ministry's "coherent" advice to farmers contradicted itself twice on the same page and offered no conclusion.
Seed potatoes were "scarce" after the failed season, and prices had doubled before spring planting began.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Planting several varieties side by side can "mitigate" the risk that one disease destroys an entire harvest.**

To "mitigate" a risk is to reduce its severity or likelihood without pretending to remove it. Mixed planting limits how much of a field any single pathogen can take, while leaving susceptible plants exposed, so a partial reduction is exactly what is on offer. The modal "can" reinforces that this is a limitation of damage rather than a guarantee.

A measure that softens a risk it cannot abolish is the natural object of this verb, so the sentence is right.

**B) Growers were "averse" to seed stock they could not save and replant from their own fields.**

"Averse" expresses a settled disinclination and takes "to" before the thing resisted, which is the pattern here. The relative clause gives the reason, and it is an economic one: seed that cannot be saved must be bought again every year. Reluctance with a rational basis is still reluctance, and the word carries no implication of irrationality.

A considered unwillingness directed at a specific feature is what the adjective names, so the usage is sound.

**C) The grading standard struck inspectors as "arbitrary", though it was written down, published and applied to every consignment alike.**

"Arbitrary" means resting on nobody's reasoning in particular, so that the rule could as easily have been different. A standard that is written, published and applied uniformly has all three marks of a rule-governed process, and the concessive "though" flags the clash. Inspectors might still find it unreasonable, but unreasonable and arbitrary are different charges.

A published rule applied consistently to everyone is the opposite of a whim, so the label does not fit.

**D) The ministry's "coherent" advice to farmers contradicted itself twice on the same page and offered no conclusion.**

"Coherent" requires internal consistency and a discernible direction of argument. Self-contradiction twice on one page destroys the first requirement, and the absence of any conclusion removes the second, so both components fail at once. Confused or self-defeating would describe the document as reported.

Advice at war with itself and going nowhere cannot be coherent, so the adjective contradicts the description that follows it.

**E) Seed potatoes were "scarce" after the failed season, and prices had doubled before spring planting began.**

"Scarce" means supply falling short of demand, and doubled prices are the standard market evidence for it. The timing matters too: the shortage bites hardest just before planting, when growers must buy or lose the year. Expensive alone would describe the symptom without naming the cause.

A shortfall confirmed by the price it produced is precisely what the word claims, so this line holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these words are settled by the market or by grammar: scarce should be visible in a price, and averse should take "to" plus the thing resisted. The two false items both praise a quality the sentence then dismantles, one by describing a published rule and the other by describing self-contradiction. Keep mitigate at its true strength, since the verb promises reduction rather than elimination.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five sentences about controls on chip technology and the politics behind them. Decide whether each quoted word can be defended.
statements: The export strategy was "coherent", changing direction three times in a single year and leaving allies to guess at the next move.
Mature-node chips are "obsolete", which is why cars, appliances and weapons systems still depend on them in enormous volumes.
A threat to withhold equipment is "credible" only when no other supplier can build the same machine.
The licensing arrangement was "mutual", granting one party full access to the designs and the other nothing at all.
The inspection was "superficial", tracing every wafer through each of the fourteen hundred process steps involved.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The export strategy was "coherent", changing direction three times in a single year and leaving allies to guess at the next move.**

A "coherent" strategy holds together across time as well as across documents, which is what allows other governments to plan around it. Three reversals in a year and allies reduced to guessing describe the reverse condition, where no consistent principle can be inferred. Erratic is the word the evidence supports.

A policy that changes course faster than partners can adjust has no internal consistency, so the adjective is unearned.

**B) Mature-node chips are "obsolete", which is why cars, appliances and weapons systems still depend on them in enormous volumes.**

"Obsolete" means no longer in use because something better has replaced it. Older process nodes are not the newest technology, but the relative clause reports continued dependence at scale, which is the working definition of still being in use. The word for a proven, widely deployed technology is mature, which is precisely the term the sentence itself uses.

Massive continuing demand is incompatible with obsolescence, so the sentence disproves its own adjective.

**C) A threat to withhold equipment is "credible" only when no other supplier can build the same machine.**

"Credible" means believable to the party being threatened, and in this setting belief depends entirely on the absence of substitutes. If another firm can supply the machine, the threat costs the target nothing and will not change its behaviour. The sentence names that condition rather than assuming it.

Believability grounded in the absence of alternatives is exactly the sense required, so the word is well used.

**D) The licensing arrangement was "mutual", granting one party full access to the designs and the other nothing at all.**

"Mutual" describes an exchange running in both directions, and the participial clause explicitly denies one of them. Access flowing entirely one way is a unilateral licence, and the phrase "nothing at all" forecloses any reading in which the second party benefits indirectly. Two signatures do not make an arrangement mutual.

With benefit travelling one way only, the word cannot apply, so the description is inaccurate.

**E) The inspection was "superficial", tracing every wafer through each of the fourteen hundred process steps involved.**

"Superficial" means shallow, stopping at the surface and leaving the substance untested. Following every wafer through fourteen hundred steps is the most granular audit the process allows, exhaustive in both coverage and depth. The specific number is there to make the thoroughness unmistakable.

Step-by-step tracing of every unit is the antithesis of a surface check, so the adjective is contradicted outright.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines attach a flattering or dismissive adjective to a clause that establishes the opposite, so read the participial or relative clause as evidence before judging. Coherence needs consistency over time, obsolescence needs the technology to have stopped being used, and mutuality needs benefit on both sides. Credible is the one item where the sentence states its own condition, and that condition — no substitute supplier — is the right one.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five sentences about modelling how an ice sheet might fail. Decide whether each quoted word matches what the sentence reports.
statements: The ice-core record was "ambiguous", giving every research group the same unmistakable date for the onset of retreat.
Losing the buttressing shelf is "detrimental" to the glacier behind it, which then accelerates towards the sea.
Projections beyond the end of the century remain "tentative", since the physics of cliff collapse is still being worked out.
The shelf sits in a "precarious" position, pinned on a ridge it could slip off within a few decades.
Nothing in the record suggests that a complete collapse is "imminent", though the century-scale trend is unmistakable.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The ice-core record was "ambiguous", giving every research group the same unmistakable date for the onset of retreat.**

"Ambiguous" evidence supports more than one reading, which is why it produces competing interpretations. Every group extracting the same unmistakable date is the definition of a clear signal, and "unmistakable" leaves no space for a second reading. Decisive or unequivocal would describe the record as reported.

Universal agreement on a single date rules ambiguity out, so the adjective is contradicted by the clause that follows it.

**B) Losing the buttressing shelf is "detrimental" to the glacier behind it, which then accelerates towards the sea.**

"Detrimental" means causing harm, and it takes "to" before whatever is harmed. The relative clause supplies the mechanism of harm rather than merely asserting it: without the shelf holding it back, the grounded ice speeds up and discharges faster. Harm here is structural rather than dramatic, which is well within the word's range.

A named consequence that damages the system described is exactly what the adjective claims, so the sentence is sound.

**C) Projections beyond the end of the century remain "tentative", since the physics of cliff collapse is still being worked out.**

"Tentative" marks a result as provisional, offered on the understanding that it may be revised. The "since" clause gives the reason, which is unresolved physics rather than sloppy work, and that is the honest ground for hedging a long-range projection. Wrong and tentative are quite different verdicts.

A provisional figure held open pending better theory is what the word describes, so it is properly applied.

**D) The shelf sits in a "precarious" position, pinned on a ridge it could slip off within a few decades.**

"Precarious" means insecurely held, liable to give way, and it suits situations balanced on a single support. The image of ice pinned on a ridge it might slip off is that instability made physical, with a timescale attached to show the risk is real rather than theoretical. Fragile would miss the sense of being balanced on something.

A structure resting on one support that could fail is precarious in the literal sense, so the word fits.

**E) Nothing in the record suggests that a complete collapse is "imminent", though the century-scale trend is unmistakable.**

"Imminent" is a claim about timing, meaning very close at hand rather than merely likely eventually. The sentence uses the word carefully by denying nearness while affirming a long-run direction, which is a distinction scientists are usually at pains to preserve. Denying imminence is not denying the trend.

Separating what is close from what is coming is exactly the work this adjective does, so the sentence is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: The set turns on the difference between certainty and timing: tentative and imminent are hedged claims about knowledge and nearness, while ambiguous is a claim that the evidence itself points two ways. Test that last one against how much the researchers agree, since unanimity destroys it. For detrimental and precarious, look for a named mechanism of harm or a single support that could give way.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five sentences about working conditions and findings far below the surface. Decide whether each quoted word is used in the required sense.
statements: Pressure housings are "integral" to every deep-sea camera, since the electronics implode within minutes without them.
Food is "scarce" below a thousand metres, which is why so many animals there move slowly and grow late.
It is "plausible" that most bioluminescence serves defence, given how many species flash only once disturbed.
Red lighting can "mitigate" the disturbance a submersible causes, because many deep-water species cannot see that wavelength.
The chief scientist was "candid" about the failed dive, publishing the equipment log alongside the results that survived.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Pressure housings are "integral" to every deep-sea camera, since the electronics implode within minutes without them.**

"Integral" identifies a part without which the whole cannot function, as opposed to a useful accessory. The "since" clause proves necessity in the strongest available form: remove the housing and the instrument destroys itself. Essential would be a fair synonym, but integral adds the sense of being built into the design.

A component whose removal ends the device is integral in the exact sense, so the word is right.

**B) Food is "scarce" below a thousand metres, which is why so many animals there move slowly and grow late.**

"Scarce" means in short supply relative to need, and the sentence traces the consequences of that shortage into the animals' physiology. Slow movement and delayed growth are energy-saving responses, which is the biological signature of an environment where meals are rare. The evidence supports the label rather than restating it.

Short supply shown through the adaptations it forces is a strong use of the word, so the sentence holds.

**C) It is "plausible" that most bioluminescence serves defence, given how many species flash only once disturbed.**

"Plausible" claims reasonableness rather than proof, which is the right strength for an inference drawn from behaviour. Flashing on disturbance is consistent with a defensive function, though other explanations remain open, and the hedge preserves that openness. A stronger word would misrepresent what observation alone can establish.

A well-supported but unproven explanation is exactly what the adjective marks, so the usage is correct.

**D) Red lighting can "mitigate" the disturbance a submersible causes, because many deep-water species cannot see that wavelength.**

To "mitigate" is to lessen something harmful without claiming to remove it entirely. Red light reduces the visual disruption for many species, while noise, pressure waves and the vehicle itself still register, so partial relief is precisely what is offered. The modal "can" keeps the claim appropriately modest.

A measure that reduces but does not eliminate the disturbance is what the verb describes, so the sentence works.

**E) The chief scientist was "candid" about the failed dive, publishing the equipment log alongside the results that survived.**

"Candid" means frank in a way that exposes rather than protects the speaker. Releasing the equipment log from a failed dive invites scrutiny of the team's own preparation, which nobody is required to volunteer. Publishing the failure next to the salvaged findings is what turns an admission into an act of openness.

Evidence of one's own setback made public is candour in the fullest sense, so the word suits the scientist described.
tasks.solution_overview: Each word here is anchored by a clause that explains it, so read "since", "because" and "given how" as invitations to check the reasoning rather than skip it. Integral demands that removal break the system, scarce should show up in behaviour or price, and mitigate must stop short of promising a cure. Plausible and candid are about honesty of a kind: one about not overclaiming, the other about not concealing.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: A closing set of five sentences on industries in transition. Decide whether each quoted word is used in the sense the surrounding detail supports.
statements: The statistical office issued a "succinct" note on sector reclassification, filling three hundred pages with annexes and worked examples.
Analysts warned that the region's manufacturing base would "erode" gradually rather than disappear in one dramatic closure.
"Adverse" currency movements wiped out the margin on exports that had looked comfortable only a quarter earlier.
A long-range forecast stays "credible" only if its assumptions are published alongside the numbers it produces.
Retraining grants helped "exacerbate" the transition, easing thousands of workers into growing sectors within two years.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The statistical office issued a "succinct" note on sector reclassification, filling three hundred pages with annexes and worked examples.**

"Succinct" praises a text for saying what is needed and stopping, so length is the one thing it cannot tolerate. Three hundred pages of annexes and worked examples may be admirably thorough, but thoroughness and brevity are separate virtues. Comprehensive is the compliment the document has actually earned.

A three-hundred-page note cannot be brief whatever else it is, so the adjective is the wrong choice here.

**B) Analysts warned that the region's manufacturing base would "erode" gradually rather than disappear in one dramatic closure.**

To "erode" is to wear away slowly, and the metaphor carries its geological sense of loss that is barely visible from day to day. The sentence draws exactly that contrast, setting incremental decline against a single closure that everyone would notice. This is also why erosion is politically dangerous: there is no moment at which alarm is obviously due.

Slow attrition set explicitly against sudden collapse is what the verb names, so the usage is right.

**C) "Adverse" currency movements wiped out the margin on exports that had looked comfortable only a quarter earlier.**

"Adverse" means running against the interests of the party described, and it sits naturally in front of nouns such as conditions, weather or movements. The sentence demonstrates the harm rather than assuming it, since a comfortable margin has been erased in a single quarter. Keep it distinct from "averse", which would need a person and the preposition to.
