Both expressions are used in their conventional senses and point at the same expected recovery, so the sentence holds.
tasks.solution_overview: The false items in this set are built from phrasal verbs whose particles carry the meaning, so the test is whether the particle belongs. A market opening is filled, while a form or a blank is filled in, and lost competitive distance is gained or made up rather than simply made. The remaining phrases — deal a blow, stop short of, pick up — are fixed units used with their standard objects, and each fits the commercial situation described.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five lines from a methods discussion about evidence and peer review. Several phrases borrow a verb from a neighbouring idiom; decide which lines are intact.
statements: The team replicated the findings in a larger sample before publishing.
Studies with null results are less likely to see the light of day, which skews the literature.
The authors pulled attention to a bias that had gone unnoticed in earlier reviews.
Peer reviewers rose several objections to the statistical model.
The result should be handled with a pinch of salt until independent teams confirm it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The team replicated the findings in a larger sample before publishing.**

Findings are replicated, and replication is the technical term for repeating a study to see whether the same result appears; the phrase "replicate the findings" is used across every empirical discipline. A larger sample is the standard way to strengthen such a repetition.

The verb carries its precise methodological sense and the sample detail supports it, so the sentence is exactly what a methods section would say.

**B) Studies with null results are less likely to see the light of day, which skews the literature.**

To "see the light of day" is the fixed idiom for finally being published or made public, and unpublished research is one of its most common subjects. "Skew" is the right technical verb for a body of evidence tilted away from the truth by selective publication.

The idiom and the statistical term work together to describe publication bias in the usual way, so this line holds.

**C) The authors pulled attention to a bias that had gone unnoticed in earlier reviews.**

Attention is drawn to something, and the related phrases — call attention to, bring attention to — all use verbs of directing rather than of force. "Pull" belongs with physical effort, so it turns a scholarly act of pointing something out into a tug of war.

**Tip:** Draw attention to a problem; you can also draw a distinction and draw a conclusion, but never pull any of them.

The authors are highlighting an overlooked flaw, so the sentence should read "the authors drew attention to a bias."

**D) Peer reviewers rose several objections to the statistical model.**

Objections are raised, and raise is the transitive verb that takes an object; "rise" is intransitive and describes something going up by itself, as when temperatures rise or a share price rises. Because the reviewers are acting on the objections rather than watching them float upwards, the transitive form is required.

**Trap:** Raise and rise differ in grammar as well as meaning: if there is an object after the verb, it has to be raise.

The reviewers put forward criticisms of the model, so the correct wording is "peer reviewers raised several objections to the statistical model."

**E) The result should be handled with a pinch of salt until independent teams confirm it.**

The idiom is "take something with a pinch of salt," meaning to treat a claim with reserve; the version with a grain of salt is the common variant. "Handle" is a real verb of caution, as in handling a claim carefully, but it does not belong inside this fixed phrase, and the mixture leaves the idiom half-formed.

The advice being given is exactly the sceptical reception the original idiom names, so the sentence needs "the result should be taken with a pinch of salt."
highlights: handled with a pinch of salt
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these items swap the verb inside a phrase that most readers store whole, which is why they slip past on a first reading. Attention is drawn rather than pulled, objections are raised rather than risen, and scepticism is expressed by taking something with a pinch of salt. Check also whether the verb can take an object at all: some of the near-misses use an intransitive verb where a transitive one is required.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five lines from the management of a long, expensive engineering programme. One item changes the preposition a noun demands; decide which line that is.
statements: The programme ran over budget, and managers had to make a case for further funding.
Every extra year in flight sets new demands to the ageing power system.
Ground crews ran a series of checks before committing to the manoeuvre.
The agency struck a deal with a partner network to keep the antennas available.
Long-range operations of this kind push the limits of what ageing hardware can do.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The programme ran over budget, and managers had to make a case for further funding.**

A project "runs over budget" when spending exceeds the allocation, and one "makes a case for" something when arguing for it before a decision-maker; both are fixed. The preposition "for" introduces what is being argued in favour of, which here is additional money.

The overspend and the argument that follows from it are described in the phrases the register supplies, so the sentence is sound.

**B) Every extra year in flight sets new demands to the ageing power system.**

Demands are placed on or made on something, and the preposition "on" carries the image of a load pressing down on a system with limited capacity. "Set" belongs with targets, standards and deadlines, and "to" points at a recipient, so the pairing turns a growing burden into something handed over politely.

**Tip:** Place demands on a system, but set a target for it.

The hardware is being loaded more heavily as it ages, so the natural wording is "places new demands on the ageing power system."

**C) Ground crews ran a series of checks before committing to the manoeuvre.**

Checks and tests are run, and "run a series of checks" is the standard operational phrase for a sequence of verifications performed in order. "Commit to" is likewise the settled expression for locking in an irreversible decision.

Both phrases belong to operations language and the sequence they describe is the usual one, so the line holds.

**D) The agency struck a deal with a partner network to keep the antennas available.**

A deal is struck, in the same family as striking a bargain or striking an accord; the verb suggests an agreement concluded at a definite moment. The partner named after "with" is the second party the phrase requires.

The negotiated arrangement and its counterparty are expressed exactly as the idiom expects, so the sentence is idiomatic.

**E) Long-range operations of this kind push the limits of what ageing hardware can do.**

Limits and boundaries are pushed, and "push the limits of" is the settled phrase for operating at or beyond the edge of designed capability. The clause after "of" names the capability in question, which is the shape this phrase normally takes.

The strain on hardware working past its design life is precisely the situation the idiom describes, so the wording stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Programme management writing has a settled verb for each stage: budgets are overrun, cases are made, checks are run, deals are struck and limits are pushed. Demands, by contrast, are placed or made on something, and the preposition that follows is the detail worth checking here. Test each phrase by asking whether the noun is receiving a load or receiving a gift, since that distinction decides between on and to.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five sentences about competition, margins and the pricing decisions that follow. Decide whether each combination is the one commercial reporting uses.
statements: The platform captured market share by undercutting established sellers for two years.
Thin margins left the retailer little room to absorb higher freight costs.
Regulators are weighing whether the firm abused its dominant position.
The company passed the increase on to customers within a fortnight.
A long spell of discounting has eaten into profits across the sector.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The platform captured market share by undercutting established sellers for two years.**

Market share is captured, gained or won, and "capture market share" is the standard phrase for taking custom away from incumbents. "Undercut" is the precise verb for selling below a rival's price, which is the mechanism the sentence gives for that capture.

The pairing and the explanation of how the share was taken belong to the same commercial vocabulary, so the line is sound.

**B) Thin margins left the retailer little room to absorb higher freight costs.**

A firm "absorbs" a cost when it takes the hit itself instead of raising prices, and "thin margins" is the settled description of a narrow gap between cost and price. The two phrases explain each other, since it is the thinness of the margin that limits the capacity to absorb.

Both expressions are used in their normal commercial senses, so the sentence reads as a trade report would write it.

**C) Regulators are weighing whether the firm abused its dominant position.**

"Abuse a dominant position" is the term of art in competition law, distinct from merely holding one, which is not itself unlawful. "Weigh" is the standard verb for an authority considering a case before deciding.

The legal phrase is used with its exact technical force and the surrounding verb fits the procedural stage, so this line holds.

**D) The company passed the increase on to customers within a fortnight.**

Costs are "passed on to" the next party in the chain, and the phrase is the direct counterpart of absorbing them; the particle and the preposition together make the direction explicit. Customers are the usual endpoint of that transfer in retail pricing.

The sentence sends the cost outward rather than inward, which is exactly what the phrase is built to express, so the wording is right.

**E) A long spell of discounting has eaten into profits across the sector.**

To "eat into" savings, margins or profits is the fixed phrase for a gradual erosion of a financial cushion, and it takes a sustained cause rather than a single event. A long stretch of discounting is precisely that kind of slow drain.

The idiom, the timescale and the financial object all match, so the sentence needs no repair.
highlights: passed the increase on to customers
tasks.solution_overview: Competition reporting distinguishes carefully between who takes a cost and who hands it on, and these lines are built on that distinction. Share is captured or won, costs are absorbed by the firm or passed on to the buyer, a dominant position is abused, and profits are eaten into. Judge each item by asking whether the verb sends the money in the direction the sentence intends.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five lines from a monetary history written in a fairly figurative style. Metaphors are only allowed in their conventional shapes here; decide which lines respect that.
statements: Cheap credit and pent-up demand can kindle inflation long after the original shock has passed.
The finance ministry moved to stem the outflow of reserves before confidence broke.
Devaluation gave the export sector a shot in the leg, though imported inputs grew dearer.
Officials believed a modest rate rise would put the brake to the slide in the currency.
The episode set a precedent that later crisis managers were quick to cite.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Cheap credit and pent-up demand can kindle inflation long after the original shock has passed.**

In economic reporting the usual fire verbs with inflation are "stoke," "fuel" or "ignite"; those are the pairings readers expect for prices already under pressure. "Kindle" more often starts a small fire or an abstract interest, so with a macroeconomic process already under way it sounds less idiomatic than the stock alternatives.

**Tip:** Prefer fuel, stoke or ignite with inflation; reserve kindle mainly for interest and enthusiasm.

The sentence describes loose money feeding a rise in prices, so the natural wording expected here is "can stoke inflation long after the original shock has passed."

**B) The finance ministry moved to stem the outflow of reserves before confidence broke.**

To "stem" is to hold back a flow, and it pairs naturally with outflows, losses and tides; "stem the outflow" is the standard phrase for stopping money leaving a country or an institution. The clause about confidence supplies the crisis setting where that phrase belongs.

The metaphor of a flow being checked matches both the verb and the noun, so the sentence is written as monetary history should be.

**C) Devaluation gave the export sector a shot in the leg, though imported inputs grew dearer.**

The idiom for a sudden stimulus is "a shot in the arm," borrowed from an injection that revives a patient; the leg version collides with "a shot in the foot," which means self-inflicted damage. Because the two phrases point in opposite directions, the invented middle term leaves the reader unsure whether exporters were helped or harmed.

**Trap:** Anatomy matters in idioms: a shot in the arm revives, a shot in the foot wounds.

A cheaper currency plainly helped exporters here, so the sentence should read "gave the export sector a shot in the arm."

**D) Officials believed a modest rate rise would put the brake to the slide in the currency.**

The fixed expression is "put the brakes on something," with the plural noun and the preposition "on"; the shorter alternative is simply to slow or check the slide. Changing the preposition breaks the driving image, since brakes are applied to a moving thing rather than handed to it.

The intention described is to halt a fall in the exchange rate, so the idiomatic version is "would put the brakes on the slide in the currency."

**E) The episode set a precedent that later crisis managers were quick to cite.**

A precedent is set, and the phrase belongs with setting a standard or an example; once set, a precedent is then followed or cited, which is exactly the sequence the relative clause describes. Nothing in the sentence disturbs that shape.

The two halves use the conventional verbs on either side of the noun, so this line is idiomatic as it stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Figurative economics still runs on fixed forms: the fire metaphor for inflation, the medical metaphor for stimulus and the driving metaphor for slowing a market each favour conventional wording. Ask whether the verb or noun in front of you is the usual member of that metaphor family or a near-synonym from the same field. A word that would pass in literal prose is often the weaker choice once the phrase has hardened into an idiom.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five lines weighing how much a behavioural pilot can prove. Two of them alter a phrase so lightly that the sentence still scans; decide which ones.
statements: The default option exerts a quiet influence that most participants never notice.
Officials were careful not to overstate the case for a nationwide rollout.
Critics say enthusiasm has run ahead of the evidence and that officials have jumped at conclusions.
The trial ran into obstacles, and the unit had to cut its losses short.
The evidence stands up to scrutiny even after the sample was reweighted.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The default option exerts a quiet influence that most participants never notice.**

Influence is exerted, exercised or wielded, and "exert influence" is the formal choice when the effect is indirect rather than commanded. "Quiet" fits the frame neatly, since an influence can be described as subtle, considerable or decisive without disturbing the phrase.

A default that shapes behaviour without anyone noticing is exactly the kind of pressure this verb names, so the sentence stands.

**B) Officials were careful not to overstate the case for a nationwide rollout.**

To "overstate the case" is the settled phrase for claiming more than the evidence supports, and it sits alongside making the case and stating the case; the preposition "for" then introduces the proposal being argued. Caution about extrapolating from a pilot is the classic context for that warning.

The phrase and its preposition are both conventional, and they describe the officials' restraint precisely, so the line holds.

**C) Critics say enthusiasm has run ahead of the evidence and that officials have jumped at conclusions.**

The idiom for reasoning too fast is "jump to conclusions," where the preposition marks the destination reached in a single leap. "Jump at" is a real phrase, but it means to accept something eagerly, as in jumping at an offer, so the substitution turns hasty reasoning into keen acceptance.

**Trap:** Jump at an opportunity, but jump to a conclusion — the preposition changes the whole charge.

The criticism is that officials reasoned too quickly from thin evidence, so the wording should be "officials have jumped to conclusions."

**D) The trial ran into obstacles, and the unit had to cut its losses short.**

Two idioms have been folded together: "cut your losses" means to stop investing in something failing, while "cut something short" means to end it earlier than planned. Each would work here on its own, but the merged version leaves the object of "cut" doing double duty and belongs to neither pattern.

The unit abandoned a failing trial rather than truncating an event, so the clean version is "the unit had to cut its losses."

**E) The evidence stands up to scrutiny even after the sample was reweighted.**

To "stand up to scrutiny" is the fixed phrase for evidence that survives close examination, and it belongs with withstanding pressure and bearing examination. Reweighting the sample is precisely the kind of test that phrase anticipates.

The idiom is used with its usual object and a plausible robustness check, so the sentence is sound as written.
tasks.solution_overview: At this level the alterations are a single preposition or a single extra word, so the whole sentence still reads smoothly and only the phrase itself gives the error away. Recall the standard forms — jump to conclusions, cut your losses, exert influence, stand up to scrutiny — and compare them element by element with what is on the page. Where an idiom has absorbed a word from a neighbouring idiom, the meaning usually blurs slightly, and that blur is the clue.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five lines about funding long-horizon research and the risks nobody wants to own. Only one phrase here is untouched; the others have absorbed a word from somewhere else.
statements: Funding bodies are reluctant to underwrite research whose payoff lies decades away.
Grant committees make a judgement call, yet few members want to bear the brunt for a failure.
Sceptics say the projections do not hold up water when tested against the last decade of observations.
Field seasons are short, so teams must take the most of every calm week.
Without new funding, the monitoring network will slowly run to a halt.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Funding bodies are reluctant to underwrite research whose payoff lies decades away.**

To "underwrite" a project is to guarantee its costs and accept the downside if it fails, which is the exact financial relationship between a funder and a long-shot programme. "Payoff" is the standard companion noun for the eventual return on such a commitment.

The verb names the risk-bearing role precisely and the time horizon explains the reluctance, so the sentence is idiomatic.

**B) Grant committees make a judgement call, yet few members want to bear the brunt for a failure.**

The phrase is "bear the brunt of" something, where the brunt is the heaviest part of an impact and "of" names the impact itself. Blame, by contrast, is taken or carried for an outcome, so the sentence has borrowed the preposition from one phrase and the noun from another.

**Tip:** Bear the brunt of a shock, but take the blame for a mistake.

The members are avoiding responsibility for a bad decision, so the sentence needs "few members want to take the blame for a failure."

**C) Sceptics say the projections do not hold up water when tested against the last decade of observations.**

English has "hold water," meaning an argument that survives examination, and "hold up," meaning something that remains valid under pressure; both are correct on their own. Combining them produces a phrase that reads like a slip of the tongue, because "hold water" is a closed idiom that admits no extra particle.

The claim is that the projections fail when checked against data, so the clean version is "the projections do not hold water when tested against the last decade of observations."

**D) Field seasons are short, so teams must take the most of every calm week.**

The idiom is "make the most of" an opportunity, and it belongs with making the best of a situation; "take" appears in the neighbouring phrase take advantage of, which is why the two get crossed. Because make governs the superlative noun in this expression, swapping in take leaves the phrase incomplete.

Short weather windows are exactly the opportunity the original idiom is used about, so the sentence should read "teams must make the most of every calm week."

**E) Without new funding, the monitoring network will slowly run to a halt.**

Something "grinds to a halt" when it slows to a stop under friction, while "run out of" describes a supply that has been exhausted; the sentence has merged the verb of the second into the frame of the first. Since a network starved of money slows gradually, the grinding image is the one the sentence wants.

**Trap:** Grind to a halt and run out of money are neighbours in meaning but never share a verb.

The slow stoppage described here is what the settled idiom names, so the line needs "the monitoring network will slowly grind to a halt."
tasks.solution_overview: Every false line here is a hybrid of two correct expressions, so the repair is to decide which of the two the sentence actually needs. Bear the brunt of damage against take the blame for a failure, hold water against stand up, make the most of an opportunity against take advantage of it, and grind to a halt against run out of money. Naming both parents of the blend is the quickest route to the version English would print.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five lines on industrial subsidies, sourcing risk and currency management. Judge each phrase against the version a specialist would write.
statements: Subsidy programmes on this scale inevitably invite scrutiny from trading partners.
The ministry earmarked funds for plants that agreed to train local engineers.
Officials say the strategy will bring fruit only after a decade of steady investment.
A single-source supplier leaves the whole sector hostage to one plant's fortunes.
Firms that hedge their currency exposure sleep more soundly when rates swing.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Subsidy programmes on this scale inevitably invite scrutiny from trading partners.**

Scrutiny is invited, attracted or come under, and "invite scrutiny" is the standard way to say that an action makes examination inevitable without anyone requesting it. Trading partners are the natural source named after "from."

The phrase carries exactly the sense of unintended but predictable attention that the sentence needs, so it holds as written.

**B) The ministry earmarked funds for plants that agreed to train local engineers.**

To "earmark funds for" a purpose is the settled budgetary phrase for reserving money in advance of spending it, and the preposition "for" introduces the intended use. The conditional clause about training is the kind of qualifying condition such allocations usually carry.

The verb belongs to public finance and is used with its usual preposition and object, so the line is sound.

**C) Officials say the strategy will bring fruit only after a decade of steady investment.**

The idiom is "bear fruit," where bear keeps its old sense of producing a crop, exactly as a tree bears fruit; the phrase names results that appear long after the effort. "Bring" belongs to a different family, as in bringing benefits or bringing relief, and it cannot enter this fixed expression.

**Tip:** A plan bears fruit; only the harvest is brought anywhere.

The sentence is about delayed returns on long investment, which is precisely the idiom's territory, so it should read "the strategy will bear fruit only after a decade of steady investment."

**D) A single-source supplier leaves the whole sector hostage to one plant's fortunes.**

The phrase "hostage to" describes a party whose fate is controlled by something outside its power, as in the fuller expression hostage to fortune. Concentrated sourcing creates exactly that dependence, and "leave someone hostage to" is the standard construction.

The metaphor of captivity fits the dependence being described and appears in its conventional form, so the sentence is idiomatic.

**E) Firms that hedge their currency exposure sleep more soundly when rates swing.**

Exposure is hedged, and the phrase "hedge currency exposure" is the technical term for using contracts to limit losses from exchange rate moves. "Swing" is the usual verb for rates moving sharply in both directions.

Both the finance term and its companion verb are the standard ones, so the sentence reads as a treasury report would put it.
tasks.solution_overview: Specialist vocabulary carries most of the weight in this set: funds are earmarked, scrutiny is invited, exposure is hedged, and a dependent party is left hostage to another's fortunes. The one weak link is an agricultural metaphor whose verb is fixed by long use, so a sensible-sounding alternative still rings false. Ask in each case whether the phrase is the one the field uses or merely a reasonable paraphrase of it.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five lines from a cautious assessment of working-time reform. The phrasing is deliberately idiomatic; decide whether each expression is in its accepted form.
statements: The pilot lent weight to the argument that shorter hours need not cost output.
Employers who resisted at first came round once the retention figures arrived.
Consultants warn against reading too much into a single year of data.
The scheme gathered momentum as larger firms signed up.
Sceptics remain unconvinced, arguing that the trials cherry-picked willing participants.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The pilot lent weight to the argument that shorter hours need not cost output.**

Evidence "lends weight to" a claim, and the phrase pictures support being added to one side of a scale; add weight to is the common variant. An argument is the standard object, and the that-clause spells out which argument is being supported.

The verb, the noun and the preposition all appear in their usual positions, so the sentence is well formed.

**B) Employers who resisted at first came round once the retention figures arrived.**

To "come round" is the settled phrasal verb for someone who changes an initially hostile view, and it often appears with a trigger introduced by "once" or "after." Retention data is precisely the sort of evidence that produces such a change of mind.

The phrase carries the sense of gradual conversion the sentence needs, so the wording stands.

**C) Consultants warn against reading too much into a single year of data.**

To "read too much into" something is the fixed phrase for over-interpreting thin evidence, and "warn against" takes a gerund in exactly the way the sentence uses it. A single year of results is the classic object of that caution.

Both expressions keep their conventional grammar and combine into ordinary analytical advice, so the line holds.

**D) The scheme gathered momentum as larger firms signed up.**

Momentum is gathered, gained or built, and "gather momentum" is the usual choice when growth feeds on itself; the same phrase serves campaigns, movements and recoveries. Firms joining in sequence is the mechanism that supplies the momentum.

The idiom is used with an appropriate subject and a cause that explains the acceleration, so the sentence is sound.

**E) Sceptics remain unconvinced, arguing that the trials cherry-picked willing participants.**

To "cherry-pick" is to select only the favourable cases, and it is the standard verb for the methodological complaint being made here. Willing volunteers are the textbook example of a sample chosen for a flattering result.

The verb names the selection bias exactly, and the criticism it supports is coherent, so this line needs no repair.
tasks.solution_overview: Idiomatic writing is not the same as loose writing, and every phrase here is a recognised unit with a settled shape. Evidence lends weight to an argument, an opponent comes round, an analyst reads too much into thin data, a movement gathers momentum, and a biased selection is cherry-picked. Check the particle or preposition attached to each one, since that is where an otherwise fluent sentence usually goes wrong.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: A final mixed set from corporate reporting: recovery, concealment, failed deals and stalled negotiations. Two phrases have been rebuilt out of the wrong parts; decide which.
statements: The report paints a picture of an industry that has lost its footing and cannot find back its balance.
Executives were accused of sweeping the losses beneath the carpet until the auditors arrived.
The merger fell through when the competition authority refused to clear it.
Talks broke down over pensions and resumed only after mediation.
The board took stock of a difficult year before setting new targets.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The report paints a picture of an industry that has lost its footing and cannot find back its balance.**

Balance is regained or recovered once it has been lost, and English has no phrase "find back"; the pattern with back attaches to win back, claw back or get back, none of which takes balance in this figurative sense. The first half of the sentence is fine, since an industry can certainly lose its footing.

**Tip:** Lose your footing, then regain your balance — the recovery verb is regain, not find.

The industry is struggling to steady itself after a shock, so the natural wording is "cannot regain its balance."

**B) Executives were accused of sweeping the losses beneath the carpet until the auditors arrived.**

The idiom is "sweep something under the carpet," or under the rug in American usage, and the preposition is part of the fixed phrase. "Beneath" is a perfectly good synonym in ordinary description, but idioms resist synonym substitution, and swapping it in makes the expression sound translated.

The accusation is straightforward concealment of losses, so the sentence should read "sweeping the losses under the carpet until the auditors arrived."

**C) The merger fell through when the competition authority refused to clear it.**

A deal, a sale or a merger "falls through" when it collapses before completion, and the phrase is the standard one in corporate reporting. "Clear" is likewise the technical verb for a regulator approving a transaction.

Both expressions are used in their usual senses and the refusal explains the collapse, so the sentence holds.

**D) Talks broke down over pensions and resumed only after mediation.**

Negotiations "break down" when they collapse in disagreement, and the preposition "over" introduces the sticking point; talks are then resumed or restarted. The pairing with mediation is exactly the sequence the phrase usually reports.

Every element belongs to the standard vocabulary of industrial disputes, so the line is idiomatic.

**E) The board took stock of a difficult year before setting new targets.**

To "take stock of" a situation is the settled phrase for reviewing where things stand before deciding what comes next, and it survives from the literal counting of inventory. Setting targets is the natural follow-on action once that review is complete.

The idiom is used in its reflective sense with a suitable object, so the sentence closes the set on solid ground.
highlights: sweeping the losses beneath the carpet
tasks.solution_overview: The last set mixes recovery and concealment metaphors with the plain phrasal verbs of deal-making. Balance is regained rather than found back, and inconvenient facts are swept under the carpet rather than beneath it, so a single substituted word is enough to break each image. The remaining lines use fall through, break down and take stock in their standard senses, where the particle carries the whole meaning.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five claims about formal vocabulary used in reports on working time, research findings and logistics. Decide whether each description of meaning or usage is accurate.
statements: In a report on the four-day week, "subsequent" surveys are the rounds carried out before the trial began.
"Substantiate" is the verb a policy brief needs when a claimed productivity gain has to be backed with evidence rather than simply asserted.
A pricing study that "corroborates" an earlier finding has shown that finding to be mistaken.
A ministry that calls its emissions target "tentative" is announcing a figure that is already fixed in law.
When a supply-chain review says a distributor has "consolidated" its warehouses, it means the distributor has spread its stock across many new sites.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on the four-day week, "subsequent" surveys are the rounds carried out before the trial began.**

"Subsequent" points forward: it labels whatever follows the event just mentioned, so subsequent surveys are the follow-up rounds run after the trial has begun. The rounds carried out beforehand would be the prior or preliminary ones, and a report that mixed the two would reverse its own timeline.

**Tip:** Read "subsequent" as "coming next" and the direction stays fixed.

Nothing that precedes the trial can be subsequent to it, so the rounds described here are the prior surveys under another word's name.

**B) "Substantiate" is the verb a policy brief needs when a claimed productivity gain has to be backed with evidence rather than simply asserted.**

"Substantiate" means to support a claim with evidence, which is exactly the obligation a brief takes on when it asserts that a shorter week raised output. Repeating the claim in more confident language is assertion, not substantiation, and formal writing keeps the two apart. The verb belongs to audits, reports and academic prose, where evidence is expected to be produced rather than promised.

Backing a claim with evidence is the whole content of the verb, and that is the obligation this brief is described as meeting.

**C) A pricing study that "corroborates" an earlier finding has shown that finding to be mistaken.**

To corroborate is to confirm: a second study corroborates an earlier finding when its results point the same way and add weight to it. Showing the earlier finding to be mistaken is the opposite move, and formal writing reaches for "contradict" or "refute" there. Research prose depends on the distinction, since corroboration builds a case while contradiction dismantles one.

**Trap:** The word sounds severe, but it always supports rather than attacks.

Corroboration adds weight to the earlier finding rather than knocking it down, so a study that showed the finding mistaken would be said to contradict it.

**D) A ministry that calls its emissions target "tentative" is announcing a figure that is already fixed in law.**

"Tentative" marks something provisional and open to revision, which is why draft figures and unconfirmed dates attract the word. A target already fixed in law would be called binding, statutory or definitive, and no ministry would hedge a legal commitment with an adjective that invites change. The register matters as much as the meaning: tentative signals caution to the reader of a formal announcement.

An adjective that advertises room for revision cannot describe a figure settled in statute, so the target announced here would have to be called binding.

**E) When a supply-chain review says a distributor has "consolidated" its warehouses, it means the distributor has spread its stock across many new sites.**

"Consolidate" means to bring parts together into a single, stronger whole, so consolidating warehouses means closing several sites and concentrating stock in fewer of them. Spreading stock across many new locations is dispersal or diversification, the opposite operation. Logistics reporting favours the verb precisely because it signals fewer and larger nodes rather than more of them.

Consolidation leaves fewer sites holding more stock, so reading it as dispersal turns the review's report of the distributor upside down.
tasks.solution_overview: Each item here turns on the direction a formal verb or adjective points: forward or backward in time, towards support or towards attack, towards concentration or towards dispersal. Test each one by substituting a plain-English paraphrase and asking whether the sentence still describes the same event. Where the paraphrase reverses the picture, the definition offered has been turned around.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Five judgements about formal words that recur in contracts, regulatory notices and research summaries. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: A clause described as "ambiguous" in a trade contract is one that can be read in only a single way.
A finance ministry that "allocates" forty million to rail upgrades has set that sum aside for a stated purpose.
In a research summary, a "caveat" is a guarantee that the findings will hold in every market studied.
"Deem" is the formal verb for treating something as having a particular status, as when a regulator deems a supplier compliant.
Emissions that are "offset" by a reforestation programme have been doubled rather than counterbalanced.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A clause described as "ambiguous" in a trade contract is one that can be read in only a single way.**

"Ambiguous" describes wording that supports more than one reading, which is why lawyers hunt for it in contracts and courts have to resolve it. A clause open to only one reading is unambiguous, plain or unequivocal, and those are the adjectives a drafter aims for. The whole risk the word names is that two parties can each read the same line differently.

A single available reading is the mark of unambiguous drafting, which leaves this description of the clause attached to the wrong adjective.

**B) A finance ministry that "allocates" forty million to rail upgrades has set that sum aside for a stated purpose.**

To allocate is to assign a resource to a designated use, and budget documents use the verb because it records a decision about destination rather than about spending itself. The money is earmarked for rail upgrades and cannot be quietly redirected without a further decision. Nothing in the verb implies the cash has already been paid out, only that its purpose has been fixed.

Earmarking money for a named purpose is all the budget verb claims, and that is what the ministry has done here.

**C) In a research summary, a "caveat" is a guarantee that the findings will hold in every market studied.**

A "caveat" is a warning or limiting condition attached to a statement, the sentence that begins "these results hold only if…" and narrows what has just been claimed. A guarantee does the reverse by widening confidence, and careful research writing would call that an assurance. Readers scan for caveats precisely because they mark where a finding stops travelling.

**Trap:** A caveat restricts a claim; it never underwrites one.

A note that narrows a finding cannot at the same time guarantee it, so the summary's caveat is being read as its own opposite.

**D) "Deem" is the formal verb for treating something as having a particular status, as when a regulator deems a supplier compliant.**

"Deem" is a high-register verb meaning to regard or treat something as being of a certain kind, and regulatory language leans on it because the judgement itself creates the status. A supplier deemed compliant is treated as compliant for the purposes of the rule, whatever a later inspection might show. Plain speech would say "count as" or "consider," but formal notices keep the shorter Latinate verb.

Conferring a status by judgement is the work this verb does in regulatory prose, which is just how the finding of compliance operates.

**E) Emissions that are "offset" by a reforestation programme have been doubled rather than counterbalanced.**

To offset something is to balance it with an equal and opposite quantity, so offset emissions are cancelled out on the ledger rather than increased. Doubling is amplification, which is what the word deliberately excludes. Climate and accounting prose both rely on the balancing sense, since an offset only makes sense against a debit.

Offsetting cancels a quantity out rather than multiplying it, so the arithmetic in this account of the reforestation programme runs the wrong way.
tasks.solution_overview: Formal vocabulary often carries a built-in limit or reservation, and these items test whether you can hear it. Ask whether the word narrows a claim, sets money or status aside, or balances one quantity against another, and check that the definition offered keeps that function intact. A definition that turns a limiting word into a guarantee has changed its job.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Five statements about formal adjectives and nouns that appear in policy papers and technical reports. Decide whether each statement describes the word correctly.
statements: A subsidy that "alleviates" fuel poverty has made the problem sharper for the households receiving it.
Risks called "inherent" in a supply chain are ones bolted on from outside and easily removed.
Calling a stable power supply a "prerequisite" for chip fabrication means the supply must be in place before fabrication can proceed.
When a statute leaves a decision to the regulator's "discretion," the regulator may judge each case on its own merits.
Describing the collapse in global air traffic during the pandemic as "unprecedented" claims that nothing comparable had happened before.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A subsidy that "alleviates" fuel poverty has made the problem sharper for the households receiving it.**

"Alleviate" means to make something painful or burdensome less severe; it eases a problem without necessarily solving it. A measure that sharpened hardship would be said to aggravate or exacerbate it, and policy evaluations keep those verbs strictly apart when they report effects. The whole point of a fuel subsidy is relief, which is the sense the verb carries.

Relief rather than aggravation is what the verb reports, so a subsidy that sharpened hardship would have to be said to exacerbate fuel poverty.

**B) Risks called "inherent" in a supply chain are ones bolted on from outside and easily removed.**

"Inherent" describes a property that belongs to something by its nature and cannot be detached from it, such as the exposure that comes with relying on a single overseas supplier. Risks bolted on from outside are external, incidental or imported, and they can be removed without changing the system itself. The adjective is chosen in formal analysis precisely to mark what cannot be engineered away.

**Tip:** Inherent risk is built in; external risk is added on.

A risk that can simply be unbolted was never inherent in the supply chain, which is where this description parts company with the adjective.

**C) Calling a stable power supply a "prerequisite" for chip fabrication means the supply must be in place before fabrication can proceed.**

A "prerequisite" is a condition that has to be satisfied first, so naming stable power a prerequisite places it earlier in the chain than fabrication itself. The word carries genuine sequence and necessity, unlike "advantage" or "bonus," which describe something merely helpful. Technical documents use it when a project cannot begin at all until the condition is met.

Necessity plus sequence is what the noun packs in, and both are present in this reading of what chip fabrication requires.

**D) When a statute leaves a decision to the regulator's "discretion," the regulator may judge each case on its own merits.**

"Discretion" is the freedom to decide according to one's own judgement within a granted power, which is why statutes use it when they want flexible rather than mechanical enforcement. Where no judgement is permitted, drafting says the regulator "shall" act and the duty becomes mandatory. Leaving a matter to discretion therefore invites case-by-case reasoning rather than a fixed formula.

Case-by-case judgement is the freedom the statute hands over, so this reading of the regulator's position is right.

**E) Describing the collapse in global air traffic during the pandemic as "unprecedented" claims that nothing comparable had happened before.**

"Unprecedented" means without precedent: no earlier instance of the same kind is on record. Applied to a collapse in air traffic, it makes a strong historical claim rather than merely reporting that the fall was large. Careful writers reserve it for genuine firsts because the word cannot be softened by degree, which is why "very unprecedented" reads so badly.

A claim that nothing comparable has happened before is what the adjective puts on the page, and that is just how the collapse is being described.
tasks.solution_overview: These five words are chosen for what they claim about the world: whether a problem eases or sharpens, whether a property is built in or bolted on, what has to be in place first, how much freedom a decision-maker keeps, and how strong a historical claim is being made. Name the opposite of each word, then ask whether the sentence has quietly described that opposite instead. Where the opposite fits better, the description has been turned around.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five short definitions of formal terms drawn from regulation, economics and public reporting. Decide whether each definition matches the word.
statements: A rule that "compels" exporters to file customs data still leaves them free to skip the filing when it is inconvenient.
An "incentive" in policy design is something that makes a chosen action more attractive to the people it targets.
In economic analysis, a "marginal" change is the effect of one additional unit rather than the total effect.
A report that "omits" the pilot regions has left them out of its account.
A tribunal that "nullifies" an export licence has stripped that licence of legal force.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A rule that "compels" exporters to file customs data still leaves them free to skip the filing when it is inconvenient.**

"Compel" is one of the strongest obligation verbs in formal English: it removes choice and leaves the party with a duty rather than an option. A rule that permitted exporters to skip filing would be described as encouraging or inviting them to file, and drafters choose those weaker verbs deliberately. Regulatory language is graded, and readers are expected to hear the difference between may, should and must.

A duty that may be skipped when convenient is no longer compulsion, so the rule described here would be reaching for a far weaker verb.

**B) An "incentive" in policy design is something that makes a chosen action more attractive to the people it targets.**

An "incentive" works on motivation: it changes the pay-off attached to an action so that the target group has a reason to choose it. Tax credits for insulation and bonuses for early filing are typical instances, and none of them forces anyone's hand. Policy writing separates incentives from mandates for exactly this reason, since one persuades and the other compels.

Changing how attractive an action looks is the mechanism the noun names, and that is what the definition credits it with.

**C) In economic analysis, a "marginal" change is the effect of one additional unit rather than the total effect.**

In economics "marginal" is a technical adjective about increments: marginal cost is the cost of producing one more unit, and marginal benefit the gain from consuming one more. The everyday sense of "minor" survives elsewhere, but analytical prose keeps the incremental meaning in view. Reading a marginal figure as a total is one of the commonest misreadings of an economics table.

**Tip:** In analysis, marginal means "one more," not "barely worth noticing."

The increment rather than the total is what the technical adjective picks out, which is the reading offered here.

**D) A report that "omits" the pilot regions has left them out of its account.**

"Omit" means to leave something out, whether by oversight or by choice, and formal reporting uses it because it states the gap without accusing anyone of concealment. If the pilot regions are absent from the tables, they have been omitted. The stronger verbs "suppress" or "withhold" would carry an implication of deliberate hiding that this neutral word avoids.

Leaving the pilot regions out of the account is all the verb reports, and the definition asks nothing more of it.

**E) A tribunal that "nullifies" an export licence has stripped that licence of legal force.**

To "nullify" is to make something void, so a nullified licence has no legal effect and cannot be relied on afterwards. The verb belongs with "invalidate" and "annul" rather than with "suspend," which merely pauses an instrument that remains alive. Legal writing needs the harder word when an authority wipes out force rather than freezing it.

Wiping out legal force rather than pausing it is the tribunal's act as this verb describes it, so the definition lands.
tasks.solution_overview: Obligation, motivation and legal force are the themes running through this set, and each word sits at a particular strength on that scale. Check whether the definition preserves the strength of the original: an obligation that becomes optional, or a small change that becomes a total one, has drifted. The technical economic sense of one adjective is also worth separating from its everyday sense.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal verbs used when rules tighten, ease or make matters worse. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Mitigate" is the formal verb for making a harm less severe, as when new sea defences mitigate flood damage to a coastal port.
A contract that "stipulates" quarterly audits sets those audits down as a required condition of the agreement.
When a law "mandates" recycled content in packaging, it makes that content compulsory rather than voluntary.
A central bank that "curtails" its bond purchases has cut them back.
Tariffs that "exacerbate" a semiconductor shortage make an already difficult situation worse.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Mitigate" is the formal verb for making a harm less severe, as when new sea defences mitigate flood damage to a coastal port.**

"Mitigate" reduces the severity of something bad without claiming to remove it, which is why climate and risk documents pair it with damage, impact and loss. Sea defences do not stop storms; they limit what the storms cost, and that partial relief is the sense the verb was made for. Its register is firmly formal, the written counterpart of everyday phrases such as "take the edge off."

Limiting a harm rather than erasing it is the work the sea-defence example calls for, so the account of the verb is sound.

**B) A contract that "stipulates" quarterly audits sets those audits down as a required condition of the agreement.**

To "stipulate" is to state something explicitly as a condition of an agreement, so a stipulated audit is not a suggestion but a term the parties are bound by. The verb belongs to contracts and regulations rather than conversation, where "say" or "put in" would do the same job less precisely. Its force comes from the fact that a stipulation can be enforced.

A binding term written into the agreement is what a stipulation creates, and that is where the quarterly audits now stand.

**C) When a law "mandates" recycled content in packaging, it makes that content compulsory rather than voluntary.**

"Mandate" as a verb makes something obligatory by authority, so mandated recycled content is a legal floor that producers must reach. A voluntary target would be described as recommended, encouraged or aspirational, and the contrast between the two is a staple of environmental policy debate. The noun sense, an authority to act, shares the same root idea of a command.

Obligation by authority is the core of the verb, and that is the effect the packaging law is described as having.

**D) A central bank that "curtails" its bond purchases has cut them back.**

"Curtail" means to cut short or reduce in scope, and monetary policy reporting uses it for a deliberate scaling back of an ongoing programme. A bank curtailing purchases is still buying, just less, which distinguishes the verb from "halt" or "terminate." Its formality suits official commentary, where "cut back" would sound too conversational.

Scaling a programme back while keeping it alive is the sense in play for these bond purchases, so the account holds.

**E) Tariffs that "exacerbate" a semiconductor shortage make an already difficult situation worse.**

"Exacerbate" means to make an existing problem more severe, and it needs that pre-existing problem to attach itself to. A shortage already under way that deepens when tariffs raise input costs is the textbook shape for the verb. Formal analysis prefers it to "make worse" because it signals aggravation of a known condition rather than the creation of a new one.

The shortage was already under way and the tariffs deepen it, which is the aggravation pattern this verb names.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is built from verbs of intervention: some soften a harm, some create a duty, some shrink an activity and one deepens a problem. Read each sentence for the direction of travel, then ask whether a plain paraphrase such as "make worse" or "cut back" fits the same slot. Consistent direction between verb and paraphrase is the signal that the account is sound.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Five descriptions of formal verbs and adjectives used when writers assign causes, set conditions or support an argument. Decide whether each description is right.
statements: "Attribute" is the verb an economist needs when assigning a rise in output to a particular cause, as in attributing higher yields to improved logistics.
To say that shared standards "underpin" the trading system is to say that they weaken its foundations.
A survey question designed to "elicit" honest answers is one intended to suppress responses.
Saying that the evidence "warrants" further investigation means the evidence rules such investigation out.
Funding described as "contingent" on a successful audit will be released only if the audit is satisfactory.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Attribute" is the verb an economist needs when assigning a rise in output to a particular cause, as in attributing higher yields to improved logistics.**

"Attribute" links an outcome to a cause, and the formal pattern is to attribute something to something else, which is why analysts attribute a yield increase to better logistics rather than merely noting the two together. The verb states a causal judgement while remaining more cautious than "prove," so it suits writing that must argue rather than assert. Its plainer cousin "put down to" carries the same idea in a much lower register.

Linking the yield rise to a named cause is the move the verb makes, so this description of the economist's usage is right.

**B) To say that shared standards "underpin" the trading system is to say that they weaken its foundations.**

"Underpin" is a construction metaphor: to underpin something is to support it from below, so shared standards that underpin trade are holding the system up. Weakening the foundations is the work of "undermine," a verb that looks similar but digs away rather than props up. Formal prose keeps the pair distinct because a single letter changes an argument's direction.

**Trap:** Underpin supports; undermine erodes. The two are opposites, not variants.

Standards that hold the trading system up cannot be weakening its foundations; that reading has quietly substituted "undermine."

**C) A survey question designed to "elicit" honest answers is one intended to suppress responses.**

To "elicit" is to draw something out, whether a response, an admission or a reaction, so a question designed to elicit honest answers is engineered to bring them into the open. Suppressing responses is the opposite intention and would be described as deterring or discouraging them. Research methodology uses the verb constantly, since instrument design is largely the art of eliciting what people actually think.

A question built to draw honest answers out is doing the reverse of suppressing them, so this account of the design fails.

**D) Saying that the evidence "warrants" further investigation means the evidence rules such investigation out.**

When evidence "warrants" an action it justifies it: there is now sufficient ground for the step to be taken. The verb is a favourite of formal recommendations because it stops short of demanding while clearly licensing. Ruling investigation out would call for "precludes" or "does not justify," which sit at the far end of the same scale.

Warranting an investigation licenses it, so evidence described this way is inviting the further work rather than closing it off.

**E) Funding described as "contingent" on a successful audit will be released only if the audit is satisfactory.**

"Contingent" makes one thing depend on another, and the collocation "contingent on" flags a condition that has not yet been satisfied. Funding contingent on a successful audit therefore remains uncommitted until the auditor reports favourably. Grant agreements prefer the adjective to a phrase such as "only if it works out" because it makes the dependency an enforceable term.

Money held back until the audit reports well is the dependency the adjective sets up, so the account of the funding is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Most of these words describe a relation rather than an action: cause to effect, foundation to structure, question to answer, evidence to next step, or money to condition. Picture the relation the word sets up and check that the description keeps it pointing the same way. Where a supporting word has been given a destructive sense, the reversal is the error.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five statements about hedging and precision in academic register, taken from research summaries and statistical reporting. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: In a briefing note, the "salient" features of a reshoring proposal are the ones that stand out as most significant for the decision at hand.
Calling a rival explanation "plausible" asserts that it has been proved correct.
"Provisional" trade figures published a month after a quarter ends are expected to change once fuller data arrives.
In economic statistics, "aggregate" demand refers to the demand of one individual household considered in isolation.
A research council that "disseminates" its findings is spreading them to a wider audience.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a briefing note, the "salient" features of a reshoring proposal are the ones that stand out as most significant for the decision at hand.**

"Salient" marks what stands out from the surrounding detail, and in professional writing it points to the features that matter for the decision rather than merely the ones that are interesting. A briefing note has to compress, so naming the salient points is a claim about relevance and prominence together. The everyday equivalent, "the main things," loses the sense of something projecting from the background.

Prominence and decision-relevance are both carried by the adjective, which is how the briefing note's salient features should be read.

**B) Calling a rival explanation "plausible" asserts that it has been proved correct.**

"Plausible" sits low on the certainty scale: it says an explanation is credible and worth entertaining, not that it has been established. Proof would be reported with "demonstrated," "confirmed" or "verified," and reviewers notice when those words are used for evidence that only reaches plausibility. The adjective is a hedge, which is precisely why cautious authors reach for it.

**Tip:** Plausible means "could be true," never "has been shown true."

Credibility is as far as the adjective reaches, so calling the rival explanation plausible leaves it well short of proved.

**C) "Provisional" trade figures published a month after a quarter ends are expected to change once fuller data arrives.**

"Provisional" figures are published on the understanding that they are incomplete and subject to revision, which is standard practice for early estimates. The word protects the statistician and warns the reader in a single adjective, and later releases are labelled revised or final. Expecting movement in the numbers is therefore part of what the label communicates.

The label exists to warn that the numbers will move, so expecting revision in these early trade figures is reading it correctly.

**D) In economic statistics, "aggregate" demand refers to the demand of one individual household considered in isolation.**

"Aggregate" means combined into a total, so aggregate demand is the demand of an entire economy summed across households, firms and government. A single household in isolation is the individual or micro case, the level at which the aggregate is built up. Confusing the two collapses the distinction between macroeconomics and microeconomics that the adjective exists to mark.

Summing across the whole economy is what the adjective does, so a household taken in isolation belongs to the micro case instead.

**E) A research council that "disseminates" its findings is spreading them to a wider audience.**

To "disseminate" is to scatter widely, and in institutional language it covers publishing, briefing and circulating results so that they reach beyond the team that produced them. Funders now write dissemination requirements into grants because findings locked in a filing cabinet have no effect. The register is formal but the idea is simple enough that "spread" paraphrases it neatly.

Pushing results out beyond the team that produced them is the verb's whole job, and that is what the council is described as doing.
tasks.solution_overview: Academic writing grades its confidence carefully, and several of these items sit on that scale between possible, provisional and proven. Others test whether a term looks at a whole or at a single case. Ask how much certainty or how much coverage the word claims, and any definition that inflates either one shows itself.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal verbs from procurement, finance and treaty-making. Decide whether each account matches how the verb is used.
statements: A hospital trust that "procures" ventilators through a framework agreement is obtaining them by a formal purchasing process.
A manufacturer that "forgoes" an available subsidy has claimed that subsidy in full.
A board that "defers" a decision until the audit is complete has postponed it rather than cancelled it.
A lender that "waives" a late-payment fee has chosen not to enforce a right it holds.
A parliament that "ratifies" a trade agreement gives it formal approval so that it can take effect.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A hospital trust that "procures" ventilators through a framework agreement is obtaining them by a formal purchasing process.**

"Procure" is the formal counterpart of "buy," reserved for organised acquisition under rules: tenders, framework agreements and audit trails. Public-sector writing uses it because procurement is a regulated process, not simply a transaction, and the whole vocabulary of suppliers and bids follows from it. Saying the trust bought ventilators would be true but would lose the institutional machinery the verb implies.

Buying under a rule-bound process is what the verb signals, which fits the trust's framework agreement neatly.

**B) A manufacturer that "forgoes" an available subsidy has claimed that subsidy in full.**

To "forgo" something is to do without it voluntarily, so a manufacturer that forgoes a subsidy has left the money unclaimed. Claiming it in full is the opposite decision, and the accounts would then record income rather than an opportunity given up. Economists like the verb because forgone benefit is the shape of opportunity cost.

**Trap:** Forgo is a decision to abstain, not a synonym for receive.

A manufacturer that forgoes the subsidy walks away from the money, so describing it as claimed in full inverts the decision.

**C) A board that "defers" a decision until the audit is complete has postponed it rather than cancelled it.**

"Defer" moves something later in time while keeping it alive on the agenda, which is why boards defer decisions pending information they expect to receive. Cancellation would be reported with "abandon" or "withdraw," and minutes distinguish the two because a deferred item must return. The verb also carries a note of orderly process that "put off" lacks.

The decision is pushed back but still live on the agenda, which is the distinction the board's language preserves.

**D) A lender that "waives" a late-payment fee has chosen not to enforce a right it holds.**

To "waive" a fee is to relinquish the right to charge it, a voluntary act by the party who could have insisted. The lender is not saying the fee was never owed; it is declining to collect what it could lawfully demand. Contract language relies on the verb because a waiver in one instance does not necessarily surrender the right in future.

Declining to enforce a charge it could lawfully have demanded is what the lender's waiver amounts to, so the account is right.

**E) A parliament that "ratifies" a trade agreement gives it formal approval so that it can take effect.**

"Ratify" is the formal act by which an agreement already negotiated is confirmed by the body with authority to bind the state. Signature settles the text; ratification brings it into force, and treaties routinely wait years between the two. The verb belongs to constitutional and diplomatic register, where approval must be recorded rather than assumed.

Confirmation that lets a negotiated agreement operate is the parliamentary act described, so the account holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Each verb here records a decision taken by an institution: to buy, to give up, to postpone, to relax a right, or to approve. The tests are whether the decision is positive or negative, and whether it is temporary or final. Substituting a plain paraphrase such as "put off" or "give up" makes the direction of each decision audible.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Five claims about verbs of oversight, argument and approval in official writing. Decide whether each claim describes the verb correctly.
statements: A supplier that "complies with" the emissions standard has been found to be in breach of it.
A minister who "delegates" authority to an agency has taken that authority back into their own hands.
To "scrutinise" a budget line is to approve it without examination.
An economist who "endorses" a carbon-pricing scheme is publicly supporting it.
In careful academic usage, to "refute" a claim is simply to deny it firmly, with no evidence required.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A supplier that "complies with" the emissions standard has been found to be in breach of it.**

To "comply with" a standard is to meet its requirements, so a compliant supplier is on the right side of the rule. A breach would be reported with "contravenes," "violates" or "fails to meet," and enforcement documents keep the two vocabularies rigidly separate because consequences follow from the label. The fixed preposition is worth noting as well: one complies with a rule, never complies a rule.

Compliance puts the supplier on the right side of the standard, so a finding of breach would need contravenes or violates instead.

**B) A minister who "delegates" authority to an agency has taken that authority back into their own hands.**

"Delegate" passes authority downwards or outwards to another body while the delegating minister retains ultimate responsibility. Taking power back is revocation or recall, an opposite movement that administrative law treats as a separate act. The whole architecture of agencies rests on the outward direction the verb describes.

Authority handed to an agency has moved outward rather than back to the minister, so reclaiming it would be reported as revocation.

**C) To "scrutinise" a budget line is to approve it without examination.**

To "scrutinise" is to examine closely and critically, which is the opposite of nodding something through. Committees exist to scrutinise spending precisely because approval without examination is the failure they are meant to prevent. The verb belongs to a family with "audit" and "examine" rather than with "endorse."

Close and critical examination is the content of the verb, so unexamined approval is the failure scrutiny exists to prevent rather than its meaning.

**D) An economist who "endorses" a carbon-pricing scheme is publicly supporting it.**

To "endorse" is to declare public support for something, lending one's name and reputation to it. In formal debate an endorsement is a position on the record, which is why economists who endorse a scheme are expected to defend it. The commercial sense of signing the back of a cheque shares the same idea of adding one's name.

Support put on the public record is what the verb reports of the economist, so the claim is accurate.

**E) In careful academic usage, to "refute" a claim is simply to deny it firmly, with no evidence required.**

In careful usage "refute" means to disprove: the claim is defeated by argument or evidence, not merely rejected. Firm denial without support is "deny" or at most "dispute," and academic readers notice when the stronger verb is used for the weaker act. Reviewers often flag the slip because it quietly upgrades an opinion into a demonstration.

**Tip:** You can deny anything at will, but you can only refute what you can disprove.

Refutation requires the disproof that firm denial never supplies, so this account lets the verb off far too lightly.
tasks.solution_overview: Regulatory and academic prose distinguishes sharply between observing a rule, handing power on, examining closely, backing publicly and defeating an argument. Ask who is doing what to whom in each sentence, and whether the described action would leave the same paper trail. Verbs of scrutiny in particular never mean automatic acceptance.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five statements about the formal vocabulary of reasoning, evidence and admission. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: An author who "concedes" a weakness in the sample is admitting a point that works against their own argument.
A reader who "infers" a conclusion from a table is drawing it out of the evidence rather than being told it directly.
A report that "implies" a link between screen time and productivity has suggested that link through its wording without stating it outright.
To "presume" that a rule applies is to take it as true in advance of confirmation.
An auditor who "ascertains" the true stock level has established it by checking.
tactical_explanations:
**A) An author who "concedes" a weakness in the sample is admitting a point that works against their own argument.**

"Concede" means to grant a point that costs you something, which is why it appears in the limitations section of a paper rather than in its abstract. The verb signals intellectual honesty: the author sees the objection and admits its force before a critic raises it. A neutral "notes" would report the same fact without acknowledging the damage.

Granting a point that costs the author something is the move the verb marks, and a weak sample is exactly such a point.

**B) A reader who "infers" a conclusion from a table is drawing it out of the evidence rather than being told it directly.**

To "infer" is to reach a conclusion from evidence by reasoning, and it is the reader or analyst who does the inferring. A table does not infer anything; it supports inferences drawn by whoever reads it. Formal writing guards the distinction because an inference belongs to a person and can therefore be challenged as unwarranted.

The reasoning belongs to the reader who works the conclusion out of the table, which is the account given here.

**C) A report that "implies" a link between screen time and productivity has suggested that link through its wording without stating it outright.**

To "imply" is to convey something without asserting it, so the implying is done by the text or its author rather than by the audience. A report that juxtaposes two findings and lets the connection hang in the air has implied a link while retaining deniability. Editors watch for the move because implied claims escape the evidential standards applied to stated ones.

**Tip:** The writer implies; the reader infers. The traffic runs in opposite directions.

Suggestion without assertion is the manoeuvre the report is credited with, so the statement reads the verb correctly.

**D) To "presume" that a rule applies is to take it as true in advance of confirmation.**

To "presume" is to accept something as true for the moment because it is reasonable to do so, pending confirmation. Legal and administrative writing depends on presumptions, which set a default that further evidence can displace. The verb is stronger than "guess" because it rests on grounds, and weaker than "establish" because it has not been verified.

A default accepted ahead of confirmation is what a presumption is, and that is how the rule is being taken here.

**E) An auditor who "ascertains" the true stock level has established it by checking.**

"Ascertain" means to find out with certainty by checking, which is why audit reports prefer it to a vaguer "work out." The auditor who ascertains stock has counted or verified rather than estimated, and the word implicitly claims that the number can now be relied on. Its high register carries an assurance that plainer verbs do not.

Checking until the figure can be relied on is the auditor's act as this verb describes it, so the statement fits.
tasks.solution_overview: This group covers what writers and readers do with evidence: give ground, draw conclusions, hint at links, assume in advance, and check a fact into certainty. Notice who performs each action, since some of these verbs belong to the writer and others to the reader. Keeping the roles straight is the fastest route through the set.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Five descriptions of formal verbs that describe growth, reduction, composition and necessity. Decide whether each description is correct.
statements: A packing workforce "augmented" by seasonal hires has been reduced in size.
Returns that "diminish" as more capital is added to a fixed plant are growing steadily larger.
To say that three northern regions "constitute" the pilot programme is to say that they were excluded from it.
Saying that a merger "entails" job losses presents those losses as a necessary consequence of it.
A licence clause that "precludes" resale prevents resale from taking place.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A packing workforce "augmented" by seasonal hires has been reduced in size.**

"Augment" means to add to something that already exists, so a workforce augmented by seasonal hires is larger than before, not smaller. Reduction would be reported with "cut," "pared back" or "reduced," and payroll documents cannot afford ambiguity between the two. The verb keeps a slightly formal tone, which is why it appears in staffing reports rather than in conversation.

Addition rather than subtraction is the direction the verb sets, so a workforce described as augmented has grown, not shrunk.

**B) Returns that "diminish" as more capital is added to a fixed plant are growing steadily larger.**

To "diminish" is to become smaller, and diminishing returns is the classic economic case: each extra unit of capital added to a fixed plant yields less than the one before. Total output may still rise, but the increments shrink, which is exactly what the participle records. Growth in the increments themselves would be increasing returns, a different phenomenon with different policy implications.

**Trap:** Diminishing returns can accompany rising output; what falls is the gain from each extra unit.

The increments are what shrink under diminishing returns, so describing those returns as steadily larger reverses the classic case.

**C) To say that three northern regions "constitute" the pilot programme is to say that they were excluded from it.**

"Constitute" says what something is made up of: the three regions are the parts that together form the programme. Exclusion would need "are omitted from" or "fall outside," the opposite relation between part and whole. Formal writing chooses this verb when membership is being defined rather than merely illustrated.

The regions are named as the components that make up the programme, so reading the verb as exclusion misstates membership.

**D) Saying that a merger "entails" job losses presents those losses as a necessary consequence of it.**

"Entail" states a necessary consequence: if the merger goes ahead, the job losses follow as part of the package rather than as a possibility. Weaker verbs such as "may involve" or "could lead to" would leave room for a different outcome, and negotiators listen for exactly that difference. The word is at home in legal and analytical prose where consequences must be pinned down.

Necessary consequence rather than a mere possibility is what the verb asserts of the job losses, so the description is right.

**E) A licence clause that "precludes" resale prevents resale from taking place.**

To "preclude" is to make something impossible in advance, so a clause precluding resale shuts the door before anyone reaches it. The verb is stronger than "discourages" and more formal than "stops," and contracts use it because it describes a bar rather than a penalty. A precluded action is not merely punished after the fact; it is not permitted at all.

Ruling the action out ahead of time is the bar the clause creates, so this reading of the licence holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Size and logical necessity are the two axes in this set: some verbs make a quantity larger or smaller, while others state what something is made of or what must follow from it. Try replacing each verb with a plain equivalent such as "add to," "shrink," "make up" or "rule out" and see whether the sentence keeps its shape.
