A definition that inverts the plain equivalent is the one to distrust.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five judgements about formal verbs of enabling, blocking, starting and stopping, including one question of register in official documents. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: A customs system that "facilitates" cross-border trade makes that trade easier to carry out.
Port congestion that "impedes" deliveries is speeding those deliveries up.
A notice reporting that production "ceased" in March states that it stopped then.
In a formal tender document, "the works kicked off in April" is more appropriate than "the works commenced in April."
Saying that new rules "render" an old permit invalid uses "render" in its formal sense of causing something to become a particular way.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A customs system that "facilitates" cross-border trade makes that trade easier to carry out.**

"Facilitate" means to make a process easier or smoother, which is why trade agreements have whole chapters headed trade facilitation. The verb does not claim to create the trade, only to remove friction from it, and that modest scope is part of its usefulness. In plainer register the same idea appears as "help along."

Easing the process without claiming to create the trade is what the verb promises, so the judgement of the customs system is sound.

**B) Port congestion that "impedes" deliveries is speeding those deliveries up.**

To "impede" is to obstruct or slow progress, so congestion that impedes deliveries is holding them back. Acceleration would be reported with "expedites" or "speeds," and logistics writing needs the contrast because delay and dispatch have opposite cost consequences.

**Tip:** Impede and expedite are natural opposites; both are formal, and only one of them helps.

An obstruction verb cannot describe deliveries speeding up, so congestion that impedes them is holding them back.

**C) A notice reporting that production "ceased" in March states that it stopped then.**

"Cease" is the formal verb for stopping, common in notices, statutes and corporate announcements where "stop" would sound too plain. Production that ceased in March came to an end at that point, whether or not it later resumed. The verb reports the fact of stopping without commenting on the reason.

A stop in March is what a notice of ceased production records, so the judgement is accurate.

**D) In a formal tender document, "the works kicked off in April" is more appropriate than "the works commenced in April.".**

"Commence" is the register-appropriate verb for a tender document, matching the formality of the contract language around it. "Kicked off" is a sporting idiom that has spread into workplace speech, but it reads as casual in a document that may be produced in a dispute. Register mismatch of this kind rarely changes the meaning, yet it undermines the authority of the text.

The formal setting calls for the Latinate verb, so the preference runs the wrong way — "the works commenced in April" is the appropriate line.

**E) Saying that new rules "render" an old permit invalid uses "render" in its formal sense of causing something to become a particular way.**

"Render" in formal usage means to cause something to be in a given state, as in rendering a permit invalid or a clause unenforceable. It takes an object plus a complement, which is the exact pattern here, and legal drafting favours it for describing the effect of one instrument on another. The everyday sense of rendering assistance or rendering an account is a separate branch of the same verb.

Causing the permit to become invalid is the construction in play, so this use of render fits.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these items ask whether a verb helps or hinders, and two ask when an activity starts or stops. One asks a different question altogether: whether the phrasing suits the formality of a tender document. Keep meaning and register apart, since a word can be perfectly accurate and still be wrong for the setting.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Five statements about the careful vocabulary of meaning, prevalence and unproven claims. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: In technical writing, a symbol that "denotes" quantity stands for it explicitly, whereas a term that connotes wealth merely carries an association.
An interest rate that "prevails" in a market is the one generally in force there.
Forecasters who "anticipate" a slowdown expect it and are planning around it before it arrives.
A statement that a firm "allegedly" mis-sold insurance policies reports an accusation that has not been proved.
A document that "purports" to be an official audit is thereby confirmed as genuine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In technical writing, a symbol that "denotes" quantity stands for it explicitly, whereas a term that connotes wealth merely carries an association.**

"Denote" is the explicit relation between a sign and what it stands for, which is why a variable denotes quantity in a formula. "Connote" covers the associations a word drags along with it, such as the overtones of comfort or status attached to a term for wealth. Technical prose needs both because definitions live in the first relation while rhetoric lives in the second.

Explicit reference set against carried association is the distinction the pair marks, so the statement is right.

**B) An interest rate that "prevails" in a market is the one generally in force there.**

To "prevail" is to be current or predominant, so the prevailing rate is the one generally applying in that market at that time. The verb's other sense, to win out, shares the idea of one thing coming out on top of the alternatives. Financial writing uses the participle constantly in phrases such as prevailing conditions and prevailing wage.

Generally in force is what the verb claims of the rate, so this reading of the market stands.

**C) Forecasters who "anticipate" a slowdown expect it and are planning around it before it arrives.**

"Anticipate" in formal use means to expect something and to act in advance of it, which is more than the bare prediction carried by "expect." Forecasters who anticipate a slowdown are already adjusting positions and provisions rather than simply issuing a number. The extra element of preparation is what earns the longer word its place.

Expectation combined with advance planning is the sense described, so the account of the forecasters is accurate.

**D) A statement that a firm "allegedly" mis-sold insurance policies reports an accusation that has not been proved.**

"Allegedly" marks a claim as asserted but not established, and journalism and regulatory notices rely on it to report accusations without adopting them. The adverb protects the writer while keeping the reader informed that a formal process has yet to conclude. Removing it would turn a reported accusation into a stated finding.

**Tip:** Allegedly reports the accusation and withholds the endorsement.

An unproven accusation is what the adverb signals, so the statement fits the insurance claim as reported.

**E) A document that "purports" to be an official audit is thereby confirmed as genuine.**

To "purport" is to claim something about oneself that may or may not be true, which is why the verb is used when authenticity is in question. A document purporting to be an official audit presents itself as one; whether it is genuine remains open. Careful writers reach for the verb exactly when they want to describe an appearance without vouching for it.

The word withholds confirmation rather than granting it, so a purported audit is precisely one not yet shown to be real.
tasks.solution_overview: Precision about what is stated, what is merely usual and what remains unproven runs through this task. Watch in particular for words that keep a claim at arm's length, since they never confirm the thing they describe. Asking whether the writer has committed to the truth of the claim resolves most of the set.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal connectors and hedging adverbs common in academic and official prose. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: "Ostensibly" reports the reason given in public while leaving room for a different underlying motive, as in "a levy ostensibly designed to fund research."
"Notwithstanding the shipping delay, the consignment cleared customs on time" uses a formal connector meaning "despite."
"Albeit" introduces a concessive qualification, as in "industrial output rose, albeit slowly."
"Thereby" links an action to the result it produces, as in "the central bank cut rates, thereby easing credit conditions."
"Whereby" introduces the means or arrangement by which something happens, as in "a scheme whereby firms trade emission permits."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Ostensibly" reports the reason given in public while leaving room for a different underlying motive, as in "a levy ostensibly designed to fund research.".**

"Ostensibly" describes how something is presented rather than how it is, so it quietly opens a gap between the stated purpose and the real one. A levy ostensibly designed to fund research invites the reader to wonder what else it funds, without the writer having to make an accusation. Analysts value the adverb for that reason: it registers doubt while keeping the sentence defensible.

Stated reason held at a distance is what the adverb conveys, so the account of the levy is right.

**B) "Notwithstanding the shipping delay, the consignment cleared customs on time" uses a formal connector meaning "despite.".**

"Notwithstanding" is a high-register equivalent of "despite," common in contracts, statutes and formal correspondence. It concedes the obstacle, here the shipping delay, and then reports the outcome that occurred anyway. It can also follow its noun, as in "the delay notwithstanding," which is a construction worth recognising in legal text.

Concession of an obstacle in formal dress is the connector's role, so the shipping-delay sentence uses it correctly.

**C) "Albeit" introduces a concessive qualification, as in "industrial output rose, albeit slowly.".**

"Albeit" compresses "although it be" into a single word and attaches a qualification to what was just claimed. Output rose, albeit slowly, concedes the weakness of the rise while keeping the positive claim intact. It attaches to a phrase rather than a full clause, which is what separates it from "although."

A concessive qualification attached to the rise is what the word introduces, so the account is accurate.

**D) "Thereby" links an action to the result it produces, as in "the central bank cut rates, thereby easing credit conditions.".**

"Thereby" points from an action to the consequence that flows from it, and the following verb normally appears as an -ing form. A rate cut that thereby eased credit conditions presents the easing as the direct result of the cut rather than a coincidence. The adverb keeps the causal link tight without the extra clause that "and as a result" would require.

Action linked to its resulting effect is the relation the word builds, so the rate-cut example holds.

**E) "Whereby" introduces the means or arrangement by which something happens, as in "a scheme whereby firms trade emission permits.".**

"Whereby" introduces the mechanism or arrangement through which something operates, and it typically follows a noun such as scheme, system or process. A scheme whereby firms trade permits tells the reader how the scheme works, not merely where or when. Substituting "by which" gives the same sense in slightly plainer clothing.

The means-of-operation reading is what the connector supplies, so the emissions-permit scheme is described correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Connectors do quiet but decisive work: they concede, contrast, signal a result or introduce the mechanism behind an arrangement. The way to test each one is to read the sentence with a plain equivalent such as despite, though, so or by which, and check that the logical relation survives. One adverb in the set also carries a note of scepticism worth listening for.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five claims about adjectives used to judge whether plans, models and results hold up. Decide whether each claim describes the adjective correctly.
statements: A resettlement plan described as "feasible" has been judged impossible to carry out with the resources available.
A business model called "viable" is one that cannot survive without permanent emergency support.
A statistical finding described as "robust" collapses as soon as the model specification is changed.
Growth described as "sustained" lasted a single quarter before reversing.
An effect described as "negligible" is too small to matter for the conclusion being drawn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A resettlement plan described as "feasible" has been judged impossible to carry out with the resources available.**

"Feasible" means capable of being done, a judgement about practicality given time, money and skills. Something impossible with current resources is infeasible or impracticable, and appraisal documents make the call explicitly because funding follows from it. Note that feasibility says nothing about whether the plan is wise, only whether it can be executed.

Practicability is what the adjective asserts, so attaching it to an impossible plan contradicts the word.

**B) A business model called "viable" is one that cannot survive without permanent emergency support.**

"Viable" means able to survive and function on its own, which for a business model means covering its costs without a permanent drip of rescue funding. A model dependent on emergency support indefinitely is the standard example of non-viability, and restructuring reviews turn on precisely that test. The biological root, able to live, is a useful reminder of the standard involved.

**Trap:** Viable is about independent survival, not about current survival with help.

Permanent dependence is the opposite of what the adjective certifies, so the claim about the business model fails.

**C) A statistical finding described as "robust" collapses as soon as the model specification is changed.**

"Robust" describes a result that holds up when the assumptions around it are varied, which is why papers report robustness checks. A finding that disappears when the specification changes is fragile or sensitive, and honest authors say so. The adjective is a claim about resilience under testing rather than about the size of the effect.

Surviving changes to the model is the whole point of the word, so a collapsing finding cannot carry it.

**D) Growth described as "sustained" lasted a single quarter before reversing.**

"Sustained" means kept up over an extended period, so sustained growth implies a run of consecutive periods rather than one good quarter. A single quarter followed by reversal would be described as a brief uptick or a one-off, and forecasters distinguish the two because trend and blip carry different policy implications. Duration is doing the work in this adjective.

One quarter followed by a reversal is what the word rules out, so the growth described here is not sustained.

**E) An effect described as "negligible" is too small to matter for the conclusion being drawn.**

"Negligible" marks a quantity small enough to be safely ignored in the argument at hand, which is a judgement about relevance as well as size. Analysts use it to justify leaving a factor out of a model without pretending the factor is literally zero. Its formality suits reports where "tiny" would sound imprecise.

Too small to affect the conclusion is the verdict the adjective delivers, so the claim about the effect is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Every adjective in this set is a verdict on strength or size: can it be done, can it survive, does it hold when tested, did it last, does it matter. Reading each claim, check whether the verdict described is positive or negative, and whether the sentence around it agrees. An adjective of endurance attached to something that collapsed is a mismatch worth catching.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Five claims about the vocabulary of relevance, method and error in research writing. Decide whether each claim is correct.
statements: Detail described as "pertinent" to an inquiry is detail that has no bearing on it.
"Extraneous" variables in a trial are factors outside the one under study that may nonetheless affect the result.
A qualifying threshold described as "arbitrary" was fixed without a principled reason for that exact figure.
Measurement error described as "systematic" is random noise that cancels out across a large sample.
A review described as "rigorous" applied strict and thorough standards throughout.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Detail described as "pertinent" to an inquiry is detail that has no bearing on it.**

"Pertinent" means directly relevant to the matter in hand, which is why inquiries ask for pertinent documents and set the rest aside. Material with no bearing on the question is irrelevant or immaterial, the terms a chair would use to rule it out. The adjective is formal but its test is practical: does this detail help decide the question.

Relevance is the whole content of the word, so defining pertinent detail as unrelated inverts it.

**B) "Extraneous" variables in a trial are factors outside the one under study that may nonetheless affect the result.**

"Extraneous" variables come from outside the relationship being studied yet can still move the outcome, which is why designs try to control or randomise them. Weather, seasonality and selection effects are typical instances in economic and clinical trials alike. The word marks origin rather than importance: extraneous does not mean harmless.

Outside the study but capable of shaping the result is the definition in use, so the claim about those variables is right.

**C) A qualifying threshold described as "arbitrary" was fixed without a principled reason for that exact figure.**

Calling a threshold "arbitrary" says the precise cut-off rests on choice rather than on evidence, even when the choice is defensible administratively. A rule granting support below a certain income is not thereby wrong, but nothing in the data makes that figure rather than a nearby one the correct one. Reviewers raise the point because results that shift with the cut-off are fragile.

**Tip:** Arbitrary attacks the exact number, not the idea of drawing a line.

A cut-off chosen without a principled basis for that exact figure is what the adjective describes, so the claim holds.

**D) Measurement error described as "systematic" is random noise that cancels out across a large sample.**

"Systematic" error pushes measurements consistently in one direction, so it survives averaging and biases the result no matter how large the sample. Noise that cancels out is random error, the far more forgiving problem. The distinction matters because more data cures one and entrenches the other.

**Trap:** Only random error washes out with sample size; systematic error scales with it.

The definition offered describes random error that washes out, so it misidentifies systematic measurement error.

**E) A review described as "rigorous" applied strict and thorough standards throughout.**

"Rigorous" describes work carried out to demanding standards of care, with methods that can withstand inspection. A rigorous review documents its search, states its criteria and applies them consistently rather than impressionistically. The adjective is a claim about process, which is why authors have to show the process to earn it.

Strict and thorough standards are what the word certifies, so the description of the review is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Method words carry technical baggage that their everyday senses do not, and this set tests whether you can hear it. Ask whether the word concerns what belongs in the study, what sits outside it, how a boundary was chosen, or how an error behaves across many observations. The technical sense usually turns out to be narrower than the conversational one.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Five statements about formal words for agreeing, objecting, arguing for and discouraging, including one word that faces both ways. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: Two peer reviewers who "concur" on a manuscript have reached the same judgement about it.
A committee member who records a "dissent" is confirming full agreement with the majority view.
An economist who "advocates" congestion charging is arguing against its introduction.
A penalty designed to "deter" late filing is designed to encourage more of it.
"Sanction" can mean both to authorise and to penalise, so a formal sentence has to supply enough context to show which sense is intended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Two peer reviewers who "concur" on a manuscript have reached the same judgement about it.**

"Concur" is the formal verb for agreeing, and it appears in reviews, judgments and minutes where "we think the same" would be too casual. Reviewers who concur have arrived at matching conclusions, whether or not they reasoned identically. Note the fixed preposition when a person is named: one concurs with a colleague.

Shared judgement is what the verb records of the reviewers, so the statement is sound.

**B) A committee member who records a "dissent" is confirming full agreement with the majority view.**

A "dissent" is a recorded disagreement, most familiar from courts where a dissenting judge sets out why the majority is wrong. Registering one is a formal act that puts objection on the record rather than a private grumble. Agreement with the majority is concurrence, its exact counterpart in the same vocabulary.

The noun records objection rather than assent, so a dissent cannot confirm agreement with the majority.

**C) An economist who "advocates" congestion charging is arguing against its introduction.**

To "advocate" something is to argue publicly in its favour, which is why the noun form names a person who speaks for a cause or a client. An economist advocating congestion charging is making the case for it, not against it. Careful writers also note that the verb takes a direct object in formal use: one advocates a policy rather than advocating for it in most edited prose.

Arguing in favour is the direction the verb sets, so an economist who advocates congestion charging is backing it.

**D) A penalty designed to "deter" late filing is designed to encourage more of it.**

To "deter" is to discourage an action by making it unattractive, usually through the prospect of a cost. Late-filing penalties exist precisely to reduce late filing, and deterrence is the standard name for that mechanism in tax and regulatory design. Encouraging the behaviour would call for an incentive, which works on the opposite side of the ledger.

Discouragement is the purpose the verb names, so a penalty designed to deter late filing cannot be meant to encourage it.

**E) "Sanction" can mean both to authorise and to penalise, so a formal sentence has to supply enough context to show which sense is intended.**

"Sanction" is genuinely two-faced: as a verb it can mean to give official approval, and as a noun it commonly means a punitive measure such as a trade restriction. Only the surrounding words settle which sense is live, so a board that sanctions a project approves it while a state under sanctions is being punished. Careful drafters often avoid the word altogether where money or liability turns on the reading.

**Tip:** With "sanction," read the sentence, not the word.

The double sense and the need for disambiguating context are both real features of the term, so this warning is well founded.
tasks.solution_overview: This set is about stance: who agrees, who objects, who argues in favour and what a penalty is meant to achieve. Ask which side of a debate each verb places its subject on, and whether a penalty is meant to increase or decrease the behaviour it targets. One noun in the group carries two opposed senses, so context has to do the deciding.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five accounts of terms that describe how clearly something is stated and what kind of evidence stands behind it. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: A warranty that is "explicit" is stated openly in the text rather than left to be understood.
An assumption that is "implicit" in a forecasting model is present in the reasoning but never stated outright.
Wages reported in "nominal" terms have not been adjusted for inflation.
"Empirical" evidence is reasoning conducted purely from first principles, without observation or measurement.
"Anecdotal" evidence rests on individual reports rather than on systematically collected data.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A warranty that is "explicit" is stated openly in the text rather than left to be understood.**

"Explicit" means spelled out, and in contract drafting an explicit warranty is one the buyer can point to on the page. The opposite, an implied warranty, arises by operation of law without being written down, which is exactly why the distinction matters commercially. Formal writing prizes explicitness because unstated terms are the ones that end up in dispute.

Stated openly in the text is what the adjective claims of the warranty, so the account is right.

**B) An assumption that is "implicit" in a forecasting model is present in the reasoning but never stated outright.**

"Implicit" describes something genuinely present in the reasoning yet never put into words, such as a stability assumption a forecast quietly relies on. The reader must reconstruct it, which is why critiques often begin by making implicit assumptions explicit. It is not the same as vague: an implicit assumption can be perfectly definite once excavated.

Present but unstated is the sense in play for the forecasting assumption, so the account holds.

**C) Wages reported in "nominal" terms have not been adjusted for inflation.**

In economics "nominal" means measured at current prices with no inflation adjustment, while "real" figures strip inflation out. A nominal wage rise of three per cent during four per cent inflation is a real fall, which is the whole reason the pair exists. Reports that omit the label invite the reader to mistake one for the other.

**Tip:** Nominal is the number on the payslip; real is what it buys.

No inflation adjustment is what the term signals, so wages reported as nominal are being read correctly.

**D) "Empirical" evidence is reasoning conducted purely from first principles, without observation or measurement.**

"Empirical" evidence comes from observation, measurement or experiment rather than from reasoning alone. Argument from first principles is theoretical or a priori work, valuable but categorically different, and papers separate their theoretical and empirical sections for that reason. The word makes a claim about where the knowledge came from.

The definition offered describes theory rather than observation, so it names the wrong category for empirical evidence.

**E) "Anecdotal" evidence rests on individual reports rather than on systematically collected data.**

"Anecdotal" evidence consists of individual cases and reports that were not gathered by any systematic method, which limits how far conclusions can travel from them. It can be genuinely informative as a prompt for study, but it cannot support a general claim about a population. The adjective is a warning label rather than a dismissal.

Individual reports without systematic collection are what the term denotes, so the account of anecdotal evidence is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these items contrast what a text says outright with what it leaves unsaid, and two contrast evidence gathered by observation with evidence of other kinds. One economic adjective distinguishes figures adjusted for inflation from figures that are not. Naming the opposite of each term is a quick way to check that the account has it right.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Five judgements about choosing the right level of formality in official reports and contracts. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: In a formal report, "the agency will endeavour to reduce waiting times" is register-appropriate where "the agency will have a go at cutting waiting times" would not be.
"Assist" is the formal counterpart of "help out," so a written evaluation says that the programme assists recipient governments rather than gives them a hand.
"Obtain" is the formal verb for acquiring something, as in obtaining a licence before operations commence.
A contract stating that the lease will "terminate" on 31 December reports that it comes to an end on that date, and the verb suits legal register better than "finish up."
"Approximately twelve per cent" is the register-appropriate way to hedge a figure in a formal report, where "round about twelve per cent" would read as conversational.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a formal report, "the agency will endeavour to reduce waiting times" is register-appropriate where "the agency will have a go at cutting waiting times" would not be.**

"Endeavour" is a formal verb of committed effort, and it carries the useful implication that the agency is bound to try without guaranteeing the outcome. "Have a go at" conveys much the same idea in speech but sounds flippant in a document that may be quoted back at its author. The choice is about the seriousness the text needs to project, not about the facts it reports.

The formal verb matches the report's setting while the idiom clashes with it, so the judgement on endeavour is sound.

**B) "Assist" is the formal counterpart of "help out," so a written evaluation says that the programme assists recipient governments rather than gives them a hand.**

"Assist" belongs to the written register of programme documents and evaluations, where "help out" and "give a hand" would jar against the surrounding prose. The meanings overlap almost completely, which is what makes the choice purely one of tone. Institutions also prefer the formal verb because it collocates cleanly with nouns such as assistance and technical assistance.

The formal option is the one that fits a written evaluation, so assist rather than help out is the right call.

**C) "Obtain" is the formal verb for acquiring something, as in obtaining a licence before operations commence.**

"Obtain" is the neutral formal verb for coming into possession of something, and licensing language uses it because "get" reads as too loose for a legal precondition. Pairing it with "commence" keeps the whole sentence at a consistent level, which is part of good formal style. Mixing registers within one clause is more conspicuous than choosing a formal word in the first place.

**Tip:** Keep the register steady across a sentence; a single casual verb undoes the rest.

The formal acquisition verb is right for a licensing requirement, so obtain before operations commence holds.

**D) A contract stating that the lease will "terminate" on 31 December reports that it comes to an end on that date, and the verb suits legal register better than "finish up.".**

"Terminate" is the standard contractual verb for bringing an agreement to an end, and it supports the related nouns termination and termination date that the rest of the document will use. "Finish up" would communicate the fact but would look out of place beside clauses about notice and remedies. Consistency with the surrounding legal vocabulary is the reason for the choice.

Ending on the stated date, expressed in contract register, is what the clause achieves, so terminate rather than finish up is right.

**E) "Approximately twelve per cent" is the register-appropriate way to hedge a figure in a formal report, where "round about twelve per cent" would read as conversational.**

"Approximately" is the formal hedge for a figure that is close but not exact, and it signals deliberate imprecision rather than carelessness. "Round about" says the same thing in a conversational voice that would undercut a report's authority. Reports also gain from consistency, since readers come to expect one hedging term throughout a document.

The formal hedge is the one that suits a written report, so approximately rather than round about is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Register, not meaning, is the pivot of this task: the informal versions offered would all be understood, but they would sit wrongly in a document meant to carry authority. Ask what setting each sentence belongs to and whether the phrasing matches the seriousness of the surrounding text. Latinate verbs and hedges of precision are the usual markers of the formal choice.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five descriptions of adjectives that grade strictness, caution and stability. Decide whether each description matches the adjective.
statements: Capital rules described as "stringent" are loosely drafted and easy for a bank to satisfy.
An enforcement regime called "lenient" imposes the maximum available penalty in every case.
A "prudent" reserve policy is one that takes large risks in pursuit of the highest available returns.
A currency described as "volatile" holds a steady value from one month to the next.
A supply chain described as "resilient" can absorb a disruption and recover its function.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Capital rules described as "stringent" are loosely drafted and easy for a bank to satisfy.**

"Stringent" means strict and demanding, so stringent capital rules set a high bar that banks must work to clear. Loosely drafted requirements would be described as lax or permissive, and supervisory reports use the contrast constantly when comparing jurisdictions. The adjective carries an implication of tight drafting as well as high standards.

Strictness is the content of the word, so a description of easy compliance contradicts stringent capital rules.

**B) An enforcement regime called "lenient" imposes the maximum available penalty in every case.**

"Lenient" describes enforcement that goes easier than it might, imposing lighter penalties or exercising forbearance. Maximum penalties in every case is the severe or punitive end of the same scale. Regulators are compared on exactly this dimension, which is why the pair of adjectives is so common in supervisory commentary.

Mildness rather than maximum severity is what the word conveys, so a lenient regime cannot be imposing every maximum penalty.

**C) A "prudent" reserve policy is one that takes large risks in pursuit of the highest available returns.**

"Prudent" describes cautious management that guards against downside risk, which is the standard by which reserve and provisioning policies are judged. Large risks taken for high returns would be called aggressive or speculative, and fiduciary language treats that as a criticism rather than a compliment. The related phrase, the prudent person standard, makes the cautious sense explicit.

Caution is the whole point of the adjective, so pairing prudent with risk-seeking behaviour misdescribes it.

**D) A currency described as "volatile" holds a steady value from one month to the next.**

"Volatile" means liable to sharp and unpredictable movement, which is why the word attaches to currencies, commodity prices and equity indices in unsettled periods. Steadiness from month to month is stability, and traders price the difference directly through measures of volatility. The adjective describes the size of swings rather than their direction.

Instability is what the word reports, so a currency described as volatile cannot be holding a steady value.

**E) A supply chain described as "resilient" can absorb a disruption and recover its function.**

"Resilient" describes the capacity to take a shock and return to working order, which for a supply chain means alternative suppliers, buffer stock or spare capacity. It is not the same as robust, which suggests resisting the shock in the first place; resilience allows for damage followed by recovery. Post-pandemic supply-chain reviews lean on the word for exactly this reason.

Absorbing a disruption and recovering is what the adjective claims, so this description of the supply chain fits.
tasks.solution_overview: Each adjective here occupies a position on a scale, and the distractors work by sliding the word to the far end of its own scale. Test them by asking what the opposite adjective would be and whether the sentence describes that opposite instead. Only one of these descriptions leaves the word where it belongs.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Five statements about formal adjectives from trade policy and public finance. Decide whether each statement describes the adjective correctly.
statements: A "reciprocal" tariff reduction is one in which each side lowers barriers in return for the other doing the same.
A "unilateral" export ban is imposed by one state acting on its own, without the agreement of its trading partners.
A "punitive" rate of duty is one set deliberately low in order to reward compliant exporters.
"Remedial" measures are those intended to correct a problem that has already been identified.
Spending described as "discretionary" is fixed by statute and cannot be varied by the department that administers it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "reciprocal" tariff reduction is one in which each side lowers barriers in return for the other doing the same.**

"Reciprocal" describes an arrangement in which each party does for the other what the other does for it, which is the basic architecture of a negotiated tariff deal. The word implies exchange rather than generosity, and negotiators use it to insist that concessions be matched. Its opposite in this setting is a unilateral cut, given without anything in return.

Matched concessions on both sides are what the adjective describes, so the reciprocal tariff cut is read correctly.

**B) A "unilateral" export ban is imposed by one state acting on its own, without the agreement of its trading partners.**

"Unilateral" means done by one party alone, so a unilateral ban takes effect on one state's own decision regardless of what partners think. Bilateral and multilateral describe the alternatives, involving two parties or many, and trade commentary depends on the three-way contrast. The adjective says nothing about whether the action is justified, only about how many hands are on it.

One state acting alone is the sense in play, so this description of a unilateral ban is exact.

**C) A "punitive" rate of duty is one set deliberately low in order to reward compliant exporters.**

"Punitive" means intended to punish, so a punitive duty is set high enough to hurt the exporter it targets. A low rate designed to reward good behaviour would be a preferential or concessionary rate, which sits at the other end of the scale. Trade disputes turn on the difference, since punitive measures invite retaliation in a way that preferences do not.

Punishment rather than reward is what the adjective signals, so a deliberately low duty cannot be punitive.

**D) "Remedial" measures are those intended to correct a problem that has already been identified.**

"Remedial" work responds to a fault that has already come to light, whether a compliance failure, a defect or a shortfall. The word looks backwards to the problem and forwards to the correction, which is why inspection reports pair it with action plans and deadlines. Preventive measures, by contrast, address a problem that has not yet occurred.

**Tip:** Remedial repairs what went wrong; preventive stops it happening.

Correcting an identified problem is the function named, so the statement about remedial measures is accurate.

**E) Spending described as "discretionary" is fixed by statute and cannot be varied by the department that administers it.**

"Discretionary" spending is the portion a department can decide about, in contrast to mandatory or statutory spending that legislation fixes in advance. The whole budgetary point of the label is the freedom it marks, which is why discretionary lines are the first casualties in a squeeze. A statutory entitlement cannot be trimmed by administrative choice.

The definition offered describes mandatory spending instead, so it names the opposite of discretionary outlays.
tasks.solution_overview: Trade and budget language encodes who acts, why a measure was set at its level, and how much freedom an official retains. Ask whether an action is taken alone or by exchange, whether a charge is meant to punish or to reward, and whether spending is fixed by law or chosen year by year. Two of these adjectives have been given the meaning of their natural opposites.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Five accounts of formal terms for obligation, charges and amounts building up over time. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: A small firm "exempt" from the reporting requirement is the one most tightly bound by it.
A company "liable" for an environmental levy has been released from any obligation to pay it.
A borrower who "incurs" additional charges has become subject to them.
Interest that "accrues" daily on an outstanding balance disappears from that balance each day.
A tax authority that "remits" a penalty has cancelled the obligation to pay it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A small firm "exempt" from the reporting requirement is the one most tightly bound by it.**

"Exempt" places someone outside an obligation that would otherwise apply, which is why thresholds relieve small firms of reporting duties that bind larger ones. Being tightly bound is the position of a firm within scope, the opposite side of the same rule. Regulatory drafting keeps exemptions explicit because everyone else is assumed to be covered.

Standing outside the requirement is what the adjective grants, so an exempt firm is the least tightly bound, not the most.

**B) A company "liable" for an environmental levy has been released from any obligation to pay it.**

"Liable" means legally responsible, so a company liable for a levy is on the hook to pay it. Release from the obligation would be reported with "exempt," "discharged" or "relieved," and tax notices distinguish the two because money follows from the label. The word can also describe exposure to a penalty, as in liable to a fine.

Responsibility rather than release is the content of the term, so a liable company remains on the hook for the levy.

**C) A borrower who "incurs" additional charges has become subject to them.**

To "incur" is to bring something upon oneself, usually a cost, charge or liability, by taking some action or missing a deadline. A borrower who incurs charges now owes them, and the verb records the moment the obligation attached. It pairs almost exclusively with unwelcome nouns: expenses, debts, penalties, risk.

Becoming subject to the charges is what the verb reports, so the borrower who incurs them is described correctly.

**D) Interest that "accrues" daily on an outstanding balance disappears from that balance each day.**

To "accrue" is to accumulate over time, so interest accruing daily is being added to what is owed rather than removed from it. The verb underlies accrual accounting, where amounts are recognised as they build up rather than when cash changes hands. Anything disappearing from the balance would be repaid, written off or discharged.

**Trap:** Accrue always adds; the accumulation is the whole idea.

Daily accumulation is the opposite of disappearing from the balance, so interest that accrues is being added.

**E) A tax authority that "remits" a penalty has cancelled the obligation to pay it.**

In this legal and revenue sense, to "remit" a penalty is to cancel or refrain from exacting it, an exercise of the authority's power to let the charge go. The commoner commercial sense of remitting funds, meaning to send payment, belongs to the same root but points the other way, so context decides. Statutory language keeps both senses alive, which is why revenue notices spell out what is being remitted.

Cancelling the obligation is the revenue sense in play here, so the authority that remits the penalty is letting it go.
tasks.solution_overview: Financial and legal language is precise about who owes what and when the obligation attaches, and these items test that precision. Ask whether the person is inside or outside the duty, whether a charge is being taken on or written off, and whether an amount is building up or draining away. Substituting a plain paraphrase such as "let off" or "builds up" makes the direction clear.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five statements about how findings, rulings and prices are labelled according to how settled they are. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: "Preliminary" results are early findings released before the full analysis has been completed.
A "definitive" ruling settles the question and is not expected to be revisited.
Prices described as "indicative" are offered as a guide rather than as a firm commitment to trade at them.
Evidence described as "inconclusive" has settled the matter beyond further dispute.
A "hypothetical" scenario in a bank stress test is constructed for analysis rather than describing an event that actually occurred.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Preliminary" results are early findings released before the full analysis has been completed.**

"Preliminary" marks a stage rather than a verdict: the work has produced something worth reporting, but the full analysis is still running. Readers are expected to treat the numbers as liable to change, which is why conference papers and early data releases carry the label. It is a close relative of provisional, differing mainly in emphasising position in a sequence.

Early findings ahead of the complete analysis are what the label announces, so the statement about preliminary results is right.

**B) A "definitive" ruling settles the question and is not expected to be revisited.**

"Definitive" claims finality: the question has been resolved and no further round is anticipated. Courts, standards bodies and reference works use the word sparingly because it forecloses reopening. Its contrast with provisional and interim is what gives it force in formal writing.

Settling the matter for good is the content of the adjective, so a definitive ruling is expected to stay put.

**C) Prices described as "indicative" are offered as a guide rather than as a firm commitment to trade at them.**

"Indicative" prices are illustrative, showing roughly where a deal might be struck without binding anyone to trade there. Markets rely on the distinction between indicative and firm quotes, and mistaking one for the other is a costly error. The adjective performs the same guiding function elsewhere, as in indicative timetables and indicative budgets.

Guidance rather than commitment is what the label conveys, so indicative prices are being read correctly.

**D) Evidence described as "inconclusive" has settled the matter beyond further dispute.**

"Inconclusive" says the evidence failed to settle the question: it points in more than one direction or falls short of the standard required. Evidence that closed the matter would be conclusive or decisive, and the negative prefix is doing all the work between the two. Research summaries use the word honestly, to report that the study cannot support a firm answer.

**Tip:** The prefix reverses the verdict; inconclusive evidence leaves the question open.

An unsettled question is what the term reports, so inconclusive evidence has not closed the matter.

**E) A "hypothetical" scenario in a bank stress test is constructed for analysis rather than describing an event that actually occurred.**

"Hypothetical" scenarios are built deliberately for testing, describing conditions that could occur rather than ones that have. Stress testing depends on them: a severe but plausible downturn is imagined precisely so that resilience can be measured before the real thing arrives. The word marks the constructed status of the scenario, not its implausibility.

Constructed for analysis rather than historically observed is the distinction drawn, so the stress-test scenario is hypothetical.
tasks.solution_overview: Every term in this task sits somewhere on a line running from provisional to final, and the position is what the writer is communicating. Ask whether the label invites revision or closes the question, and whether a figure is offered for guidance or as a commitment. A negative prefix in the set flips one word to the unsettled end of the line.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Five accounts of the formal vocabulary used to describe how quantities move in relation to one another. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: Regional income levels that "converge" are moving closer together over time.
Model projections that "diverge" give increasingly different answers as the forecast horizon lengthens.
To report that two series "correlate" is to say that they move together, without by itself establishing that one causes the other.
Freight rates that "fluctuate" move up and down rather than following a single steady path.
A currency that "stabilises" after intervention has settled into a steadier range.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Regional income levels that "converge" are moving closer together over time.**

"Converge" describes lines approaching one another, and in economics it names the process by which poorer regions catch up with richer ones. The claim is about the gap narrowing, not about the levels being equal, so convergence can be slow and still real. Growth economists devote whole literatures to whether it happens at all.

Moving closer together is the pattern the verb traces, so regional incomes that converge are described correctly.

**B) Model projections that "diverge" give increasingly different answers as the forecast horizon lengthens.**

"Diverge" is the mirror image: paths that separate rather than approach, which is what happens to projections when small differences in assumptions compound over time. Reporting that models diverge at long horizons is a statement about growing uncertainty rather than about any single model being wrong. Climate and macroeconomic forecasting both show the pattern clearly.

Increasingly different answers over a longer horizon are what divergence means, so the account of the projections holds.

**C) To report that two series "correlate" is to say that they move together, without by itself establishing that one causes the other.**

To "correlate" is to vary together in a measurable way, which is a statement about association and nothing more. The standing caution that correlation does not establish causation exists because the two are so easily conflated in careless prose. A correlation is consistent with causation running either way, or with a third factor driving both.

**Tip:** Correlation reports company, not consequence.

Association without an automatic causal claim is what the verb licenses, so the caution about correlation is accurate.

**D) Freight rates that "fluctuate" move up and down rather than following a single steady path.**

"Fluctuate" describes irregular movement in both directions, which is why it suits freight rates responding to fuel costs, capacity and season. The verb makes no claim about an underlying trend; a series can fluctuate while drifting upwards overall. Its usefulness lies in describing the shape of the movement rather than its destination.

Up-and-down movement rather than a steady path is what the verb reports, so fluctuating freight rates fit.

**E) A currency that "stabilises" after intervention has settled into a steadier range.**

To "stabilise" is to become or be made steady, so a currency that stabilises after intervention is moving within a narrower band than before. The verb is neutral about the level reached: stabilising at a lower value is still stabilising. What it claims is a reduction in the size of the swings.

Settling into a steadier range is the outcome described, so a currency that stabilises after intervention is read correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: These verbs describe patterns over time: coming together, moving apart, moving in step, moving unevenly, and settling down. Picture the shape each one would trace on a chart and check that the account matches the picture. One item also raises the standing caution that moving together is not the same as one thing causing the other.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Five judgements about high-register connectors and Latin expressions found in legal and academic writing. Decide whether each judgement is correct.
statements: "Hitherto" means up to the present time or up to the point being described, as in a market hitherto closed to foreign banks.
"Henceforth" refers to the period before an announcement rather than the period following it.
"Insofar as the available data allow" signals that a claim is being advanced without any limitation on its scope.
Writing that a subsidy is not objectionable "per se" claims that it is objectionable in every form it could take.
A "de facto" standard is one that prevails in practice even though no law or formal agreement requires it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Hitherto" means up to the present time or up to the point being described, as in a market hitherto closed to foreign banks.**

"Hitherto" looks backwards from a moment in the text, covering everything up to that point, which is why it pairs naturally with a change that is about to be described. A market hitherto closed to foreign banks was closed until the opening being reported. The word is firmly literary and legal in register; ordinary prose would say "until now."

Up to this point is the span the adverb covers, so the market hitherto closed is described correctly.

**B) "Henceforth" refers to the period before an announcement rather than the period following it.**

"Henceforth" faces the other way: it means from this time forward, and it typically announces a rule that starts applying now. The period before the announcement would be covered by hitherto or previously, so the two adverbs divide the timeline between them. Statutory notices use henceforth precisely to mark the moment a new regime begins.

The adverb governs the period after the announcement, so henceforth cannot refer to the period before it.

**C) "Insofar as the available data allow" signals that a claim is being advanced without any limitation on its scope.**

"Insofar as" limits a claim to the extent that some condition holds, so tying an assertion to the available data restricts rather than widens it. The phrase is a hedge in formal dress, and reviewers read it as an admission that the evidence only reaches so far. An unlimited claim would drop the qualifier altogether.

**Trap:** Insofar as narrows the claim; it never enlarges it.

Scope is being restricted rather than left open, so insofar as the data allow is a hedge, not a blank cheque.

**D) Writing that a subsidy is not objectionable "per se" claims that it is objectionable in every form it could take.**

"Per se" means in itself or by its very nature, so saying a subsidy is not objectionable per se concedes that the instrument as such is acceptable while leaving room for objection to particular uses of it. The phrase is a careful narrowing device, common in competition law and policy analysis. Reading it as a universal condemnation reverses the concession being made.

The expression exempts the thing in itself while preserving case-by-case criticism, so not objectionable per se is not a universal condemnation.

**E) A "de facto" standard is one that prevails in practice even though no law or formal agreement requires it.**

"De facto" describes what holds in practice, as opposed to "de jure," which describes what holds in law. A de facto standard has been adopted widely enough to govern behaviour without any regulator mandating it, which is common in technology markets. The pair lets a writer separate practical reality from formal status in two words.

Prevailing in practice without legal backing is what the phrase marks, so a de facto standard is read correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: The expressions here are compact, and their compactness is what makes them easy to misread: each one either fixes a point in time, limits the scope of a claim, or separates what is true in practice from what is true in law. Unpack each into a plain paraphrase such as until now, from now on, to the extent that, in itself, or in practice. If the paraphrase changes the sentence's reach, the judgement has gone wrong.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five claims about formal nouns used in regulation, treaty drafting and budgeting. Decide whether each claim describes the noun correctly.
statements: A "moratorium" on deep-sea mining licences is an instruction to issue those licences faster.
A ruling described as setting a "precedent" establishes a pattern that later cases are expected to follow.
A "safeguard" clause in a trade agreement removes a country's ability to respond to a sudden surge of imports.
A "threshold" in a regulation is the level at which an obligation begins to apply.
A "contingency" in a project budget is an allowance held against events that may or may not occur.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "moratorium" on deep-sea mining licences is an instruction to issue those licences faster.**

A "moratorium" is a temporary and usually official suspension of an activity, imposed while questions about it are resolved. A moratorium on mining licences therefore stops new licences from being granted for a period, which is the reverse of acceleration. The word carries a built-in expectation that the pause will end, unlike a ban.

Suspension rather than acceleration is what the noun imposes, so a moratorium on licences stops them rather than speeding them up.

**B) A ruling described as setting a "precedent" establishes a pattern that later cases are expected to follow.**

A "precedent" is an earlier decision treated as a guide for later ones, and the whole doctrine of consistency in adjudication rests on it. Regulators and courts weigh whether a case sets a precedent because the consequences reach far beyond the parties in front of them. The adjective unprecedented, meaning without any such earlier instance, is built from the same idea.

A pattern for later cases is what the noun establishes, so a ruling that sets a precedent is described correctly.

**C) A "safeguard" clause in a trade agreement removes a country's ability to respond to a sudden surge of imports.**

A "safeguard" clause preserves a country's freedom to act, typically by allowing temporary restrictions when imports surge and injure a domestic industry. It is an escape hatch written into the agreement, not a surrender of policy space. Negotiators insist on such clauses precisely because they make deeper commitments politically possible elsewhere in the text.

**Tip:** A safeguard protects the party that invokes it; it does not disarm them.

The clause grants a response rather than removing one, so a safeguard preserves rather than strips the country's options.

**D) A "threshold" in a regulation is the level at which an obligation begins to apply.**

A "threshold" marks the point at which something begins, so a regulatory threshold is the level of turnover, emissions or headcount at which a duty switches on. Firms below it are outside the obligation and firms above it are inside, which is why the exact figure attracts so much argument. The noun keeps its architectural sense of a doorway one crosses.

The switching-on level is what the term names, so a regulatory threshold is the point at which the duty begins.

**E) A "contingency" in a project budget is an allowance held against events that may or may not occur.**

A "contingency" is provision made for something that might happen, which in budgeting means money set aside for risks that have been identified but not confirmed. Nothing about the noun implies the event will occur; it implies only that prudence requires cover. The related adjective contingent, meaning dependent on something else, shares the same uncertainty.

An allowance against uncertain events is what the budget line holds, so the contingency is described correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Each noun here names a device that governs future action: a pause, a pattern for later cases, a protective escape route, a trigger level, or money held in reserve for the unexpected. Ask what the device is for and whether the claim preserves that purpose. Two of these have been described as doing the opposite of what they exist to do.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Five descriptions of adjectives used to judge how clear an argument is and whether it can be defended. Decide whether each description is correct.
statements: Trial findings described as "equivocal" point clearly in one direction.
An "unequivocal" commitment is one hedged with enough qualifications to be read either way.
A negotiating position described as "tenable" cannot be defended against criticism.
An assumption called "untenable" has survived every attempt to challenge it.
A "spurious" correlation is one that shows up in the data without reflecting any genuine underlying relationship.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Trial findings described as "equivocal" point clearly in one direction.**

"Equivocal" findings point in more than one direction at once, leaving the reader unable to draw a single conclusion. Results that point clearly one way are unequivocal or unambiguous, and trial reports keep the distinction sharp because treatment decisions follow from it. The root, equal voices, is a useful reminder that two readings are speaking at the same volume.

Competing readings rather than a clear direction are what the adjective reports, so equivocal findings do not point one way.

**B) An "unequivocal" commitment is one hedged with enough qualifications to be read either way.**

"Unequivocal" means admitting of only one interpretation, which is why diplomatic and corporate statements are praised or attacked on precisely this ground. A commitment loaded with qualifications is hedged, equivocal or heavily caveated, the opposite condition. The negative prefix here removes the doubt rather than adding it.

Single-reading clarity is the content of the adjective, so a hedged commitment cannot be called unequivocal.

**C) A negotiating position described as "tenable" cannot be defended against criticism.**

"Tenable" describes a position that can be held, one that survives the objections brought against it. A position that collapses under criticism is untenable, and the pair maps neatly onto the military image of ground that can or cannot be defended. Formal argument uses the adjective to concede that a view is arguable without conceding that it is correct.

Defensibility is what the word grants, so a tenable negotiating position is one that can be held under criticism.

**D) An assumption called "untenable" has survived every attempt to challenge it.**

"Untenable" says the position cannot be maintained: the objections have proved decisive and the assumption has to be abandoned. Something that survived every challenge would be tenable, robust or well supported. Papers use the harsher word at the point where they discard an assumption rather than merely doubt it.

**Trap:** The prefix carries the verdict; untenable means the argument has already lost.

Surviving challenge is the reverse of what the word records, so an untenable assumption has already fallen.

**E) A "spurious" correlation is one that shows up in the data without reflecting any genuine underlying relationship.**

A "spurious" correlation is a statistical association without a real relationship behind it, typically produced by coincidence, a shared trend or a third variable driving both series. The classic examples pair unrelated time series that both happen to rise year after year. The adjective is a judgement about authenticity rather than about the strength of the measured association.

A relationship that is apparent rather than genuine is what the term names, so a spurious correlation is read correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Two pairs here differ only by a negative prefix, and the prefix is the whole argument. Read each word for whether it opens a question or closes it, and whether a position can be held under pressure or has already fallen. One final adjective concerns a relationship that looks real in the data but is not.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Five statements about the formal vocabulary of employment, fiscal policy and market conditions. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: Reducing headcount "through attrition" means allowing staff numbers to fall as people leave and are not replaced.
A programme of "austerity" involves cutting public spending, typically in order to reduce a deficit.
Consumer demand described as "buoyant" is strong and holding up well.
Trading on the exchange described as "subdued" was unusually active and heavy.
Inflation expectations described as "entrenched" have become firmly established and hard to shift.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Reducing headcount "through attrition" means allowing staff numbers to fall as people leave and are not replaced.**

"Attrition" in workforce planning means the gradual loss of staff through resignation and retirement, so reducing headcount through attrition avoids compulsory redundancies. The employer simply declines to refill posts as they empty, which is slower but far less contentious. The military sense of wearing an opponent down shares the same idea of loss over time.

Natural departures left unreplaced are the mechanism the phrase describes, so reducing headcount through attrition is right.

**B) A programme of "austerity" involves cutting public spending, typically in order to reduce a deficit.**

"Austerity" names a policy of restraint in public spending, usually adopted to bring borrowing down, and it has become the standard label for post-crisis consolidation programmes. The word is descriptive rather than technical, which is part of why it is politically loaded. Its opposite in this setting is fiscal expansion or stimulus.

Spending cuts aimed at the deficit are what the term covers, so this description of an austerity programme is accurate.

**C) Consumer demand described as "buoyant" is strong and holding up well.**

"Buoyant" carries the image of something floating high, so buoyant demand is strong and resisting downward pressure. Commentary pairs the adjective with demand, markets and revenues when they hold up better than expected. Its natural opposites, flat or depressed, would report the same variable performing poorly.

Strength that is holding up is the picture the adjective paints, so buoyant consumer demand is read correctly.

**D) Trading on the exchange described as "subdued" was unusually active and heavy.**

"Subdued" describes activity that is quieter and weaker than usual, which is why it attaches to thin trading sessions and soft demand. Unusually heavy activity would be reported as brisk, active or heavy, and market commentary keeps the vocabularies apart because they signal opposite conditions to a reader scanning quickly. The word suggests something held down rather than merely small.

Quiet trading is what the adjective reports, so pairing subdued with unusually heavy activity contradicts the term.

**E) Inflation expectations described as "entrenched" have become firmly established and hard to shift.**

"Entrenched" describes something dug in and resistant to change, so entrenched inflation expectations have settled into how firms and households plan. Central bankers fear the condition because dislodging it costs far more than preventing it. The metaphor of a trench captures both the firmness and the difficulty of removal.

Firmly established and hard to shift is what the adjective conveys, so entrenched inflation expectations fit.
tasks.solution_overview: Reports on labour markets and public finances use a compact set of terms for shrinking a workforce quietly, tightening budgets, and describing activity as strong, weak or stubbornly fixed. Ask what each word tells you about direction and about strength, and be alert to one adjective that has been paired with conditions of the opposite kind. The rest describe exactly what their plain paraphrases suggest.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five accounts of terms that classify claims and objections in academic and policy argument. Decide whether each account is accurate.
statements: A "substantive" objection to a proposal concerns its merits rather than the manner in which it was handled.
A "procedural" objection concerns how a decision was reached rather than whether the decision itself was right.
A "normative" claim states what ought to be the case, as when an economist argues that regional inequality should be reduced.
In that same contrast, a "positive" statement describes what is the case and can in principle be tested against evidence.
"Qualitative" evidence describes characteristics and reasons in words rather than measuring them in numbers.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "substantive" objection to a proposal concerns its merits rather than the manner in which it was handled.**

"Substantive" points to the substance of a matter: the merits, the content, the thing itself rather than the wrapping around it. A substantive objection says the proposal is wrong, not that it arrived late or was tabled by the wrong committee. The adjective is also used to mark real as opposed to token change, as in substantive reform.

Merits rather than handling is the division the word draws, so a substantive objection is described correctly.

**B) A "procedural" objection concerns how a decision was reached rather than whether the decision itself was right.**

"Procedural" concerns the route by which a decision was reached, including notice, consultation and voting rules. A procedural objection can succeed even when the underlying decision is popular, because the process itself failed. Administrative law depends on the separation, since courts often review process where they will not review merits.

How the decision was made rather than whether it was correct is the scope of the term, so the procedural objection holds.

**C) A "normative" claim states what ought to be the case, as when an economist argues that regional inequality should be reduced.**

"Normative" claims are about what ought to be, and they rest on values that evidence alone cannot settle. Arguing that inequality should be reduced is a normative position however much data accompanies it. Economists flag the label so that readers can see where description ends and advocacy begins.

A claim about what ought to be is what the term identifies, so the normative argument about inequality is accurate.

**D) In that same contrast, a "positive" statement describes what is the case and can in principle be tested against evidence.**

"Positive" in this technical contrast has nothing to do with optimism: it marks a statement about what is the case, framed so that evidence could in principle confirm or refute it. A claim that a tax rise reduced consumption by two per cent is positive; a claim that it should not have been imposed is normative. Keeping the two apart is the first discipline of economic writing.

**Tip:** Positive describes; normative prescribes. Optimism plays no part in either.

A testable description of what is the case is the sense in play, so the positive statement is read correctly.

**E) "Qualitative" evidence describes characteristics and reasons in words rather than measuring them in numbers.**

"Qualitative" evidence works in categories, descriptions and reasons rather than in measured quantities, which is why interviews and case studies fall under the heading. It answers how and why questions that a table of figures cannot, and mixed-method work uses it alongside quantitative data rather than instead of it. The contrast is about the form of the evidence, not its quality despite the similarity of the words.

Description in words rather than measurement in numbers is the distinction drawn, so qualitative evidence fits.
tasks.solution_overview: Argument in formal settings is sorted by type before it is judged on strength: merits against process, what ought to be against what is, and evidence in words against evidence in numbers. Ask what kind of claim is being made rather than whether it is convincing. Getting the category right is what these five terms are for.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: A final set of five statements about formal words describing the scale and pace of change. Decide whether each statement is accurate.
statements: A "comprehensive" review of trade policy covers the whole of its subject rather than a selected part of it.
Reform described as "incremental" is delivered in a single sweeping change.
A "wholesale" restructuring of a ministry is a sweeping change affecting the organisation as a whole.
A "piecemeal" approach to regulation proceeds according to a single coordinated plan.
A risk described as "systemic" threatens the functioning of an entire financial system rather than one firm within it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A "comprehensive" review of trade policy covers the whole of its subject rather than a selected part of it.**

"Comprehensive" claims full coverage of the field in question, which is a strong promise and one readers test. A review that examined tariffs but ignored services would be partial or selective, whatever its title says. The adjective is about breadth rather than depth, so a comprehensive review can still be shallow in places.

Covering the whole subject is what the word undertakes, so a comprehensive review is described correctly.

**B) Reform described as "incremental" is delivered in a single sweeping change.**

"Incremental" change arrives in small successive steps, each building modestly on the last, which is the opposite of a single sweeping move. Policy analysis contrasts incrementalism with radical or big-bang reform precisely because the political economy of the two differs so sharply. Nothing in the word suggests the total change is small; only that it is delivered gradually.

**Tip:** Incremental describes the pace of delivery, not the size of the destination.

Step-by-step delivery is what the adjective specifies, so incremental reform is not a single sweeping change.

**C) A "wholesale" restructuring of a ministry is a sweeping change affecting the organisation as a whole.**

"Wholesale" used adjectivally of change means done on a large scale and across the board, as in wholesale restructuring or wholesale replacement of a management team. The commercial sense of selling in bulk to retailers is a separate branch of the word, and context keeps them apart without difficulty. Here the adjective reports the breadth of the shake-up.

Sweeping change across the organisation is what the word conveys, so wholesale restructuring is apt.

**D) A "piecemeal" approach to regulation proceeds according to a single coordinated plan.**

"Piecemeal" describes action taken bit by bit without an overall design, and it is nearly always a criticism when applied to regulation. A single coordinated plan would be described as systematic, integrated or coherent, the very qualities the word says are missing. The complaint behind it is that fragments accumulate into something no one designed.

Uncoordinated fragments rather than a unified plan are what the adjective reports, so piecemeal regulation is misdescribed here.

**E) A risk described as "systemic" threatens the functioning of an entire financial system rather than one firm within it.**

"Systemic" risk threatens the operation of a whole system, which in finance means the failure of one institution cascading through the connections that bind the rest. Regulators separate it from firm-specific risk because the tools required are entirely different. It is worth keeping apart from systematic, which describes something done according to a method or an error that runs consistently in one direction.

Danger to the system as a whole is what the adjective identifies, so systemic risk is read correctly.
tasks.solution_overview: Scope and pace are the two questions running through this closing task: does the change cover everything or only parts, and does it arrive all at once or step by step. Two of the words describe sweeping coverage, two describe fragmentary or gradual action, and one names risk that spreads through a whole system. Matching each word to the right corner of that grid settles the set.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Five claims about pairs of near-synonyms used in workplace and business writing. Decide whether each account of their overlap and difference is accurate.
statements: "Wage" and "salary" are fully interchangeable, so an assembly worker paid by the hour and a manager paid a fixed annual sum are described with the same word in careful reporting.

"Strategy" names the overall plan a ministry commits to, while "tactic" names one concrete move used to carry it out, so a decarbonisation strategy can be delivered through a public procurement tactic.
Because "client" and "customer" overlap, an accountancy firm's long-standing advisory relationships are normally called its "customers" in professional writing.
"Keen" is only ever a criticism in business English, so telling a recruiter that a candidate is keen to relocate signals reluctance.
"Fewer" and "less" differ only in formality, which is why careful writers prefer "less delivery delays" in a formal supply-chain report.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Wage" and "salary" are fully interchangeable, so an assembly worker paid by the hour and a manager paid a fixed annual sum are described with the same word in careful reporting.**

Both words name pay for work, and real employment arrangements sometimes blur the boundary. In careful reporting, however, a wage is typically calculated by the hour, day or shift, whereas a salary is a fixed sum quoted for a longer period, usually a year. Salaried staff may receive overtime, but that possibility does not erase the usual contrast in how their basic pay is expressed.

The terms overlap broadly but are not fully interchangeable, so using one label for both payment structures loses a useful distinction.

**B) "Strategy" names the overall plan a ministry commits to, while "tactic" names one concrete move used to carry it out, so a decarbonisation strategy can be delivered through a public procurement tactic.**

A strategy sets the direction and the reasoning behind it, usually over years and across departments. A tactic is one of the moves chosen to serve that direction, and it can be replaced without the larger aim changing. Buying only low-emission vehicles is exactly that kind of move inside a wider climate plan.

Scope is what separates the pair, and the sentence keeps each word at its own level, so the description is sound.

**C) Because "client" and "customer" overlap, an accountancy firm's long-standing advisory relationships are normally called its "customers" in professional writing.**

Both words name someone who pays for something, but the professions have settled on client for continuing relationships built on advice, expertise and confidentiality.
