Customer suits one-off buyers of goods and standard services, which is the language of retailers and utilities. A firm advising the same organisation for years sits squarely in the first group.

Continuing professional advice calls for clients, so the wording recommended here reads as a downgrade of the relationship rather than a neutral alternative.

**D) "Keen" is only ever a criticism in business English, so telling a recruiter that a candidate is keen to relocate signals reluctance.**

Keen most often means eager or enthusiastic, and keen to plus a verb is one of the standard ways of reporting willingness. The adjective has a second sense of sharp, as in a keen eye for irregular invoices, but neither reading is negative. A candidate described as keen to relocate is being presented as ready and willing.

Enthusiasm rather than reluctance is what the phrase conveys, so the negative reading offered here misses the ordinary meaning of the word.

**E) "Fewer" and "less" differ only in formality, which is why careful writers prefer "less delivery delays" in a formal supply-chain report.**

The choice between them turns on whether the noun can be counted, not on how formal the sentence is. Delays arrive one at a time and take a plural, so they call for fewer, while an uncountable mass such as congestion or capacity takes less. Formality has no bearing on the rule, and casual speech breaks it as often as official prose.

Countability decides this pair, so the recommended phrasing fails and careful reporting asks for fewer delivery delays.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these lines test structure rather than meaning, so ask whether pay is calculated from hours or fixed by the year, whether a plan sets direction or executes it, and whether a noun can be counted at all. The client and customer contrast turns on how continuing and advisory the relationship is, while keen is worth checking against both of its ordinary senses, eager and sharp. Substituting the other member of each pair into the sentence usually makes the mismatch audible.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Each line below compares two words that report the same act in a different tone or register. Judge whether the comparison matches standard usage.
statements: "Refuse" is the blunter of the two verbs, while "decline" is the more formal and face-saving choice, so a supplier that declines an invitation to tender sounds politer than one that refuses it.
"Readership" is the word for the people who watch a televised policy briefing, while "audience" is reserved for the subscribers of a newspaper.
"Purchase" is the more formal partner of "buy," so a procurement report may record that a hospital purchased ventilators where a message to a colleague would say it bought them.
"Issue" is always harsher than "problem," which is why a diplomat who raises an issue is understood to be escalating a dispute.
"Remuneration" is the everyday, informal word for pay and would look out of place in a company's annual report.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Refuse" is the blunter of the two verbs, while "decline" is the more formal and face-saving choice, so a supplier that declines an invitation to tender sounds politer than one that refuses it.**

Both verbs report a no, which is why they are so often swapped. Refuse states the rejection flatly and can suggest resistance, while decline wraps the same answer in courtesy and often leaves the reason unspoken. Formal correspondence leans on the second for exactly that reason.

Politeness rather than the content of the answer is what separates them, and the sentence lines the pair up correctly, so it holds.

**B) "Readership" is the word for the people who watch a televised policy briefing, while "audience" is reserved for the subscribers of a newspaper.**

Readership counts the people who read a publication, and it belongs with newspapers, journals and reports. Audience is the wider word for those who listen to or watch something, from a broadcast briefing to a conference talk. The sentence has handed each word the other's territory.

**Trap:** Both words describe reach, which makes the swap easy to miss when the topic is media coverage.

Viewers form an audience and subscribers a readership, so the two labels here have simply been exchanged.

**C) "Purchase" is the more formal partner of "buy," so a procurement report may record that a hospital purchased ventilators where a message to a colleague would say it bought them.**

The two verbs describe the same transaction, and no difference of meaning separates them. What differs is register: purchase belongs to contracts, invoices and official reports, while buy is the everyday word in speech and informal writing. Choosing between them is a decision about the document rather than about the goods.

Register is the only variable in play, and the sentence assigns each verb to the right kind of text, so the account stands.

**D) "Issue" is always harsher than "problem," which is why a diplomat who raises an issue is understood to be escalating a dispute.**

Issue is normally the softer of the two, naming a matter that is up for discussion without insisting that something has gone wrong. Problem states plainly that there is a fault to fix, which is why it sounds more accusatory across a negotiating table. Diplomats reach for issue precisely to keep the temperature down.

The direction of the contrast is reversed here, so raising an issue signals room to talk rather than escalation.

**E) "Remuneration" is the everyday, informal word for pay and would look out of place in a company's annual report.**

Remuneration is a formal, institutional term covering salary, bonuses, pensions and benefits in kind, and annual reports devote whole sections to it. The everyday words are pay, wages and, in conversation, money. Nobody discusses their remuneration over lunch.

**Tip:** Long Latinate nouns of this kind usually mark the formal end of a register scale.

The word belongs to exactly the document the sentence rules it out of, so its account of the register is upside down.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines are decided by register and tone rather than by dictionary meaning, so ask which document each word would appear in before judging the claim. Refuse and decline both say no, purchase and buy both name a transaction, and remuneration and pay both name money; what changes is how formal or how blunt the choice sounds. The readership and audience pair is the exception, and it is settled by whether people are reading or watching.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements about word pairs that survive into official and statistical writing. Decide whether each distinction is drawn correctly.
statements: "House" points at the building, while "household" points at the people who share it, so statistics on household spending count occupants rather than roofs.
"Forecast" describes a rough calculation of a quantity that already exists, while "estimate" always projects a value into the future.
"Assist" is the more formal sibling of "help," so a public agency's guidance is more likely to say it assists applicants than that it helps them out.
"Price" is what a buyer pays, while "cost" is what production consumes, so a chipmaker can raise its price without any change in what a wafer costs to make.
"Ability" and "capability" are indistinguishable, so nothing would be gained by choosing one over the other when describing a port's potential throughput after new investment.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "House" points at the building, while "household" points at the people who share it, so statistics on household spending count occupants rather than roofs.**

A house is a physical structure and can stand empty for years. A household is the social unit living together and pooling resources, which is why surveys ask about household income, size and spending. One dwelling can contain several households, and a household can occupy something that is not a house at all.

People or bricks is the whole of the distinction, and the sentence keeps them apart, so the description works.

**B) "Forecast" describes a rough calculation of a quantity that already exists, while "estimate" always projects a value into the future.**

An estimate is an approximate value based on incomplete evidence, and it can concern the past, present or future. A forecast is specifically a reasoned statement about a future condition, such as tomorrow's weather or next year's inflation. The words can overlap when a future number is estimated, but only forecast builds the forward time reference into the label.

The sentence assigns the future meaning to the wrong word and makes estimate far too narrow, so the proposed distinction is reversed.

**C) "Assist" is the more formal sibling of "help," so a public agency's guidance is more likely to say it assists applicants than that it helps them out.**

The two verbs report the same act of support. Assist carries an official, professional tone and sits comfortably in guidance notes, job descriptions and legal text, while help is the plain everyday choice and pairs freely with particles such as out. Institutions reach for the formal option to sound impartial.

Register does the work here, and the sentence matches each verb to the setting that suits it, so the line is accurate.

**D) "Price" is what a buyer pays, while "cost" is what production consumes, so a chipmaker can raise its price without any change in what a wafer costs to make.**

A price is the amount a seller asks or a buyer pays for a product. A production cost is the value of the labour, materials, energy and capital consumed in making it, although cost can also describe expenditure from a buyer's perspective. In this manufacturing context the two figures can move independently, which is why a higher selling price can widen a margin without any change in wafer costs.

The sentence uses price for the market charge and cost for the production input, so its contextual distinction is sound.

**E) "Ability" and "capability" are indistinguishable, so nothing would be gained by choosing one over the other when describing a port's potential throughput after new investment.**

Ability and capability overlap, and either can sometimes describe what a person or system can do. Capability more readily carries a planning sense: the potential made available by particular equipment, expertise or investment, whereas ability often points to demonstrated performance. A port's throughput after new cranes are installed is therefore naturally framed as a capability that the investment would create.

Because capability can foreground conditional potential in a way ability need not, calling the pair indistinguishable misses a useful nuance in this example.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line asks you to place a word on a scale rather than to define it outright: physical against social, informal against official, present against future. House and household separate a building from its occupants, help and assist separate everyday from institutional tone, and estimate and forecast separate a present quantity from one still to come. For price and cost, and for ability and capability, decide whose perspective the sentence takes before accepting the equivalence it offers.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Five claims about how far a word stretches beyond its most literal use. Decide whether each description of the pair is accurate.
statements: "Border" usually marks a line between territories, while "boundary" can also mark the limits of an idea, so a study can push the boundaries of a discipline but not its borders.
"Sparse" and "scarce" carry exactly the same emphasis, so a thinly scattered network of charging points and a genuine shortage of lithium are described identically.
"Monitor" means to watch and record over time, while "supervise" adds authority over the people involved, so a sensor can monitor emissions but only an inspector supervises staff.
"Partly" simply says to some extent, while "partially" tends to stress that a whole is incomplete, so a partially restored grid sounds more unfinished than a partly funded scheme.
"Utilise" is the heavier, more technical partner of "use," so a policy brief saying that a laboratory utilises spare capacity sounds more formal than one saying it uses it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Border" usually marks a line between territories, while "boundary" can also mark the limits of an idea, so a study can push the boundaries of a discipline but not its borders.**

Border is overwhelmingly geographical and political: it separates one jurisdiction from the next and gets patrolled. Boundary keeps that physical use but extends comfortably into the abstract, covering the edges of a field, a definition or a remit. That is why research pushes boundaries while customs officers work at borders.

The abstract reach of one word and not the other is the point at issue, and the sentence states it correctly, so the contrast holds.

**B) "Sparse" and "scarce" carry exactly the same emphasis, so a thinly scattered network of charging points and a genuine shortage of lithium are described identically.**

Sparse is about distribution: things are present but thinly spread across space or a page. Scarce is about supply measured against demand, which is a claim about shortage rather than spacing. A charging network can be sparse while the electricity behind it is abundant, and a metal can be scarce even where it is concentrated in a single mine.

**Trap:** Both words leave an impression of not much, which hides the fact that they measure different things.

Spread and shortage are separate ideas, so the two descriptions in this sentence cannot be collapsed into one.

**C) "Monitor" means to watch and record over time, while "supervise" adds authority over the people involved, so a sensor can monitor emissions but only an inspector supervises staff.**

Monitoring is observation with a record attached, and instruments do it as readily as people. Supervising presupposes responsibility for someone's work and the standing to direct it, which is why the word implies a human in charge. Equipment can watch a chimney stack; it cannot hold anyone to account.

Authority over people is the extra ingredient in the second verb, and the sentence places it exactly there, so the line is sound.

**D) "Partly" simply says to some extent, while "partially" tends to stress that a whole is incomplete, so a partially restored grid sounds more unfinished than a partly funded scheme.**

The two adverbs overlap so heavily that many sentences accept either. Where they part company, partly divides a cause or a reason into shares, as in partly because of weather, while partially draws attention to an incomplete state of something that ought to be whole. Restoration is a process with a finished state in view, which is why the second sounds like work still outstanding.

Emphasis rather than meaning separates them, and the sentence describes that emphasis accurately, so it stands.

**E) "Utilise" is the heavier, more technical partner of "use," so a policy brief saying that a laboratory utilises spare capacity sounds more formal than one saying it uses it.**

Use is the neutral everyday verb for putting something to a purpose. Utilise can suggest making practical or effective use of something, but it is also widely chosen as a more technical-sounding substitute even when that nuance adds little. In this sentence about spare capacity, the main audible difference is the heavier institutional register.

The policy-brief version does sound more formal with utilises, so the register contrast described here is genuine.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines test how far a word can stretch beyond its most literal use and what it quietly adds when it does. Boundary reaches into abstraction where border stays on the map, monitor records where supervise commands, and utilise merely raises the tone that use already carries. For sparse and scarce, keep distribution and shortage apart, and for partly and partially, notice which one leaves a whole visibly unfinished.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Each statement pairs a narrow word with a broader one from the language of work and public programmes. Judge whether the contrast holds.
statements: "Convince" works on what someone believes, while "persuade" works on what someone does, so an audit can convince a board that a risk is real and then persuade it to act.
"Job" names a particular post, while "career" names the longer path built out of such posts, so losing a job need not end a career.
"Funds" is the institutional partner of "money," which is why a recovery programme releases funds rather than simply handing over money.
"Inform" is the formal choice and normally takes a person as its object, so a regulator informs a firm of a breach while a colleague simply tells you about it.
"Workforce" is a collective noun for everyone an employer engages, while "worker" names one of them, so a four-day week reshapes a workforce rather than a worker.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Convince" works on what someone believes, while "persuade" works on what someone does, so an audit can convince a board that a risk is real and then persuade it to act.**

The traditional careful distinction pairs convince with belief, often in a that-clause, and persuade with action, often in a to-infinitive. Modern usage does allow some overlap, especially convince someone to do something, but believing a risk exists and agreeing to act on it remain separate outcomes. The sentence stages those outcomes with the clearest conventional pattern.

Belief takes convince and action takes persuade here, so the contrast is accurately drawn without requiring the verbs to be absolute opposites.

**B) "Job" names a particular post, while "career" names the longer path built out of such posts, so losing a job need not end a career.**

A job is bounded by an employer, a title and a contract. A career runs across those boundaries and takes in training, promotions and moves between organisations. That is why redundancy is described as the loss of a job rather than the loss of a career.

Scale over time is what separates the two nouns, and the sentence draws a conclusion that follows from it, so the line is accurate.

**C) "Funds" is the institutional partner of "money," which is why a recovery programme releases funds rather than simply handing over money.**

Both words name purchasing power, but funds implies an allocated pool with a purpose and an accounting trail attached. Money is the general everyday term and carries no sense of earmarking. Public programmes talk about funds because the sums are budgeted, conditional and audited.

Allocation and formality separate the pair, and the sentence attaches each word to the setting that suits it, so the description works.

**D) "Inform" is the formal choice and normally takes a person as its object, so a regulator informs a firm of a breach while a colleague simply tells you about it.**

Tell and inform both transfer information, and both take a person as object, but inform belongs to official notification and often pairs with of. Its formality is part of why regulators, courts and employers use it in writing that may later be relied on. Tell delivers the same content in conversational clothes.

Official notice and ordinary conversation are exactly where these verbs part company, and the sentence separates them, so it holds.

**E) "Workforce" is a collective noun for everyone an employer engages, while "worker" names one of them, so a four-day week reshapes a workforce rather than a worker.**

Workforce refers to the whole body of employees and appears throughout statistics on participation and skills. Worker picks out an individual and can be counted one by one. A policy that changes the standard week applies across the group even though each person experiences it separately.

Collective against individual is the whole of the contrast, and the sentence respects it, so the wording is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Each pair here divides work between a narrow and a broad member, or between an everyday and an official one. Ask whether the sentence aims at belief or action for convince and persuade, at one post or a lifetime of them for job and career, and at one person or the whole payroll for worker and workforce. Funds and inform simply raise the register of money and tell, so the test is which kind of document the word belongs in.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Claims about how technical or how formal a word is. Decide whether each account matches careful usage.
statements: In careful economic writing, "risk" and "uncertainty" name the same thing, since both describe outcomes whose probabilities are fully known.
"Estimate" implies a calculation resting on some evidence, while "guess" implies none, so a modelled estimate of annual ice loss is not simply a guess.
"Observe" is the more casual of the two verbs, so a field report on tern colonies would say researchers saw the birds rather than that they observed them.
"Request" is the formal counterpart of "ask," so a ministry requests supporting documents in a letter while a caller simply asks for them.
"Get" is the register-appropriate verb for formal procurement writing, so a tender document would normally state that a hospital got its supplies rather than obtained them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In careful economic writing, "risk" and "uncertainty" name the same thing, since both describe outcomes whose probabilities are fully known.**

Risk is the case where outcomes can be listed and probabilities attached, which is what makes insurance and pricing possible. Uncertainty covers situations where those probabilities are not available at all, and economists have kept the terms apart for a century for that reason. It is why a policy paper can call a hazard deeply uncertain rather than merely risky.

**Trap:** Everyday speech does treat the two as synonyms, which is why the technical split is so easy to overlook.

Known odds belong to only one member of the pair, so the equation offered here erases the difference the terms exist to mark.

**B) "Estimate" implies a calculation resting on some evidence, while "guess" implies none, so a modelled estimate of annual ice loss is not simply a guess.**

An estimate is an approximate figure reached from measurements, assumptions or a stated method. A guess is ordinarily an answer offered without enough evidence or calculation, although an educated guess may draw on limited knowledge. A model of annual ice loss can be inspected, challenged and rerun, which gives its output an evidential basis that a mere guess lacks.

The modelled figure is therefore properly called an estimate rather than an unsupported guess, so the distinction works in this context.

**C) "Observe" is the more casual of the two verbs, so a field report on tern colonies would say researchers saw the birds rather than that they observed them.**

Observe is the technical verb of systematic watching and carries the sense of recording under some protocol. See is the plain everyday verb and says nothing about method. Scientific reporting therefore prefers observed, and often specifies how many hours of observation lie behind a figure.

The register labels are the wrong way round, so a field report would record that researchers observed the colonies.

**D) "Request" is the formal counterpart of "ask," so a ministry requests supporting documents in a letter while a caller simply asks for them.**

Both verbs seek something from someone, and neither is stronger than the other in force. Request is the written, official form and appears in correspondence, forms and procedures, while ask is unmarked and conversational. The setting decides which one a writer reaches for.

The sentence lines the formal verb up with official correspondence and the plain one with speech, so its account of the pair is right.

**E) "Get" is the register-appropriate verb for formal procurement writing, so a tender document would normally state that a hospital got its supplies rather than obtained them.**

Get is the most flexible and least formal verb in this family, which is why it dominates speech and almost disappears from contracts. Obtain, acquire and procure carry the formality that tender documents need while naming the same act of coming into possession. Formal writing avoids get precisely because it sounds casual.

**Tip:** If the sentence would sit in a signed document, the plain verb usually gives way to the Latinate one.

The formality ranking here is inverted, so the tender would state that the hospital obtained its supplies.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these lines turn on how technical a word is and two on how formal, so decide first whether the claim concerns method or tone. Risk and uncertainty split on whether probabilities can be attached, and estimate and guess on whether any calculation lies behind the figure. For observe, request and get, imagine the sentence inside a scientific report or a signed contract and see which member of the pair survives.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Five descriptions of near-synonyms used in regulation, pay and public health writing. Decide whether each one is accurate.
statements: "Readership" counts the people who attend a live briefing, so a think tank reporting turnout at its launch event is reporting its readership.
"Remuneration" refers to unpaid voluntary contributions, which is why board members who serve without pay still have remuneration to report.
"Continual" suggests something repeated at intervals, while "continuous" suggests no break at all, so continual outages are not the same as a continuous power supply.
"Assert" presents a claim as confident fact, while "allege" flags it as unproven, so a competition authority that alleges price-fixing has not yet asserted it as established.
"Mitigate" means to make something less severe rather than to remove it, so flood defences can mitigate damage without eliminating the hazard.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Readership" counts the people who attend a live briefing, so a think tank reporting turnout at its launch event is reporting its readership.**

Readership is built from readers and measures how many people a written publication reaches. Those who turn up to hear a speaker form an audience, and organisers count attendance rather than circulation. Nothing about a launch event involves reading at all.

The word tracks readers only, so turnout at a briefing belongs to the think tank's audience instead.

**B) "Remuneration" refers to unpaid voluntary contributions, which is why board members who serve without pay still have remuneration to report.**

Remuneration means payment for work or services and covers salary, fees, bonuses and benefits in kind. Unpaid service is the absence of remuneration, which is exactly why annual reports state when a director receives none. The word is formal rather than negative or voluntary.

Payment is built into the meaning, so unpaid service cannot be remuneration by definition.

**C) "Continual" suggests something repeated at intervals, while "continuous" suggests no break at all, so continual outages are not the same as a continuous power supply.**

Continual events stop and start: they recur often enough to be a nuisance but remain countable episodes. Continuous describes an unbroken state or process with no gaps in it. Outages are separate events, while a supply that never fails is a single uninterrupted condition.

**Tip:** If you could count the occurrences, the repeated word is the one you want.

Repetition and unbrokenness are different pictures, and the sentence sorts them correctly, so it holds.

**D) "Assert" presents a claim as confident fact, while "allege" flags it as unproven, so a competition authority that alleges price-fixing has not yet asserted it as established.**

Assert puts the speaker's own weight behind a statement and invites the reader to take it as settled. Allege reports a claim while withholding that endorsement, which is why legal and journalistic writing leans on it before any finding is made. The choice of verb is a statement about the evidence rather than about the strength of feeling.

Endorsement is exactly what separates them, and the sentence describes that gap accurately, so the contrast is well drawn.

**E) "Mitigate" means to make something less severe rather than to remove it, so flood defences can mitigate damage without eliminating the hazard.**

Mitigation reduces the force or the consequences of a problem that remains in place. Elimination removes the problem itself, which is a far stronger claim and rarely available. Barriers and drainage lower the depth and spread of flooding while the river continues to rise.

Reduction and removal are different promises, and the sentence keeps the weaker one where it belongs, so the line is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Half of this set tests whether a word's meaning has been swapped for its neighbour's, and half tests how strong a claim the word actually makes. Readership and remuneration each have a plain core, readers and payment, that the lines above quietly contradict. For continual, allege and mitigate, ask whether the sentence describes repeated events, an endorsed claim, or a problem reduced rather than removed.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Statements about pairs that differ in structure, intention or countability rather than in basic meaning. Judge each against standard usage.
statements: "Wage" typically attaches to pay calculated from hours or shifts, while "salary" is a fixed periodic sum, so overtime sits naturally with the first and awkwardly with the second.
"Ability" describes what someone can already do, while "capability" often stresses potential capacity under the right conditions, so a plant's capability can exceed its present ability to deliver.
"Postpone" implies a deliberate decision to move something to a later date, while "delay" can be accidental, so a shipment delayed by a storm was not postponed by the exporter.
"Fewer" is the careful choice before uncountable nouns, which is why a formal audit should report "fewer evidence" of price manipulation.
"Decline" softens a refusal by leaving the reason unstated, so a minister who declines to comment has still refused, only more diplomatically.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Wage" typically attaches to pay calculated from hours or shifts, while "salary" is a fixed periodic sum, so overtime sits naturally with the first and awkwardly with the second.**

A wage is typically calculated from time worked, so overtime hours can directly raise the amount due. A salary is a fixed periodic sum for a role, commonly quoted by year, although salaried employees can still qualify for overtime pay under a contract or the law. The contrast is therefore about the usual basis of basic pay, not a ban on overtime for salaried staff.

Overtime is more naturally built into wage calculation than salary calculation, so the sentence captures the normal pattern.

**B) "Ability" describes what someone can already do, while "capability" often stresses potential capacity under the right conditions, so a plant's capability can exceed its present ability to deliver.**

Ability reports a current, demonstrated competence. Capability points at what could be achieved given investment, training or favourable conditions, which is why it appears in planning documents rather than performance reviews. A factory with new equipment installed but staff still in training illustrates the gap precisely.

Present performance against unlocked potential is the difference, and the sentence builds its example on it, so the account holds.

**C) "Postpone" implies a deliberate decision to move something to a later date, while "delay" can be accidental, so a shipment delayed by a storm was not postponed by the exporter.**

Postponing is an act with an agent behind it and usually a new date attached. Delay simply reports that something happened later than planned, whatever the cause, and weather is a classic cause with no decision behind it. The two verbs therefore assign responsibility very differently.

Agency is the deciding factor, and the sentence places it correctly, so the distinction is sound.

**D) "Fewer" is the careful choice before uncountable nouns, which is why a formal audit should report "fewer evidence" of price manipulation.**

Fewer goes with plural countable nouns, so we write fewer complaints, fewer suppliers, fewer breaches. Evidence is uncountable in ordinary usage and takes less, or is recast as fewer items of evidence when a count is genuinely intended. Formality does not change which form a noun accepts.

**Trap:** Advice to prefer fewer in careful writing applies to countable nouns only; it is not a general upgrade over less.

The noun refuses the count, so the phrasing fails and an audit would report less evidence of price manipulation.

**E) "Decline" softens a refusal by leaving the reason unstated, so a minister who declines to comment has still refused, only more diplomatically.**

Declining and refusing produce the same outcome: the request is not granted. Decline is the courteous, formal option and often stands alone without explanation, which is how declined to comment became a fixed phrase in reporting. Refuse sounds more forceful and invites the question of why.

The sentence acknowledges the shared outcome and locates the difference in tone, which is exactly where it lies, so the line stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines separate near-synonyms by structure or intention rather than by meaning: how pay is calculated, whether a result is already achieved, and whether anyone chose the outcome. Wage against salary, ability against capability, and postpone against delay all reward that question. The fewer line is settled instead by whether the noun can be counted, and the decline line by tone rather than force.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each line offers an equivalence or a ranking between two words used in economics and management. Decide whether it survives inspection.
statements: "Hazard" and "risk" mean the same thing in safety writing, so a chemical's hazard and the risk of exposure to it are measured in the same way.
"Tactic" is the broader and more abstract member of the pair, so a firm's decade-long direction is its tactic and a single price cut is its strategy.
"Shortage" describes a temporary gap between supply and demand, while "scarcity" describes a lasting condition of limited supply, so a chip shortage differs from the scarcity of rare earth deposits.
"Issue" can only mean a numbered edition of a publication, so a committee cannot describe unresolved funding questions as issues.
"Efficient" and "effective" are interchangeable labels, so a programme that reaches its target while wasting most of its budget is equally well described by either.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Hazard" and "risk" mean the same thing in safety writing, so a chemical's hazard and the risk of exposure to it are measured in the same way.**

A hazard is the property of something that could cause harm, and it belongs to the substance or the situation itself. Risk combines that potential with the likelihood and severity of actual exposure, which is why assessments bring the two together. A sealed drum of a highly hazardous solvent can present very little risk.

**Tip:** Hazard asks what could hurt you; risk asks how likely and how badly.

Potential harm and expected harm are different quantities, so treating the words as one collapses the whole logic of assessment.

**B) "Tactic" is the broader and more abstract member of the pair, so a firm's decade-long direction is its tactic and a single price cut is its strategy.**

Strategy is the wide, long-horizon plan, and tactics are the specific moves that serve it. A ten-year positioning decision is exactly what a strategy names, while a discount in one quarter is a move within it. The vocabulary of scope runs in the opposite direction to the one described here.

The labels have been exchanged, so the decade-long direction is the strategy and the price cut the tactic.

**C) "Shortage" describes a temporary gap between supply and demand, while "scarcity" describes a lasting condition of limited supply, so a chip shortage differs from the scarcity of rare earth deposits.**

A shortage is a supply shortfall at a given price or in a particular period, often caused by disrupted logistics or capacity and therefore often temporary. Scarcity is the broader economic condition in which available resources are limited relative to competing wants; it can persist even when markets clear. Duration is a strong tendency rather than an exceptionless definition, but chips and rare earth deposits illustrate the usual contrast well.

The first example is a time-bound market shortfall and the second a structural limitation, so the distinction is sound in the contexts given.

**D) "Issue" can only mean a numbered edition of a publication, so a committee cannot describe unresolved funding questions as issues.**

The publication sense is real but it is one of several. Issue also names a matter under discussion, and that sense is standard in minutes, agendas and policy papers. It works as a verb too, as when a regulator issues guidance.

**Trap:** A word having a specialist sense does not lock out its everyday one.

The discussion sense is ordinary English, so restricting the noun to magazine editions does not survive contact with usage.

**E) "Efficient" and "effective" are interchangeable labels, so a programme that reaches its target while wasting most of its budget is equally well described by either.**

Effective asks a yes-or-no question: did the intended result occur? Efficient asks about the ratio between that result and the resources consumed. A programme can succeed expensively, which makes it effective and inefficient at the same time.

The example given is precisely the case where the two words come apart, so calling them interchangeable cannot hold.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line offers an equivalence or a ranking, and the work is to check it against what the words actually measure. Hazard and risk differ over whether likelihood of exposure is included, strategy and tactic over scope, and shortage and scarcity over how temporary the gap is. Efficient and effective come apart whenever a result is achieved wastefully, which is the test the last line invites you to apply.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Five contrasts drawn from finance, professional services and media measurement. Decide whether each distinction is accurate.
statements: "Client" leans towards an ongoing professional relationship, while "customer" covers ordinary buyers, so a consultancy keeps clients and a supermarket serves customers.
"Revenue" is everything a firm takes in, while "profit" is what survives after costs, so revenue can rise in a year that ends with a loss.
"Estimate" and "forecast" overlap in reporting uncertain figures, but only the forecast is explicitly about a future value, which is why a census yields estimates rather than forecasts.
"Audience" gathers listeners and viewers, while "readership" gathers readers, so a podcast series builds an audience and a journal builds a readership.
"Efficient" is about reaching a result with little waste, while "effective" is about reaching it at all, so a scheme can be effective and still be criticised as inefficient.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Client" leans towards an ongoing professional relationship, while "customer" covers ordinary buyers, so a consultancy keeps clients and a supermarket serves customers.**

Client carries the sense of advice, representation or expertise supplied over time, and it is the standard word in law, accountancy, architecture and consulting. Customer is the general term for anyone buying goods or standard services, however briefly. The two overlap where a service is both professional and transactional, but the typical cases are clear.

The sentence takes those typical cases rather than the blurred edge, so the pairing it describes is the usual one.

**B) "Revenue" is everything a firm takes in, while "profit" is what survives after costs, so revenue can rise in a year that ends with a loss.**

Revenue is income generated by the firm's ordinary business before relevant expenses are deducted; it is not literally every cash inflow, since borrowing or new investment is not revenue. Profit is what remains after the applicable costs and expenses have been subtracted. Revenue can therefore grow while faster-growing costs still leave the firm with a loss.

The statement uses everything in the ordinary sales-income sense, and its central revenue-versus-profit distinction is correct.

**C) "Estimate" and "forecast" overlap in reporting uncertain figures, but only the forecast is explicitly about a future value, which is why a census yields estimates rather than forecasts.**

Both words admit that a number is not known exactly, and both come with margins attached. The difference lies in time: estimates approximate something in the present or past that could in principle be counted, while forecasts state what is expected to happen. Census work reconstructs a population that already exists.

**Tip:** Ask whether the quantity has happened yet; that alone usually settles the choice.

Time reference is doing the work here, and it points where the sentence says it does, so the reasoning holds.

**D) "Audience" gathers listeners and viewers, while "readership" gathers readers, so a podcast series builds an audience and a journal builds a readership.**

Audience comes from hearing and has widened to cover anyone attending or watching, which is why broadcasters, speakers and platforms all measure audiences. Readership stays tied to written material and is counted from circulation or subscriptions. A publication with both a print edition and a podcast reports each figure separately.

The medium decides the noun, and the sentence matches each medium to its own word, so the contrast is right.

**E) "Efficient" is about reaching a result with little waste, while "effective" is about reaching it at all, so a scheme can be effective and still be criticised as inefficient.**

Effectiveness is judged against the objective: was the outcome achieved? Efficiency is judged against the inputs: how much was spent, wasted or duplicated on the way. Evaluations routinely find that a programme did what it set out to do at an indefensible cost.

The sentence describes exactly that combination, which is what the two words exist to distinguish, so the account is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line here rewards asking what each word measures rather than how similar the two feel. Client and customer differ in the depth of the relationship, revenue and profit in where they sit on an income statement, and audience and readership in the medium involved. Estimate and forecast split on time reference, while effective and efficient split on outcome against cost, so a success achieved wastefully satisfies only one of them.

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Claims about how strong a word's promise is, taken from statistics, public finance and guidance documents. Judge whether each one holds.
statements: "Household" refers strictly to the physical dwelling, so statistics on household income are counting buildings rather than people.
"Reduce" leaves part of the problem in place, while "eradicate" claims to remove it completely, so a scheme that halves hospital infections has reduced but not eradicated them.
"Deficit" and "debt" are two names for the same figure, so a government that halves its deficit has halved its debt.
"Recommend" carries the same force as "mandate," so guidance that recommends hybrid working has placed employers under a requirement.
"Concede" grants a point reluctantly, while "agree" carries no such reluctance, so a negotiator who concedes a clause has given ground rather than found common cause.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Household" refers strictly to the physical dwelling, so statistics on household income are counting buildings rather than people.**

Household names the group of people who live together and share expenses, which is why surveys record its size, composition and income. The building itself is a dwelling or a house, and it can stand empty or contain several households. Income belongs to people rather than to bricks.

The measure follows the occupants, so treating household as a word for the structure misreads what these statistics count.

**B) "Reduce" leaves part of the problem in place, while "eradicate" claims to remove it completely, so a scheme that halves hospital infections has reduced but not eradicated them.**

Reduction is a matter of degree and can be reported as a percentage. Eradication is absolute: nothing of the thing remains, which is why it is claimed for very few diseases. Halving a figure is a substantial reduction and nowhere near removal.

**Tip:** Absolute verbs like eradicate resist qualification; if you can add by half, you want the gradable one.

Strength of claim is what separates them, and the sentence keeps the weaker verb for the weaker result, so it is accurate.

**C) "Deficit" and "debt" are two names for the same figure, so a government that halves its deficit has halved its debt.**

A deficit is a flow measured over one period: the gap between what is spent and what is raised in a year. Debt is the stock accumulated from all past deficits and repayments. A halved deficit still adds to the total owed, only more slowly.

Flow and stock are different quantities, so the conclusion drawn here does not follow and the debt keeps growing.

**D) "Recommend" carries the same force as "mandate," so guidance that recommends hybrid working has placed employers under a requirement.**

A recommendation states what a body thinks best and leaves the decision with the reader. A mandate creates a duty, usually backed by a sanction or a reporting obligation. Employers routinely decline recommendations without breaching anything, which would be impossible if the two carried equal weight.

Force is exactly what divides the pair, so guidance that only recommends leaves employers free to say no.

**E) "Concede" grants a point reluctantly, while "agree" carries no such reluctance, so a negotiator who concedes a clause has given ground rather than found common cause.**

Agreement can be mutual and even enthusiastic; conceding implies pressure, argument or a trade. That is why reports of talks distinguish the two, counting concessions on one side and announcing agreements on both. The word chosen tells the reader how the outcome was reached.

Reluctance is built into one verb and absent from the other, and the sentence rests on precisely that, so the description is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these lines test how strong a word's claim really is, so weigh reduce against eradicate and recommend against mandate before accepting the equivalence offered. The household line asks whether the noun counts people or structures, and the deficit line whether the figure is a yearly flow or an accumulated stock. Concede adds a reluctance that agree does not, which is the kind of attitude a near-synonym can carry entirely on its own.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Five statements about words whose everyday and technical senses pull in different directions. Decide whether each account is correct.
statements: "Keen" cannot mean eager in standard English, so a report describing analysts as keen to see the next inflation figure has misused the word.
"Risk" covers outcomes whose odds can be estimated, while "uncertainty" covers those where even the odds are unknown, so an insurer can price risk but not deep uncertainty.
"Curb" implies restraining something without stopping it, while "ban" removes it outright, so a levy that curbs single-use packaging has not banned it.
"Suspend" implies a pause that can be reversed, while "terminate" ends the arrangement for good, so a licence suspended pending review has not been terminated.
"Significant" in a statistical report simply means large, so an effect reported as statistically significant is by that fact economically important.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Keen" cannot mean eager in standard English, so a report describing analysts as keen to see the next inflation figure has misused the word.**

Keen to plus a verb is one of the commonest ways of reporting eagerness in British English, and it is entirely standard in journalism and business writing. The adjective also has a sense of sharp or acute, as in a keen eye for irregular invoices, but the two coexist happily. Nothing about analysts waiting for data strains either reading.

The eager sense is ordinary rather than exceptional, so the charge of misuse cannot be sustained.

**B) "Risk" covers outcomes whose odds can be estimated, while "uncertainty" covers those where even the odds are unknown, so an insurer can price risk but not deep uncertainty.**

Pricing a policy requires a distribution of outcomes: how often the event occurs and how much it costs when it does. Where no such distribution can be built, the situation is uncertain rather than risky in the technical sense, and insurers withdraw or add exclusions. The distinction has practical consequences precisely because it is not merely verbal.

Knowable odds are the dividing line, and the sentence draws its conclusion straight from that, so the account is right.

**C) "Curb" implies restraining something without stopping it, while "ban" removes it outright, so a levy that curbs single-use packaging has not banned it.**

Curbing reduces the scale or pace of an activity while leaving it lawful. A ban prohibits the activity, so anyone who continues is in breach. A charge that makes packaging more expensive changes behaviour at the margin and nothing more.

Legality is the clean test between the two verbs, and the sentence applies it correctly, so the line holds.

**D) "Suspend" implies a pause that can be reversed, while "terminate" ends the arrangement for good, so a licence suspended pending review has not been terminated.**

Suspension stops something temporarily while a decision is taken, and the underlying arrangement survives. Termination brings it to an end, leaving nothing to restore. A review only makes sense while the licence still exists in some form.

**Tip:** If a later decision could bring the arrangement back, the pause word is the one you need.

Reversibility separates the pair, and the sentence keeps the reversible verb with the reviewable case, so the description is sound.

**E) "Significant" in a statistical report simply means large, so an effect reported as statistically significant is by that fact economically important.**

In statistics, significant means unlikely to have arisen by chance given the data, and with a large enough sample a tiny effect clears that bar. Importance is a separate judgement about the size of the effect and what it costs or saves. Careful writing keeps the two apart by reporting effect sizes alongside significance tests.

**Trap:** The everyday sense of the word does mean sizeable, which is why the technical usage misleads so reliably.

Statistical significance says nothing about magnitude, so the inference drawn in this line does not follow.
tasks.solution_overview: This set mixes claims about how much a word rules out with claims about how much it asserts. Keen has two live senses, curb and ban differ over legality, and suspend and terminate differ over whether anything can be restored. Risk and uncertainty split on whether probabilities are available, while significant carries a technical meaning that says nothing at all about the size of an effect.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Each line separates two words that are close in feel but differ in what they assert. Judge whether the separation is drawn correctly.
statements: "Keen" stretches from eager to sharp, while "eager" covers only strong desire, so a keen observer of trade policy need not be an excited one.
"Accurate" means close to the true value, while "precise" means tightly clustered, so a tide gauge can be precise to the millimetre and still be inaccurate.
"Imply" belongs to the speaker who hints, while "infer" belongs to the listener who draws the conclusion, so a cautious central banker implies a pause and markets infer one.
"Persuade that" is preferred to "convince that" in every context, so careful writers avoid saying that the evidence convinced the panel that the model was sound.
"Correlate" claims only that two series move together, while "cause" claims that one produces the other, so postal codes can correlate with income without causing it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Keen" stretches from eager to sharp, while "eager" covers only strong desire, so a keen observer of trade policy need not be an excited one.**

One adjective has two live senses and the other has one. Keen can describe enthusiasm, but applied to perception, judgement or an edge it means acute, which is the reading in a phrase like a keen observer. Eager has no such second sense and always points at wanting something.

Breadth of sense is the difference, and the sentence relies on the acute reading that only one word supports, so it is accurate.

**B) "Accurate" means close to the true value, while "precise" means tightly clustered, so a tide gauge can be precise to the millimetre and still be inaccurate.**

Accuracy compares a measurement with reality; precision describes how little a set of measurements varies among themselves. An instrument with a systematic offset repeats the same wrong number very consistently, which is precision without accuracy. Measurement science keeps the words apart for exactly this case.

**Tip:** Precision is about agreement, accuracy about truth.

The example is the textbook case of the two coming apart, so the distinction drawn here holds.

**C) "Imply" belongs to the speaker who hints, while "infer" belongs to the listener who draws the conclusion, so a cautious central banker implies a pause and markets infer one.**

Implying is something a message does: content is suggested without being stated. Inferring is something a reader or listener does with that message. The roles cannot be exchanged, which is why the two verbs take different subjects within the same story.

Direction of the act is the whole point, and the sentence assigns each verb to the right party, so the line is sound.

**D) "Persuade that" is preferred to "convince that" in every context, so careful writers avoid saying that the evidence convinced the panel that the model was sound.**

The traditional preference runs the other way: convince pairs with a that-clause about belief, while persuade pairs with an infinitive about action. Convinced the panel that the model was sound is therefore the idiomatic form rather than one to be avoided. Persuade that does occur, but it is the marked option.

The recommendation reverses the usual pattern, so the sentence it warns against is in fact the natural one.

**E) "Correlate" claims only that two series move together, while "cause" claims that one produces the other, so postal codes can correlate with income without causing it.**

Correlation is a statistical relationship and can arise from a shared third factor, from selection, or from chance. Causation asserts a mechanism by which one variable moves the other. Location and income travel together because of housing markets and history, not because an address generates earnings.

Mechanism is what the stronger word adds, and the sentence withholds it deliberately, so the claim is correctly hedged.
tasks.solution_overview: These lines separate words that are close in feel but differ in what they assert or in who performs the act. Accurate and precise part company whenever an instrument is consistently wrong, and imply and infer part company by which side of the conversation is acting. For convince and persuade, check what follows the verb, and for correlate and cause, check whether any mechanism is being claimed.

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Statements contrasting words that describe the same situation from different angles in policy and research writing. Decide whether each is accurate.
statements: "Resilient" describes something that recovers after a shock, while "robust" describes something that resists it, so a supply chain can be robust against one disruption and resilient after another.
"Prohibit" bans an action outright, while "discourage" only makes it less attractive, so a tax that discourages diesel purchases does not prohibit them.

"Anecdotal" evidence rests on scattered individual reports, while "systematic" evidence comes from a designed collection process, so a handful of employer testimonials stays anecdotal however striking it sounds.
"Hypothesis" names a proposal still to be tested, while "theory" names an explanation already supported by evidence, so a new account of glacier retreat begins as a hypothesis.

"Sparse" describes something thinly spread across space, while "scarce" describes something in short supply relative to demand, so food can be sparse on the deep seabed while skilled technicians are scarce onshore.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Resilient" describes something that recovers after a shock, while "robust" describes something that resists it, so a supply chain can be robust against one disruption and resilient after another.**

Robustness is about withstanding pressure without much change: buffers, redundancy and strong components. Resilience is about the speed and completeness of recovery once damage has occurred. Planners use both words because no system absorbs every shock.

Resisting and recovering are different capacities, and the sentence assigns each word to its own, so the contrast is well made.

**B) "Prohibit" bans an action outright, while "discourage" only makes it less attractive, so a tax that discourages diesel purchases does not prohibit them.**

A prohibition removes the legal option, and breaching it is an offence. Discouragement changes incentives while leaving the choice intact, which is what a tax does. Buyers who pay the higher price are doing nothing wrong.

Whether the act remains lawful is the test, and the sentence applies it correctly, so the line stands.

**C) "Anecdotal" evidence rests on scattered individual reports, while "systematic" evidence comes from a designed collection process, so a handful of employer testimonials stays anecdotal however striking it sounds.**

Anecdotes are chosen by whoever tells them, which is why they cannot support claims about how common something is. Systematic evidence follows a sampling plan that can be described, repeated and criticised. Vividness does not convert one into the other.

Selection method rather than persuasiveness is what matters, and the sentence holds that line, so it is accurate.

**D) "Hypothesis" names a proposal still to be tested, while "theory" names an explanation already supported by evidence, so a new account of glacier retreat begins as a hypothesis.**

A hypothesis is a specific, testable proposal that observations may support or contradict. A scientific theory is a broader explanatory framework supported by substantial evidence; it is not merely a hypothesis that has been promoted after one successful test. A newly proposed mechanism for glacier retreat begins on the testable-proposal side of that distinction.

The account has not yet earned the evidential breadth of a theory, so calling it a hypothesis is appropriate.

**E) "Sparse" describes something thinly spread across space, while "scarce" describes something in short supply relative to demand, so food can be sparse on the deep seabed while skilled technicians are scarce onshore.**

Sparse answers the question of how thinly distributed something is over an area. Scarce answers whether there is enough of it for those who want it. A resource can be widely spread and still scarce, or concentrated and abundant.

Distribution and sufficiency are separate measures, and the sentence gives each word the example that fits it, so the pairing is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line contrasts two words that describe one situation from different angles, so name the angle before judging. Robust and resilient split resistance from recovery, prohibit and discourage split the unlawful from the merely costly, and anecdotal and systematic split how the evidence was gathered. Hypothesis and theory differ by how much testing has happened, while sparse and scarce differ by whether you are measuring spread or sufficiency.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Five accounts of near-synonyms used in procurement, forecasting and scientific reporting. Decide whether each account is correct.
statements: "Procure" is the formal, institutional partner of "buy," so a defence ministry procures components while a household buys them.
"Forecast" can only describe events that have already been completed, so a meteorological service issues forecasts about last month's rainfall.
"Decline" is always ruder than "refuse," so an applicant who declines an offer has given more offence than one who refuses it.
"Consensus" means complete agreement with no dissenting voice, so a report describing a scientific consensus is claiming unanimity.
"Sanction" has only one meaning, so a body that sanctions a trade practice is always penalising it.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Procure" is the formal, institutional partner of "buy," so a defence ministry procures components while a household buys them.**

Both verbs end with goods changing hands. Procure belongs to organisations with tendering rules and contracts, and it implies a process rather than a moment. Buy is unmarked and works for any purchaser, which is why a headline can still say the ministry bought the same components.

Institutional process against everyday purchase is where these verbs differ, and the sentence contrasts exactly that, so the description works.

**B) "Forecast" can only describe events that have already been completed, so a meteorological service issues forecasts about last month's rainfall.**

A forecast is by definition a statement about what is expected to happen, whether in weather, inflation or demand. Describing rainfall that has already fallen is reporting, or at most estimating a figure never measured directly. The prefix fore- carries that future reference explicitly.

Looking ahead is built into the word, so an account of last month's rain is not a forecast at all.

**C) "Decline" is always ruder than "refuse," so an applicant who declines an offer has given more offence than one who refuses it.**

Decline is the courteous option and is standard in formal letters, which is why declined with thanks is a set phrase. Refuse is the blunter verb and can suggest resistance or even defiance. The ranking of politeness runs in the opposite direction to the one claimed.

Courtesy belongs to the first verb, so an applicant who declines has softened the answer rather than sharpened it.

**D) "Consensus" means complete agreement with no dissenting voice, so a report describing a scientific consensus is claiming unanimity.**

Consensus describes a broad, settled agreement among a group and tolerates dissent at the edges. Unanimity is the stronger word and admits no exceptions at all. Scientific bodies report consensus precisely because a minority view usually persists.

**Trap:** Reading consensus as unanimity makes a single dissenting paper look like a refutation.

Room for dissent is part of the weaker word, so equating it with unanimity overstates what such a report claims.

**E) "Sanction" has only one meaning, so a body that sanctions a trade practice is always penalising it.**

Sanction is one of the rare words that faces both ways: as a verb it often means to authorise, while as a plural noun it usually means penalties. A committee that sanctions a practice has approved it, whereas a state placed under sanctions is being punished. Only the surrounding words settle which sense is live.

Two opposed senses share the one form, so a single reading cannot be guaranteed the way this line assumes.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one line here describes its pair correctly, and the rest overstate or invert what a word carries. Check the direction of politeness in refuse and decline, the time reference built into forecast, and how much agreement consensus actually claims. Sanction is the trickiest case, since it can mean approve or penalise depending on context, while procure differs from buy only in institutional formality.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Each line claims that a distinction either exists or does not. Decide whether careful usage supports the claim.
statements: "Continual" and "continuous" are never distinguished by careful writers, so continual monitoring and continuous monitoring promise the same coverage.
"Capacity" points to how much can be handled, while "capability" points to what can be done at all, so a port can have the capability to handle liquefied gas and too little capacity to matter.
"Partly" reports that something holds to some degree, while "partially" more often marks a whole left incomplete, so a partly technical objection differs in flavour from a partially completed audit.
"Substantial" and "marginal" both describe large effects, so a marginal improvement in crop yields is a substantial one.
"Boundary" stretches to abstract limits as well as physical ones, so economists can write about the boundary between market and state without meaning a line on a map.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Continual" and "continuous" are never distinguished by careful writers, so continual monitoring and continuous monitoring promise the same coverage.**

Continual describes something that happens again and again with gaps between the occurrences. Continuous describes an unbroken run with no gaps at all. A contract promising continuous monitoring therefore commits to far more than one promising continual checks, and a supplier would notice the difference immediately.

Coverage is what changes between the two, so treating the words as one erases a difference contracts are written around.

**B) "Capacity" points to how much can be handled, while "capability" points to what can be done at all, so a port can have the capability to handle liquefied gas and too little capacity to matter.**

Capability is qualitative: do the equipment, licences and expertise exist to do this kind of work? Capacity is quantitative: how much throughput is available per week or per year. A single specialised berth answers the first question and barely registers on the second.

Kind against quantity is the split, and the sentence shows both at work in one facility, so the contrast is well drawn.

**C) "Partly" reports that something holds to some degree, while "partially" more often marks a whole left incomplete, so a partly technical objection differs in flavour from a partially completed audit.**

Where the two are not simply interchangeable, partly tends to divide a reason or a description into shares. Partially leans towards a process or state that has not reached completion, and it is the natural word beside restored, built or implemented. The difference is one of emphasis rather than of strict rule.

Emphasis is exactly what the sentence claims to be tracking, and it tracks it correctly, so the line holds.

**D) "Substantial" and "marginal" both describe large effects, so a marginal improvement in crop yields is a substantial one.**

Substantial means considerable in size or importance. Marginal, in ordinary usage, means small enough to sit at the edge of what matters, and in economics it refers to the effect of one additional unit rather than to a large total. Neither reading makes it a synonym for substantial.

The two adjectives sit at opposite ends of the scale, so a marginal gain in yields is precisely what a substantial one is not.

**E) "Boundary" stretches to abstract limits as well as physical ones, so economists can write about the boundary between market and state without meaning a line on a map.**

The physical use is the older one, marking where a field, an estate or a territory ends. The abstract use is equally standard and covers the limits of a discipline, a remit or a category. That flexibility is why the word appears throughout policy writing where border would sound odd.

The abstract reach is genuine, and the example depends on it, so the sentence is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these lines ask whether a distinction exists at all, and the honest answer differs in each case. Continual and continuous really do differ over gaps, while substantial and marginal sit at opposite ends of a size scale rather than describing one effect. For capacity, partly and boundary, decide whether the sentence measures quantity, emphasis or the reach of a word beyond its literal use.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Statements about words that carry an attitude as well as a meaning. Judge whether each description matches how the word is used.
statements: "Rigorous" praises careful thoroughness, while "rigid" criticises an unwillingness to bend, so a rigorous inspection regime is not the same as a rigid one.
"Allege" means to establish a claim beyond doubt, so a competition authority that alleges collusion has already proved it.
"Ubiquitous" simply means fairly common, so a technology found in a handful of pilot cities can fairly be called ubiquitous.
"Endorse" signals active approval, while "tolerate" signals only that something is allowed to continue, so a regulator can tolerate a pricing practice without endorsing it.
"Issue" and "crisis" carry the same weight, so a minister who calls rising energy costs an issue is announcing a crisis.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Rigorous" praises careful thoroughness, while "rigid" criticises an unwillingness to bend, so a rigorous inspection regime is not the same as a rigid one.**

The two adjectives share a root but have drifted apart in attitude. Rigorous is approving and points at standards applied consistently and in detail. Rigid is disapproving and points at rules applied without judgement, even where they no longer fit.

**Tip:** Ask whether the writer is praising or complaining; the pair splits on evaluation rather than on strictness.

Approval and complaint are carried by the words themselves, and the sentence keeps them apart, so it stands.

**B) "Allege" means to establish a claim beyond doubt, so a competition authority that alleges collusion has already proved it.**

Alleging is asserting without yet proving, which is why the word survives in legal reporting: it lets a serious accusation be published before any finding. Establishing a claim beyond doubt is what a judgment or a completed investigation does. The vocabulary of proof is quite separate.

The word marks a claim as untested, so an allegation of collusion opens the case rather than closing it.

**C) "Ubiquitous" simply means fairly common, so a technology found in a handful of pilot cities can fairly be called ubiquitous.**

Ubiquitous means present everywhere, or so widespread that it is hard to avoid, which is a far stronger claim than common. A few pilot deployments are the opposite: rare, deliberate and easy to count. Widespread or emerging would carry the intended sense without the exaggeration.

**Trap:** Strong adjectives lose their force when spent on merely noticeable quantities, and readers discount the rest of the sentence with them.

Pilot schemes fall a long way short of everywhere, so the label overstates the reach by a wide margin.

**D) "Endorse" signals active approval, while "tolerate" signals only that something is allowed to continue, so a regulator can tolerate a pricing practice without endorsing it.**

Endorsement puts the endorser's name behind the thing approved. Tolerance withholds that support and merely declines to intervene, often for want of powers or evidence. Regulators exploit the gap constantly when they publish concerns but take no action.

Support against mere permission is the difference, and the sentence separates them cleanly, so the description is sound.

**E) "Issue" and "crisis" carry the same weight, so a minister who calls rising energy costs an issue is announcing a crisis.**

Issue is the neutral, low-temperature word for a matter under discussion. Crisis claims that a situation has become acute and demands immediate action. Ministers choose the milder noun precisely to avoid that second implication.

Intensity is what separates them, so calling something an issue plays it down rather than raising the alarm.
tasks.solution_overview: Attitude and strength of claim decide this set, so ask what each word commits its user to. Rigorous approves where rigid complains, endorse supports where tolerate merely permits, and issue stays calm where crisis sounds an alarm. Allege withholds proof by design, and ubiquitous claims a reach that a handful of pilot sites cannot support.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Five contrasts of scope and tone taken from corporate reporting and public statistics. Decide whether each one is accurate.
statements: "Problem" states plainly that something has gone wrong, while "issue" is the more diplomatic word for a matter under discussion, so committees raise issues where engineers report problems.
"Strategy" sets the direction and "tactic" supplies the move, so abandoning one tactic need not mean abandoning the strategy behind it.
"Remuneration" covers the whole package of pay and benefits, while "salary" names only the fixed cash component, so a remuneration report can grow without a single salary rising.
"Household" and "house" are interchangeable in survey work, so counting households and counting houses gives the same figure in a city of shared flats.
"Audience" can extend to anyone a message reaches, while "readership" stays with written material, so a broadcaster and a journal do not measure reach with the same noun.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Problem" states plainly that something has gone wrong, while "issue" is the more diplomatic word for a matter under discussion, so committees raise issues where engineers report problems.**

Problem names a fault and implies that someone should fix it. Issue leaves the question of blame open and frames the matter as something to be talked through. Organisations drift towards the second word in minutes and public statements for exactly that reason.

Diplomatic distance is the difference, and the sentence matches each word to the setting that prefers it, so it is accurate.

**B) "Strategy" sets the direction and "tactic" supplies the move, so abandoning one tactic need not mean abandoning the strategy behind it.**

Tactics are chosen for their fit with circumstances and are replaced when circumstances change. The strategy is the standing aim that makes one tactic preferable to another. Dropping a supplier incentive while keeping a nearshoring aim is an ordinary example.

The levels are nested rather than parallel, and the sentence draws the right consequence from that, so the line holds.

**C) "Remuneration" covers the whole package of pay and benefits, while "salary" names only the fixed cash component, so a remuneration report can grow without a single salary rising.**

Salary is one line in a pay package. Remuneration adds bonuses, share awards, pension contributions and benefits in kind, which is why company reporting uses the broader word. Awards that vest can lift total remuneration in a year of frozen pay.

Scope of coverage separates the two nouns, and the sentence follows that scope to its conclusion, so it stands.

**D) "Household" and "house" are interchangeable in survey work, so counting households and counting houses gives the same figure in a city of shared flats.**

A house is a dwelling; a household is a group of people sharing living arrangements and expenses. Shared flats are the clearest case where the counts diverge, since several households can occupy one address, or one household can spread across two. Survey design treats them as separate units for that reason.

Shared occupancy pulls the two counts apart, so the identical figure predicted here would not appear.

**E) "Audience" can extend to anyone a message reaches, while "readership" stays with written material, so a broadcaster and a journal do not measure reach with the same noun.**

Audience began with listeners and now covers viewers, attendees and users of almost any medium. Readership is narrower and counts the readers of a specific publication. A journal can report both figures if it also runs a lecture series, but they answer different questions.

Breadth of medium is the deciding factor, and the sentence keeps each noun within its own range, so the account is right.
tasks.solution_overview: Scope and tone run through this set: one word in each pair reaches further or lands more softly than its partner. Issue softens problem, remuneration widens salary, and audience widens readership, while strategy sits above the tactics that serve it. The household line is the outlier, and shared accommodation is the case that shows why a dwelling and a household cannot be counted as one.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Each line weighs how much a word concedes, claims or preserves in careful academic and negotiating prose. Judge whether the weighing is right.
statements: "Concede" grants a point under pressure, while "acknowledge" simply recognises it, so a negotiator can acknowledge a rival's figures without conceding the argument.
"Ostensibly" flags a stated reason that may not be the real one, while "evidently" points to what the evidence shows, so an ostensibly technical objection may be political underneath.
"Methodology" names the study of methods and the reasoning behind a design, while "method" names the procedure itself, so calling a single sampling step a methodology inflates the word.
"Plausible" says a claim could be true, while "demonstrated" says the evidence has settled it, so a plausible mechanism for glacier retreat still needs measurement.
"Defer" pushes a decision to a later point, while "cancel" removes it altogether, so a board that defers a capital programme has kept it alive.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Concede" grants a point under pressure, while "acknowledge" simply recognises it, so a negotiator can acknowledge a rival's figures without conceding the argument.**

Acknowledging accepts that something is there: a number, a difficulty, a fact. Conceding gives up ground in a dispute, which implies that the other side gains by it. Talks routinely feature the first without the second, and communiques are drafted to keep them apart.

Loss of ground is what the stronger verb adds, and the sentence withholds it deliberately, so the distinction is sound.

**B) "Ostensibly" flags a stated reason that may not be the real one, while "evidently" points to what the evidence shows, so an ostensibly technical objection may be political underneath.**

Ostensibly reports appearances and quietly invites doubt about them. Evidently reports what can be seen or inferred from the available evidence and carries no such scepticism. Swapping the two changes the writer's stance entirely.
