Doubt is built into one adverb and absent from the other, and the sentence turns on that, so its account holds.

**C) "Methodology" names the study of methods and the reasoning behind a design, while "method" names the procedure itself, so calling a single sampling step a methodology inflates the word.**

A method is a procedure used to collect or analyse evidence. Methodology can mean the study of methods or, in research writing, the system of methods and principles that shapes a design. Usage sometimes extends methodology to methods collectively, but a single sampling step is still one method rather than an entire methodological framework.

Because the example names only one procedure, calling it a methodology would inflate its scope, so the distinction holds.

**D) "Plausible" says a claim could be true, while "demonstrated" says the evidence has settled it, so a plausible mechanism for glacier retreat still needs measurement.**

Plausibility is a judgement about coherence: the account hangs together and does not contradict what is known. Demonstration requires observations that discriminate between this account and its rivals. Many plausible mechanisms turn out to contribute nothing measurable.

Coherence and evidence are separate hurdles, and the sentence keeps the weaker word for the earlier one, so it is accurate.

**E) "Defer" pushes a decision to a later point, while "cancel" removes it altogether, so a board that defers a capital programme has kept it alive.**

Deferral leaves the item on the agenda with a new date or trigger attached. Cancellation takes it off entirely, and reviving it means starting again. Boards distinguish the two because the accounting and the signal to investors both differ.

Survival of the decision is the test, and the sentence applies it correctly, so the line holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line rewards asking how much each word concedes, claims or preserves. Concede gives ground where acknowledge only registers a fact, plausible falls short of demonstrated, and defer keeps alive what cancel destroys. Ostensibly carries a hint of doubt that evidently lacks, while methodology names the reasoning behind a method rather than serving as a grander name for it.

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Five claims that impose a restriction or an equivalence on professional vocabulary. Decide whether standard usage supports them.
statements: "Client" is barred from professional-services writing, so a legal aid body must describe the people it represents as customers.
"Convince" is the natural verb before an infinitive of action, so careful writers say that a campaign convinced households to switch tariffs rather than persuaded them.
"Capability" cannot refer to potential capacity, so describing a grid as having the capability to absorb more wind power misuses the word.
"Curtail" and "abolish" describe the same action, so a scheme whose funding is curtailed has been abolished.
"Procurement" names the whole process of sourcing and contracting, while "purchase" names the single transaction at its end, so a procurement reform touches far more than the moment of purchase.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Client" is barred from professional-services writing, so a legal aid body must describe the people it represents as customers.**

Client is the standard term in exactly this setting, since it marks a relationship built on representation and advice. Customer suggests a retail transaction and sits oddly beside legal representation. Nothing in professional usage rules the first word out; it is the expected choice.

The prohibition is invented, so the people a legal aid body represents remain its clients.

**B) "Convince" is the natural verb before an infinitive of action, so careful writers say that a campaign convinced households to switch tariffs rather than persuaded them.**

Persuade someone to do something is the established pattern for bringing about an action, while convince someone that something is true is the clearest pattern for changing a belief. Convince someone to is now standard in much modern English, especially American English, so it is not simply ungrammatical; it is nonetheless less neutral than persuade in a task testing the traditional careful distinction. Switching tariffs is an action rather than a proposition to believe.

For the register and contrast tested here, persuaded households to switch is the more natural careful choice, so the claim that convince is preferred does not hold.

**C) "Capability" cannot refer to potential capacity, so describing a grid as having the capability to absorb more wind power misuses the word.**

Potential is central to what capability means: the word describes what could be done given the right conditions, which is why planning documents are full of it. A grid that could take more renewable input once storage is added is a textbook case. Restricting the noun to demonstrated performance would leave no word for the planning sense.

Potential is part of the meaning rather than a stretch of it, so the sentence about the grid is perfectly idiomatic.

**D) "Curtail" and "abolish" describe the same action, so a scheme whose funding is curtailed has been abolished.**

Curtailing cuts something back: the scheme continues on reduced resources. Abolishing ends it, so there is nothing left to fund. Budget documents rely on the difference whenever they announce reductions rather than closures.

Survival on a smaller scale is what one verb allows and the other forbids, so the equation cannot hold.

**E) "Procurement" names the whole process of sourcing and contracting, while "purchase" names the single transaction at its end, so a procurement reform touches far more than the moment of purchase.**

Procurement covers specification, tendering, evaluation, award and contract management. A purchase is the transfer itself, which may take a minute. Reforms usually attack the earlier stages, where competition and value for money are decided.

Process against transaction is the difference, and the sentence follows it to a conclusion that fits, so the line stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines invent a restriction or an equivalence that professional usage does not recognise, so test each against the way the words appear in contracts and reports. Client is the normal word in professional services, capability routinely covers potential, and curtail leaves alive what abolish ends. For convince and persuade, let the structure after the verb decide, and for procurement, remember that it names a process rather than a moment.

tasks.title: Task 21
tasks.context: Statements about near-synonyms whose difference lies in the writer's sympathies rather than in the facts. Judge each description.
statements: "Frank" praises honesty, while "blunt" hints that the honesty arrived without tact, so a frank assessment of a pilot scheme reads better than a blunt one.
"Assertive" describes confident self-expression, while "aggressive" adds hostility, so an assertive negotiating stance is not an aggressive one.
"Incremental" change arrives in small steps, while "radical" change breaks with what came before, so a series of incremental tariff adjustments is not a radical trade policy.
"Thrifty" and "stingy" carry the same attitude, so praising a household as thrifty is the same as calling it stingy.
"Partly" and "partially" are both barred from formal writing, so an official evaluation must avoid saying that a target was partly met.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Frank" praises honesty, while "blunt" hints that the honesty arrived without tact, so a frank assessment of a pilot scheme reads better than a blunt one.**

Both adjectives describe speech that holds nothing back. Frank is approving and suggests courage and openness, while blunt adds an edge and implies that feelings were not considered. The words therefore report the same behaviour with opposite sympathies.

**Tip:** When two words describe one act, ask which side the writer has taken.

Sympathy is what separates them, and the sentence ranks them accordingly, so the description holds.

**B) "Assertive" describes confident self-expression, while "aggressive" adds hostility, so an assertive negotiating stance is not an aggressive one.**

Assertiveness means stating a position clearly and holding it without attacking the other party. Aggression pushes past that line into intimidation or attack. Training materials keep the pair distinct because the behaviours they describe are genuinely different in a room.

Hostility is the extra element in the stronger word, and the sentence declines to import it, so the contrast is right.

**C) "Incremental" change arrives in small steps, while "radical" change breaks with what came before, so a series of incremental tariff adjustments is not a radical trade policy.**

Incremental change accumulates within an existing framework and can usually be unwound step by step. Radical change replaces the framework itself. A run of small tariff moves leaves the trading system it operates in untouched.

Scale and continuity are what separate the two adjectives, and the sentence applies both, so the line stands.

**D) "Thrifty" and "stingy" carry the same attitude, so praising a household as thrifty is the same as calling it stingy.**

Thrifty is approving and describes careful, resourceful management of limited money. Stingy is disapproving and describes an unwillingness to spend or share even where it would be reasonable. The behaviour may look similar from outside, but the two words judge it in opposite directions.

**Trap:** Pairs like this are where connotation, not denotation, does all the work.

One word compliments and the other criticises, so the two descriptions could never land the same way with a reader.

**E) "Partly" and "partially" are both barred from formal writing, so an official evaluation must avoid saying that a target was partly met.**

Both adverbs are entirely standard in formal English and appear throughout official evaluations, statistics and legal drafting. The only live question between them is emphasis, with partially leaning towards incompleteness. No rule of register excludes either one.

**Trap:** A style preference between two words is easily mistaken for a ban on both.

Neither adverb is off-limits, so partly met is a normal way for an evaluation to report a mixed result.
tasks.solution_overview: Connotation carries most of this set: the same behaviour can be praised or criticised depending on which near-synonym a writer picks. Frank against blunt, assertive against aggressive, and thrifty against stingy all turn on the writer's sympathies rather than on the facts described. Incremental and radical differ in scale, while the partly line tests whether a supposed rule of register exists at all.

tasks.title: Task 22
tasks.context: Each line offers to collapse a pair that measurement usually keeps apart. Decide whether the collapse is legitimate.
statements: "Uncertainty" is simply a politer word for "risk," so a note about deep uncertainty in long-run climate projections is a note about measurable risk.
"Convince" pairs naturally with a that-clause about belief, while "persuade" pairs with an infinitive of action, so evidence convinces a committee that a policy works and persuades it to fund one.
"Emissions" and "pollution" mean the same, so a plant reporting zero emissions of carbon dioxide has reported zero pollution.

"Effective" judges whether the intended result was produced, while "efficient" judges the ratio of result to resources, so a costly programme that hits its target is effective without being efficient.
"Innovation" and "invention" are identical, so a device that never leaves the laboratory has innovated as much as one adopted across an industry.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Uncertainty" is simply a politer word for "risk," so a note about deep uncertainty in long-run climate projections is a note about measurable risk.**

Risk in technical usage presupposes that outcomes and their probabilities can be described. Deep uncertainty is the label for cases where models disagree, probabilities cannot be assigned, and even the range of possible outcomes is contested. The word is chosen for accuracy rather than for politeness.

Measurability is what one term claims and the other denies, so recasting the note as being about risk changes what it says.

**B) "Convince" pairs naturally with a that-clause about belief, while "persuade" pairs with an infinitive of action, so evidence convinces a committee that a policy works and persuades it to fund one.**

The grammar mirrors the meaning: belief is expressed in a clause, action in an infinitive. That is why convinced that and persuaded to are the settled combinations in careful prose. The sentence runs both patterns side by side in a single example.

Structure and sense agree here, and the sentence keeps them aligned, so its account of the pair is accurate.

**C) "Emissions" and "pollution" mean the same, so a plant reporting zero emissions of carbon dioxide has reported zero pollution.**

Emissions are quantities of a specified substance released, and the term is always relative to what is being measured. Pollution is the broader judgement that released material causes harm, and it covers particulates, effluent, noise and heat. A plant with no carbon dioxide output may still discharge nitrogen oxides or warmed water.

One measurement does not exhaust the other category, so the leap from a single clean figure to zero pollution does not follow.

**D) "Effective" judges whether the intended result was produced, while "efficient" judges the ratio of result to resources, so a costly programme that hits its target is effective without being efficient.**

Effectiveness is measured against the objective alone. Efficiency brings in what was consumed on the way, which is why evaluations report both. Programmes that succeed at high cost are the standard illustration of the gap.

The two criteria diverge in exactly the case described, and the sentence describes it faithfully, so the line stands.

**E) "Innovation" and "invention" are identical, so a device that never leaves the laboratory has innovated as much as one adopted across an industry.**

Invention is the creation of something new. Innovation, in the usual economic sense, is the process of putting that novelty into use where it changes practice. A prototype that never reaches a user is an invention without an innovation.

Adoption is what the second word requires, so the laboratory device falls short of the claim made for it here.
tasks.solution_overview: This set repeatedly offers to collapse a pair that measurement keeps apart. Risk and uncertainty differ over whether probabilities exist, emissions and pollution over what is being measured, and invention and innovation over whether anything was ever adopted. The two accurate lines rest on the grammar that follows convince and persuade, and on the difference between hitting a target and hitting it cheaply.

tasks.title: Task 23
tasks.context: Five contrasts between a defined term and a looser impression of the same situation. Decide whether each is drawn accurately.
statements: "Recession" has a technical threshold behind it, while "slowdown" merely reports weaker growth, so an economy can slow for a year without entering a recession.
"Issue" softens "problem" enough to keep a discussion open, so describing supply bottlenecks as issues invites negotiation rather than blame.
"Continual" and "continuous" both promise an unbroken process, so continual interruptions to a data feed would mean the feed never stopped.
"Withstand" describes surviving pressure, while "sustain" describes keeping something going, so a grid can withstand a heatwave and still struggle to sustain supply through winter.
"Ability" attaches to what a body can do, while "capacity" often measures how much, so a laboratory's ability to sequence samples is a different claim from its weekly capacity.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Recession" has a technical threshold behind it, while "slowdown" merely reports weaker growth, so an economy can slow for a year without entering a recession.**

A recession is identified using formal criteria, although there is no single universal rule: two consecutive quarters of falling output is a common benchmark, while some bodies assess a broader decline across the economy. A slowdown says only that growth has weakened and may still remain positive. An economy can therefore expand more slowly for a year without meeting any accepted recession criterion.

Because slowdown does not itself imply contraction, the distinction and the conclusion drawn from it are sound.

**B) "Issue" softens "problem" enough to keep a discussion open, so describing supply bottlenecks as issues invites negotiation rather than blame.**

Problem points at a fault and implicitly at whoever caused it. Issue frames the same difficulty as a topic the parties can work on together. Commercial correspondence uses the milder noun to protect a relationship while still raising the difficulty.

Tone shapes how a message lands, and the sentence identifies the effect of choosing the softer noun, so it holds.

**C) "Continual" and "continuous" both promise an unbroken process, so continual interruptions to a data feed would mean the feed never stopped.**

Continual describes repeated occurrences separated by gaps, which is why interruptions are the natural noun beside it. Continuous describes something running without any break. Repeated interruptions are, by definition, breaks in the feed.

The sentence contradicts itself once the words are read properly, so continual interruptions mean the opposite of an unbroken feed.

**D) "Withstand" describes surviving pressure, while "sustain" describes keeping something going, so a grid can withstand a heatwave and still struggle to sustain supply through winter.**

Withstanding is about enduring a force at a moment of stress. Sustaining is about maintaining a level of output or service over time. A network can survive a peak load and still lack the fuel or capacity for a long cold season.

**Tip:** One verb faces a shock, the other faces a duration.

The two demands are separate, and the sentence shows a system meeting one but not the other, so the contrast is well drawn.

**E) "Ability" attaches to what a body can do, while "capacity" often measures how much, so a laboratory's ability to sequence samples is a different claim from its weekly capacity.**

Ability answers whether the task is within reach at all: the skills, licences and equipment exist. Capacity answers how many, how fast or how much can be handled in a given period. A single sequencing machine settles the first question and constrains the second severely.

Kind and quantity are separate measures, and the sentence separates them, so the line is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these lines distinguish a threshold or a quantity from a looser impression, so ask what would actually be counted. Recession rests on a definition that slowdown lacks, capacity counts what ability only makes possible, and sustain covers a duration that withstand does not. The continual line fails on its own terms once repeated interruptions are recognised as gaps, while the issue line turns on tone.

tasks.title: Task 24
tasks.context: Statements about actions that look similar in a notice or on a balance sheet but differ in what survives. Judge each account.
statements: "Rescind" cancels a decision so that it no longer stands, while "amend" keeps it in force with changes, so a rescinded guideline leaves nothing behind to follow.
"Consolidate" brings existing parts under one structure, while "expand" adds new ones, so a manufacturer consolidating three plants into one has not expanded.
"Discretion" leaves a decision to an official's judgement, while "obligation" removes the choice, so an inspector with discretion to issue fines is not required to issue them.
"Divest" means to sell off a holding, while "invest" commits money to it, so a pension fund divesting from fossil fuels is doing the reverse of investing in them.
"Estimate" and "projection" both admit uncertainty, but a projection spells out the assumptions it depends on, so a projection of grid demand is conditional in a way an estimate need not be.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Rescind" cancels a decision so that it no longer stands, while "amend" keeps it in force with changes, so a rescinded guideline leaves nothing behind to follow.**

Rescinding removes an instrument from the books, and anyone who relied on it must look elsewhere. Amending edits the text while the instrument survives, so obligations continue in altered form. Official notices distinguish the two carefully because compliance depends on which has happened.

Survival of the instrument is the test, and the sentence applies it correctly, so the description holds.

**B) "Consolidate" brings existing parts under one structure, while "expand" adds new ones, so a manufacturer consolidating three plants into one has not expanded.**

Consolidation rearranges what a firm already has, often to cut duplication and fixed costs. Expansion increases what it has, whether in sites, output or markets. Merging plants may even reduce total floor space while raising utilisation.

Adding against rearranging is the difference, and the sentence follows it to the right conclusion, so it stands.

**C) "Discretion" leaves a decision to an official's judgement, while "obligation" removes the choice, so an inspector with discretion to issue fines is not required to issue them.**

A discretionary power may be exercised or withheld, though the official must be able to justify either course. An obligation makes the action mandatory whenever the trigger is met. Enforcement regimes mix the two deliberately, and knowing which applies decides whether inaction is lawful.

Whether a choice remains is the whole distinction, and the sentence preserves it, so the line is sound.

**D) "Divest" means to sell off a holding, while "invest" commits money to it, so a pension fund divesting from fossil fuels is doing the reverse of investing in them.**

Investment puts capital into an asset and takes on exposure to it. Divestment sells the asset and removes that exposure, often for financial or ethical reasons. The prefix marks the reversal explicitly.

Direction of the money is the entire point, and the sentence states it correctly, so the account is accurate.

**E) "Estimate" and "projection" both admit uncertainty, but a projection spells out the assumptions it depends on, so a projection of grid demand is conditional in a way an estimate need not be.**

An estimate is an approximate value supported by available evidence and may concern a past, present or future quantity. A projection works forward from a specified scenario: if assumptions about growth, prices or policy hold, a particular demand path follows. Estimates also rely on assumptions, but those assumptions need not define a future scenario in the way they do for a projection.

The projection is explicitly conditional on its scenario, so the contrast drawn here is useful and accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Each line separates two moves that look similar in a notice or on a balance sheet but differ in what survives afterwards. Rescind removes what amend preserves, consolidate rearranges what expand would add, and divest reverses what invest committed. Discretion and obligation split on whether a choice remains, while a projection differs from an estimate by carrying its assumptions on its face.

tasks.title: Task 25
tasks.context: Each line tests whether an absolute word has been used where a gradable one belongs. Decide whether the usage described is defensible.
statements: "Meticulous" praises attention to detail, while "pedantic" complains about attention to the wrong details, so calling an audit trail meticulous is a compliment.
"Unprecedented" simply means unusual, so a price swing larger than any in the past decade but smaller than one in the 1970s can be called unprecedented.
"Condone" and "condemn" both express disapproval, so a regulator that condones a practice has criticised it.
"Inevitable" and "likely" make the same claim, so a model that puts a high probability on ice-shelf collapse has shown it to be inevitable.
"Scarce" measures supply against demand, so water can be scarce in a region that receives plenty of rain but needs far more.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Meticulous" praises attention to detail, while "pedantic" complains about attention to the wrong details, so calling an audit trail meticulous is a compliment.**

Both adjectives describe someone who will not let a small thing pass. Meticulous treats that care as valuable and proportionate, while pedantic treats it as misdirected fuss that obscures what matters. The judgement lives in the word rather than in the behaviour.

Approval and complaint are carried by the adjectives themselves, and the sentence assigns them correctly, so it stands.

**B) "Unprecedented" simply means unusual, so a price swing larger than any in the past decade but smaller than one in the 1970s can be called unprecedented.**

Unprecedented claims that nothing of the kind has happened before, so a single earlier instance defeats it. Unusual, exceptional or largest in a decade all report rarity without that absolute claim. The example supplies its own precedent.

**Trap:** Absolute adjectives are the easiest to overreach, and one counterexample is enough to sink them.

An earlier and larger swing exists, so the strongest available word is exactly the one this case cannot support.

**C) "Condone" and "condemn" both express disapproval, so a regulator that condones a practice has criticised it.**

Condone means to accept or overlook conduct that might have been criticised, which places it on the permissive side. Condemn denounces the conduct outright. The words look alike and mean nearly opposite things, which is why they are so often swapped.

**Tip:** Condone lets it pass; condemn calls it out.

Acceptance is not criticism, so a regulator that condones a practice has declined to attack it.

**D) "Inevitable" and "likely" make the same claim, so a model that puts a high probability on ice-shelf collapse has shown it to be inevitable.**

Likely reports a probability and leaves room for the outcome not to occur. Inevitable says the outcome cannot be avoided, which no probabilistic model delivers. Reporting that stretches high probability into certainty misstates what the science says.

A high probability still leaves an alternative open, so the stronger word overstates the finding it claims to summarise.

**E) "Scarce" measures supply against demand, so water can be scarce in a region that receives plenty of rain but needs far more.**

Scarcity is a relation rather than a quantity: it compares what is available with what is wanted. Abundant rainfall can still leave a region short if agriculture, industry and cities together demand more. That is why water stress is reported as a ratio rather than a total.

Demand is half of the measure, and the sentence builds its example on exactly that, so the claim is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Three of these lines reach for an absolute word where a gradable one is warranted, so ask whether a single counterexample or a residual probability would defeat the claim. Unprecedented and inevitable both fail that test, while condone and condemn sit on opposite sides of approval despite their similar shape. Meticulous and scarce are accurate because each is used for what it really measures: proportionate care, and supply weighed against demand.

tasks.title: Task 26
tasks.context: Five statements about the attitude a word carries alongside its meaning in reporting on firms and governments. Judge each one.
statements: "Exploit" is a neutral synonym for "use," so reporting that a firm exploits its migrant workers says no more than that it employs them.
"Lobby" describes pressing decision-makers on behalf of an interest, while "advocate" can be disinterested, so an industry body lobbies where a charity may simply advocate.
"Regime" carries a colder and often disapproving tone when applied to a government, while "administration" stays neutral, so the choice between them signals the writer's stance.
"Downsizing" is a softened way of saying that jobs are being cut, so a release announcing downsizing is announcing redundancies.
"Fewer" belongs before uncountable nouns such as "information" and "capital," so a formal report should prefer fewer capital to less capital.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Exploit" is a neutral synonym for "use," so reporting that a firm exploits its migrant workers says no more than that it employs them.**

Applied to resources, exploit can indeed be neutral: a company exploits a gas field or a market opportunity. Applied to people it carries a strong charge of unfair advantage and is read as an accusation. Employ, engage or hire are the neutral verbs for a workforce.

**Trap:** A word can be neutral with one kind of object and heavily loaded with another.

With workers as its object the verb accuses, so the sentence reports far more than ordinary employment.

**B) "Lobby" describes pressing decision-makers on behalf of an interest, while "advocate" can be disinterested, so an industry body lobbies where a charity may simply advocate.**

Lobbying names organised pressure directed at people with power, and it implies a stake in the outcome. Advocacy is arguing for a cause and does not require any benefit to the advocate. The words overlap in practice, which is why registers of lobbyists have to define the term with care.

Self-interest is the element one word suggests and the other does not, and the sentence keeps them apart, so it holds.

**C) "Regime" carries a colder and often disapproving tone when applied to a government, while "administration" stays neutral, so the choice between them signals the writer's stance.**

Regime is standard and neutral in phrases such as a regulatory regime or an exchange rate regime. Applied to a national government it usually marks the writer's distance, and it clusters with words like authoritarian. Administration and government carry no such implication.

Connotation shifts with the object here, and the sentence describes that shift accurately, so the point stands.

**D) "Downsizing" is a softened way of saying that jobs are being cut, so a release announcing downsizing is announcing redundancies.**

Downsizing describes a reduction in the size of an organisation, and in practice that reduction falls on staff. The word is chosen because it sounds structural rather than personal. Redundancies, layoffs and job cuts name the same event without the cushioning.

Euphemism changes the packaging rather than the content, and the sentence sees through it correctly, so the reading is right.

**E) "Fewer" belongs before uncountable nouns such as "information" and "capital," so a formal report should prefer fewer capital to less capital.**

Fewer takes plural countable nouns: fewer applications, fewer outages, fewer suppliers. Capital and information are mass nouns and take less, whatever the formality of the document. Where a count is genuinely intended, writers add a countable noun, as in fewer capital projects.

**Tip:** If the noun cannot take a number in front of it, less is the form you need.

The nouns named here refuse the count, so the recommended phrasing fails and less capital is the correct form.
tasks.solution_overview: Most of this set is about the attitude a word smuggles in alongside its meaning. Exploit accuses when its object is people, regime distances where administration does not, and downsizing cushions what redundancies would state plainly. Lobby suggests a stake that advocate need not have, while the fewer line is settled by whether the noun can be counted at all.

tasks.title: Task 27
tasks.context: Each line equates two words that in fact exclude one another. Decide whether the equation can stand.
statements: "Categorical" and "qualified" describe the same kind of claim, so a statement hedged with conditions is a categorical one.
"Propaganda" is a neutral term for public information, so a health ministry's vaccination campaign is properly described as propaganda in formal writing.
"Rigid" and "resilient" both describe systems that cope well with shocks, so a rigid production schedule is resilient by definition.
"Assert" puts the writer's own authority behind a claim, while "allege" holds it at arm's length, so an investigator who alleges wrongdoing has not vouched for it.
"Terminate" and "suspend" describe the same action, so a contract suspended for review has already been terminated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Categorical" and "qualified" describe the same kind of claim, so a statement hedged with conditions is a categorical one.**

A categorical statement is unconditional and admits no exceptions. A qualified statement is fenced with conditions, ranges or caveats that limit when it applies. The two sit at opposite ends of how firmly a claim is made.

Hedging is precisely what removes a claim from the categorical class, so the description reverses the relationship.

**B) "Propaganda" is a neutral term for public information, so a health ministry's vaccination campaign is properly described as propaganda in formal writing.**

Propaganda now implies manipulation: material shaped to persuade rather than to inform, often with facts selected or distorted. Public information campaign, health messaging or awareness campaign are the neutral descriptions. The older neutral sense has not survived in ordinary usage.

**Trap:** Words that were once neutral keep the old definition in dictionaries long after usage has loaded them.

The loaded reading is the live one, so applying the word to a routine health campaign smuggles in an accusation.

**C) "Rigid" and "resilient" both describe systems that cope well with shocks, so a rigid production schedule is resilient by definition.**

Resilience is the capacity to absorb a shock and recover, which usually depends on slack, alternatives and room to reconfigure. Rigidity is the absence of exactly those features: a schedule that cannot flex breaks when one input fails. In this context the words are closer to opposites than to synonyms.

Inflexibility undermines recovery rather than supplying it, so the rigid schedule is the least resilient arrangement available.

**D) "Assert" puts the writer's own authority behind a claim, while "allege" holds it at arm's length, so an investigator who alleges wrongdoing has not vouched for it.**

Asserting commits the speaker: the claim is offered as true and the speaker takes responsibility for it. Alleging reports the claim while reserving judgement, which is what allows serious accusations to be published before they are tested. The verb chosen tells the reader where the evidence stands.

Commitment is the difference, and the sentence keeps the uncommitted verb for an untested accusation, so it holds.

**E) "Terminate" and "suspend" describe the same action, so a contract suspended for review has already been terminated.**

Suspension pauses performance while the contract itself remains in existence, which is what makes a review meaningful. Termination ends the contract, and the parties' obligations fall away with it. Commercial drafting keeps separate clauses for each because the consequences differ so sharply.

Something must survive for a review to restore, so a suspended contract has plainly not been terminated.
tasks.solution_overview: Four of these lines equate a word with something it actually excludes, so ask what each term rules out. Categorical excludes hedging, resilient excludes the brittleness of a rigid plan, and terminate excludes the survival that suspension preserves. Propaganda carries an accusation that neutral information campaigns do not, while assert and allege differ over whether the speaker vouches for the claim.

tasks.title: Task 28
tasks.context: Statements pairing a compliment with a criticism for the same behaviour. Decide whether each description of the pair is accurate.
statements: "Concise" and "terse" pay the same compliment, so calling a minister's answer terse praises its economy.
"Cautious" describes prudent care, while "timid" implies a lack of nerve, so a cautious investment policy is not a timid one.

"Determined" credits persistence with a purpose, while "stubborn" suggests persistence past the point of sense, so the same negotiator can be described either way depending on the writer's sympathies.
"Ambitious" and "reckless" can describe the same plan, but only the second says the risks were ignored, so calling an expansion ambitious withholds that judgement.
"Restructuring" describes reorganising how a firm operates, while "redundancies" names the job losses that may follow, so the first can be announced without conceding the second.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Concise" and "terse" pay the same compliment, so calling a minister's answer terse praises its economy.**

Concise praises brevity that keeps everything necessary. Terse describes brevity that feels curt, and it usually implies impatience or reluctance on the speaker's part. Both note that few words were used; only one approves of it.

**Tip:** When two words describe the same length of answer, the difference is almost always attitude.

Curtness is not economy, so the terse label reads as a criticism rather than praise.

**B) "Cautious" describes prudent care, while "timid" implies a lack of nerve, so a cautious investment policy is not a timid one.**

Caution weighs risks and acts accordingly, which can include acting boldly where the odds justify it. Timidity is a disposition to avoid risk regardless of what the analysis says. Fund documents use the first word because it describes a method rather than a temperament.

Judgement against nervousness is what separates them, and the sentence refuses to conflate the two, so it is accurate.

**C) "Determined" credits persistence with a purpose, while "stubborn" suggests persistence past the point of sense, so the same negotiator can be described either way depending on the writer's sympathies.**

Neither adjective disputes the facts: the person kept going. What changes is whether that persistence is presented as principled or as obstinate. Reporting on the same round of talks routinely splits along exactly this line.

The behaviour stays constant while only the evaluation moves, which is what the sentence claims, so the observation holds.

**D) "Ambitious" and "reckless" can describe the same plan, but only the second says the risks were ignored, so calling an expansion ambitious withholds that judgement.**

Ambitious reports that a plan aims high and implies the aim may be justified. Reckless adds that the danger was disregarded, which is a criticism rather than a description of scale. A plan can be both, but the two words do not assert the same thing.

Disregard for risk is the extra content, and the sentence notes that the milder word leaves it out, so the account is right.

**E) "Restructuring" describes reorganising how a firm operates, while "redundancies" names the job losses that may follow, so the first can be announced without conceding the second.**

Restructuring covers changes to reporting lines, divisions, sites or ownership, and it need not involve dismissals at all. Redundancies are the specific consequence for staff whose roles disappear. Announcements often use the broader word precisely because it postpones the sharper one.

Scope is what allows the vaguer term to come first, and the sentence identifies that, so the reading is sound.
tasks.solution_overview: Connotation and scope decide this set, and in each case the facts could stay the same while the word chosen changes the verdict. Concise and terse, cautious and timid, determined and stubborn, and ambitious and reckless each pair a compliment with a criticism. Restructuring differs from redundancies in scope rather than in tone, which is why it can be announced while the harder news is held back.

tasks.title: Task 29
tasks.context: Five contrasts between a broad term and a narrower one in climate, health and measurement writing. Judge whether each holds.
statements: "Mitigation" tackles the causes of a hazard, while "adaptation" prepares for its effects, so sea walls adapt to rising water rather than mitigating the warming behind it.
"Endemic" describes something permanently established in a place, while "epidemic" describes a sudden outbreak, so resistance that is endemic in hospitals is not an epidemic.
"Novel" claims only that something is new, while "innovative" claims it improves on what came before, so a novel pricing algorithm is not automatically an innovative one.
"Definitive" closes a question, while "provisional" marks a result as open to revision, so provisional estimates of ice loss are published precisely because no definitive figure exists yet.
"Compensation" can cover payment for work and payment for harm, while "remuneration" stays with pay for services, so damages awarded to a claimant are compensation but not remuneration.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Mitigation" tackles the causes of a hazard, while "adaptation" prepares for its effects, so sea walls adapt to rising water rather than mitigating the warming behind it.**

Climate policy uses the pair as a settled division of labour: mitigation cuts emissions, adaptation manages consequences that are already unavoidable. A barrier does nothing to the concentration of gases in the atmosphere. What it changes is what that concentration means for the town behind it.

Cause and consequence are addressed by different measures, and the sentence assigns each word correctly, so the line holds.

**B) "Endemic" describes something permanently established in a place, while "epidemic" describes a sudden outbreak, so resistance that is endemic in hospitals is not an epidemic.**

Endemic marks a constant background presence, whether of a disease, a pest or a practice. Epidemic marks a sharp rise above that baseline over a limited period. Resistant organisms circulating steadily on a ward are the first case rather than the second.

Baseline against surge is the distinction, and the sentence keeps the steady case with the steady word, so it is accurate.

**C) "Novel" claims only that something is new, while "innovative" claims it improves on what came before, so a novel pricing algorithm is not automatically an innovative one.**

Novel makes the descriptive claim that something is new or unfamiliar. Innovative normally presents the novelty as a useful advance in method or practice, although the word can be promotional and does not prove improvement by itself. A newly designed algorithm may be novel yet fail to produce any practical benefit.

Because newness alone does not justify the favourable innovative label, the sentence's distinction is sound.

**D) "Definitive" closes a question, while "provisional" marks a result as open to revision, so provisional estimates of ice loss are published precisely because no definitive figure exists yet.**

A provisional figure is released early because it is useful, with the explicit expectation that later data will refine it. A definitive figure claims that further revision is not expected. Statistical agencies label their releases for exactly this reason.

Openness to revision is the difference, and the sentence explains why the weaker label is chosen, so the account is sound.

**E) "Compensation" can cover payment for work and payment for harm, while "remuneration" stays with pay for services, so damages awarded to a claimant are compensation but not remuneration.**

Compensation is the broader noun and includes anything paid to make good a loss, from injury damages to delay payments, as well as employment packages in some varieties of English. Remuneration is confined to what is paid in return for work or services. Damages are paid for a wrong rather than for labour supplied.

Breadth of coverage is the difference, and the sentence tests it with a case only one word reaches, so the claim is accurate.
tasks.solution_overview: Every line pairs a broad word with a narrower one, or a factual claim with an evaluative one. Mitigation and adaptation divide causes from consequences, endemic and epidemic divide a steady baseline from a surge, and novel and innovative divide newness from improvement. Definitive and provisional differ over whether revision is expected, while compensation reaches cases that remuneration cannot.

tasks.title: Task 30
tasks.context: Each line tests whether a familiar word is narrower or wider than it looks. Decide whether the account given is correct.
statements: "Marginal" in economics means unimportant, so the marginal cost of producing one more chip is the cost that matters least.
"Household" gathers the people who share a dwelling, while "house" names the structure, so a survey of household energy use follows occupants rather than bricks.
"Fewer" counts items one by one, while "less" measures quantity as a mass, so careful writing prefers fewer delivery delays and less congestion.
"Estimate" fills a gap in what is already known, while "forecast" reaches into what has not happened yet, so a backdated estimate of past emissions is not a forecast.
"Boundary" is restricted to physical lines on the ground, so writing about the boundaries of a regulator's remit misuses the word.
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Marginal" in economics means unimportant, so the marginal cost of producing one more chip is the cost that matters least.**

In economics marginal means at the margin: the change produced by one additional unit. Marginal cost is therefore central to pricing and output decisions rather than peripheral to them. The everyday sense of slight is a different use of the same word.

**Trap:** The technical and everyday senses point in opposite directions here, which is why the term is so often misread.

The additional-unit reading is the one in play, so the figure named is among the most decisive in the analysis.

**B) "Household" gathers the people who share a dwelling, while "house" names the structure, so a survey of household energy use follows occupants rather than bricks.**

Energy statistics are collected per household because consumption depends on how many people live together and how they behave. The building matters only through its fabric and size. One house can contain several households, each with its own bill.

People rather than structures are the unit of measurement, and the sentence says so, so it is accurate.

**C) "Fewer" counts items one by one, while "less" measures quantity as a mass, so careful writing prefers fewer delivery delays and less congestion.**

Delays are discrete events and take a plural, which is the environment fewer requires. Congestion is a mass noun with no plural and takes less. The two examples in the sentence sit on either side of that division.

Countability decides the form, and both halves of the sentence respect it, so the line holds.

**D) "Estimate" fills a gap in what is already known, while "forecast" reaches into what has not happened yet, so a backdated estimate of past emissions is not a forecast.**

Reconstructing emissions for a year when measurement was incomplete produces an estimate: the quantity existed and is being approximated. A forecast states what is expected in a period still to come. Both carry uncertainty, but only one of them faces forward.

Time reference separates the pair, and the backdated case falls clearly on the estimate side, so the sentence is right.

**E) "Boundary" is restricted to physical lines on the ground, so writing about the boundaries of a regulator's remit misuses the word.**

Boundary is used freely for the limits of an idea, a discipline, a dataset or a legal power, alongside its physical use for fields and territories. The abstract sense is standard in policy and academic writing rather than a stretch of the word. Border is the term that stays close to the map.

The abstract use is ordinary English, so describing the limits of a remit as its boundaries is entirely idiomatic.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these lines test whether a word is narrower than it looks, and three test what is actually being counted or projected. Marginal in economics means the effect of one more unit rather than something unimportant, and boundary reaches well beyond physical lines. For household, fewer and estimate, ask whether the unit is people or buildings, countable or mass, already existing or still to come.

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence uses the highlighted word appropriately in formal English.
statements: In a report on four-day work schedules, the phrase "the stability of the system" correctly uses "stability", drawn from the adjective base "stable" and carrying -ity, in the required noun slot.
In a report on personalised online pricing, the phrase "the outcome was economics" correctly uses "economics", drawn from the noun base "economy" and carrying -ics, in the required adjective slot.

In a report on the classical gold standard, the phrase "the pattern changed beneficial" correctly uses "beneficial", drawn from the noun/verb base "benefit" and carrying -ial, in the required adverb slot.
In a report on reshored supply chains, the phrase "the predictable of the system" correctly uses "predictable", drawn from the verb base "predict" and carrying -able, in the required noun slot.

In a report on post-war European recovery, the phrase "the outcome was competition" correctly uses "competition", drawn from the verb base "compete" and carrying -ition, in the required adjective slot.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on four-day work schedules, the phrase "the stability of the system" correctly uses "stability", drawn from the adjective base "stable" and carrying -ity, in the required noun slot.**

"stable" is an adjective, and -ity lifts adjectives of that kind into abstract nouns, so "stability" names a quality instead of describing anything. The slot agrees: "the" opens a noun phrase and "of the system" has to hang off a noun inside it. Base, affix and placement therefore line up with what the claim reports.

Adjective base, noun-making suffix, noun slot — the line holds.

**B) In a report on personalised online pricing, the phrase "the outcome was economics" correctly uses "economics", drawn from the noun base "economy" and carrying -ics, in the required adjective slot.**

"economy" is indeed the noun base, and -ics does build a word from it, but what it builds is another noun: "economics" names a field of study. The slot after the linking verb "was" needs a form that describes the outcome, and that work belongs to "economic", the -ic adjective in the same family.

**Trap:** -ics nouns look plural but stay nouns — "economics is taught in year two", never "the plan was economics".

A field-naming noun cannot pass for the describing word this slot calls for, so the claim doesn't hold — "the outcome was economic".

**C) In a report on the classical gold standard, the phrase "the pattern changed beneficial" correctly uses "beneficial", drawn from the noun/verb base "benefit" and carrying -ial, in the required adverb slot.**

-ial does turn the noun/verb "benefit" into "beneficial", but the product is an adjective, so it can modify a noun rather than the verb "changed". After "the pattern changed" English wants a manner adverb, and the family reaches one by adding -ly on top of the adjective. That extra step is exactly what the phrase skips.

An adjective standing where a manner adverb belongs leaves "changed" unmodified, so the claim fails — "the pattern changed beneficially".

**D) In a report on reshored supply chains, the phrase "the predictable of the system" correctly uses "predictable", drawn from the verb base "predict" and carrying -able, in the required noun slot.**

The base is the verb "predict", and -able builds "predictable", a word for things that can be foreseen. Wedged between "the" and "of the system", though, it is being asked to name something, and an adjective cannot head a noun phrase like that; the family's noun is "prediction". Read the phrase aloud and "of the system" has nothing to attach to.

The derivation is fine but the category is not, so the wording collapses — "the prediction of the system".

**E) In a report on post-war European recovery, the phrase "the outcome was competition" correctly uses "competition", drawn from the verb base "compete" and carrying -ition, in the required adjective slot.**

"compete" is the verb base and -ition genuinely builds "competition" from it, yet the product names an activity, which makes it a noun. The claim files it in an adjective slot after "was", where a describing word is needed, and the member built for that job is "competitive". A noun can follow "was" in ordinary prose, but then it is a noun complement, not the adjective the claim advertises.

Since -ition never yields an adjective, it is the category label that fails here — "the outcome was competitive".
tasks.solution_overview: Every claim here names a base, an affix and a slot, so read the slot first: "the ... of the system" needs an abstract noun, anything after the linking verb in "the outcome was ..." has to describe the outcome, and a word following "the pattern changed" has to say how. Then test the ending on its own terms — -ity and -ition build nouns, -ial and -able build adjectives, -ics names a field — and see whether the category the claim attaches is the one the suffix actually delivers.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence uses the highlighted word appropriately in formal English.
statements: In a report on behavioural policy nudges, the phrase "the productive of the system" correctly uses "productive", drawn from the verb base "produce" and carrying -ive, in the required noun slot.
In a report on antibiotic resistance, the phrase "the outcome was innovation" correctly uses "innovation", drawn from the verb base "innovate" and carrying -ion, in the required adjective slot.

In a report on Arctic tern migration, the phrase "the pattern changed responsible" correctly uses "responsible", drawn from the adjective base "responsible" and carrying zero suffix, in the required adverb slot.

In a report on the development of powered flight, the phrase "the efficiency of the system" correctly uses "efficiency", drawn from the adjective base "efficient" and carrying -iency, in the required noun slot.

In a report on potato cultivation, the phrase "the outcome was transparent" correctly uses "transparent", drawn from the adjective base "transparent" and carrying zero suffix, in the required adjective slot.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on behavioural policy nudges, the phrase "the productive of the system" correctly uses "productive", drawn from the verb base "produce" and carrying -ive, in the required noun slot.**

-ive attaches to the verb "produce" and yields "productive", a word for describing output, so its home is before a noun or after a linking verb. The slot framed by "the" and "of the system" is reserved for a noun, and the family supplies "productivity" for that position. Nothing in the sentence gives "productive" a noun to modify.

An -ive adjective cannot head that noun phrase, so the claim comes apart — "the productivity of the system".

**B) In a report on antibiotic resistance, the phrase "the outcome was innovation" correctly uses "innovation", drawn from the verb base "innovate" and carrying -ion, in the required adjective slot.**

-ion turns the verb "innovate" into "innovation", the name of a process, and a name is a noun however central it is to the topic. The claim assigns it the adjective slot after "was", the position that says what the outcome was like, and "innovative" is the family member shaped for that.

**Tip:** When you need to describe rather than name, look for the -ive twin of an -ion noun: creation → creative, innovation → innovative.

The suffix builds a name, not a description, so the adjective claim does not stand — "the outcome was innovative".

**C) In a report on Arctic tern migration, the phrase "the pattern changed responsible" correctly uses "responsible", drawn from the adjective base "responsible" and carrying zero suffix, in the required adverb slot.**

With no suffix added, "responsible" is still the adjective it began as, and adjectives do not modify verbs. "the pattern changed" needs a word saying how the change happened, which is why the family adds -ibly to give "responsibly". Leaving the base form there means nothing is describing the verb at all.

Zero derivation keeps an adjective an adjective, so the adverb claim fails — "the pattern changed responsibly".

**D) In a report on the development of powered flight, the phrase "the efficiency of the system" correctly uses "efficiency", drawn from the adjective base "efficient" and carrying -iency, in the required noun slot.**

"efficient" is the adjective base, and the -ent → -iency shift produces "efficiency", the abstract noun for that quality. The frame wants precisely that: "the" opens a noun phrase and "of the system" depends on the noun inside it. Derivation and placement are both as the claim describes.

**Tip:** Adjectives in -ent usually take this route: efficient → efficiency, sufficient → sufficiency.

A quality noun in a noun slot, correctly traced to its adjective base, so the wording is sound.

**E) In a report on potato cultivation, the phrase "the outcome was transparent" correctly uses "transparent", drawn from the adjective base "transparent" and carrying zero suffix, in the required adjective slot.**

No suffix is involved here, and the claim says as much: "transparent" is already an adjective. After the linking verb "was" a predicative adjective is what the sentence needs, and describing an outcome as transparent is ordinary formal usage. Base, absence of affix and slot all agree.

The adjective sits in an adjective slot with nothing added or missing, so the line stands.
tasks.solution_overview: Two of these forms are the base itself with nothing added, which makes the slot test decisive: an unchanged adjective can sit after "was" but not after "changed", where manner adverbs live. For the derived forms, ask what the ending actually produces — -ive describes, -ion names a process, -iency names a quality — and only then check whether the frame is asking for a noun, an adjective or an adverb.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence uses the highlighted word appropriately in formal English.
statements: In a report on semiconductor supply chokepoints, the phrase "the resilience of the system" correctly uses "resilience", drawn from the adjective base "resilient" and carrying -ence, in the required noun slot.
In a report on Thwaites Glacier, the phrase "the outcome was sustainability" correctly uses "sustainability", drawn from the verb base "sustain" and carrying -ability, in the required adjective slot.
In a report on deep-sea bioluminescence, the phrase "the pattern changed affordably" correctly uses "affordably", drawn from the verb base "afford" and carrying -ably, in the required adverb slot.
In a report on octopus cognition, the phrase "the reliable of the system" correctly uses "reliable", drawn from the verb base "rely" and carrying -able, in the required noun slot.
In a report on economic-sector change, the phrase "the outcome was variable" correctly uses "variable", drawn from the verb base "vary" and carrying -able, in the required adjective slot.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In a report on semiconductor supply chokepoints, the phrase "the resilience of the system" correctly uses "resilience", drawn from the adjective base "resilient" and carrying -ence, in the required noun slot.**

"resilient" is the adjective, and -ence converts adjectives of that shape into abstract nouns, giving "resilience". The determiner "the" plus "of the system" leaves a noun-shaped gap, which is what the noun fills. Meaning and category both survive the derivation intact.

**Tip:** -ent adjectives pair with -ence nouns: resilient → resilience, persistent → persistence.

**B) In a report on Thwaites Glacier, the phrase "the outcome was sustainability" correctly uses "sustainability", drawn from the verb base "sustain" and carrying -ability, in the required adjective slot.**

-ability stacks two steps onto the verb "sustain" — first the adjective "sustainable", then the noun "sustainability" — so the end product names a property rather than describing one. The claim puts it in the adjective slot after "was", which is where "sustainable" belongs. The longer the suffix chain, the easier it is to lose track of the final category.

A property-naming noun cannot serve as the predicative adjective claimed, so this doesn't hold — "the outcome was sustainable".

**C) In a report on deep-sea bioluminescence, the phrase "the pattern changed affordably" correctly uses "affordably", drawn from the verb base "afford" and carrying -ably, in the required adverb slot.**

From the verb "afford" the family runs to the adjective "affordable" and then to "affordably", the -ably adverb. Because the word follows "the pattern changed", a manner adverb is exactly the category required. The chain and the slot label in the claim both check out.

A manner adverb after a verb of change, correctly traced back to "afford", so the wording stands.

**D) In a report on octopus cognition, the phrase "the reliable of the system" correctly uses "reliable", drawn from the verb base "rely" and carrying -able, in the required noun slot.**

"rely" drops its -y to give "reliable", but -able produces an adjective, not a noun. The gap between "the" and "of the system" needs a name for the quality, and the family builds it with one further step: "reliability". Without that step the determiner and the of-phrase are attached to nothing.

**Trap:** -able adjectives can look nominal after "the", yet only the -ability noun can head the phrase.

**E) In a report on economic-sector change, the phrase "the outcome was variable" correctly uses "variable", drawn from the verb base "vary" and carrying -able, in the required adjective slot.**

"vary" is the verb base and -able gives "variable", used here to mean liable to change. After the linking verb "was" a predicative adjective is required, and "variable" fills that comfortably in formal writing. The derivation reported and the category demanded are the same.

**Trap:** "variable" is also a noun in statistics, but in this frame, straight after "was", it reads as the adjective the slot wants.

tasks.solution_overview: The -able family does most of the work in this set: -able produces describing words, its partner -ably produces manner words, and -ability or -ence produces abstract nouns. Match each product against the frame it sits in, and remember that a form can be built from the stated base quite correctly and still be filed under the wrong part of speech.
